t.borgring@55.5,12.1:
In 2014, archaeologists using laser scanning of the landscape noticed a faint circle in a field near Køge, on the Danish island of Zealand, about forty kilometres south-west of Copenhagen. Excavations confirmed what they had hoped: it was a Viking ring fortress, one of a small group of perfectly circular fortresses built in Denmark in the late tenth century, probably under King Harald Bluetooth. It was named Borgring, and it was the first new ring fortress to be found in Denmark in over sixty years.

The ring fortresses, including Trelleborg, Fyrkat and Aggersborg, are a remarkable group: they are built to a precise geometric plan, with a circular rampart, four gates aligned to the points of the compass and roads dividing the interior into quarters. They were built in a short period, and their purpose is still debated, as military bases, centres of royal power, or both. Together with Borgring, they were added to the UNESCO list in 2023 as the Viking-Age Ring Fortresses.

At Borgring, the rampart has been partly reconstructed, and the outline of the fortress can be seen in the landscape. There are information boards explaining the site. It is a quiet place, surrounded by fields, and the experience is more about understanding the past than seeing impressive ruins.

Køge, about four kilometres away, is a pleasant old market town with half-timbered houses and a harbour. In 1677, the Battle of Køge Bay, a major naval victory for Denmark over Sweden, was fought just offshore. Further south, the chalk cliffs of Stevns Klint, a UNESCO site for their record of the extinction of the dinosaurs, are a dramatic sight.

The riding in Zealand is gentle, through farmland, woods and villages, with gentle curves and little traffic. The coast roads are scenic, but wind can be strong. Danish speed limits are strictly enforced. Køge has fuel and all services. Local food includes smørrebrød, open sandwiches, and pastries. Late spring and summer, with long days and mild weather, are the best seasons.
t.militello val di catania@37.3,14.8:
Militello in Val di Catania is a small town in the hills south-west of Catania, in eastern Sicily, surrounded by orange groves and olive trees, with Mount Etna visible on the horizon. Like many towns in this part of Sicily, it was devastated by the earthquake of 1693, which destroyed much of the south-east of the island, and was rebuilt in the Baroque style. Its churches and palaces are part of the UNESCO-listed Late Baroque Towns of the Val di Noto, inscribed in 2002, together with Noto, Ragusa, Modica, Caltagirone and others.

Militello has a remarkable number of churches for its size, with Baroque façades and rich interiors, and a museum with sacred art. The town was a fief of the Branciforte family, who made it a centre of culture in the seventeenth century, with a court that attracted artists and scholars. The town also has a strong connection to the actor and director Pippo Baudo, a famous Italian television presenter, who was born here.

The area around Militello is known for its oranges, especially the blood oranges of the Piana di Catania, which have a protected designation. The town also produces prickly pears and mostarda, a sweet jelly made from grape must. Nearby, Palagonia and Scordia are agricultural towns surrounded by orange groves.

The riding around Militello is good. The roads through the hills toward Caltagirone, famous for its ceramics and its staircase decorated with tiles, and toward the Monti Iblei, the plateau of south-eastern Sicily, are winding and scenic, with views over the orange groves and Etna. The roads to Palazzolo Acreide and the Pantalica gorge, with its prehistoric rock tombs, are also good. The surfaces vary, with potholes and broken sections common in rural areas. Sicilian drivers can be unpredictable, so ride defensively. Summer is hot, but the hills are cooler.

Militello has fuel and food, and Catania, about forty kilometres away, has everything. Local food includes arancini, cannoli, and pasta alla Norma, with aubergine and ricotta salata. Spring, when the orange blossom fills the air, is the best time to visit.
t.caltagirone@37.2,14.5:
Caltagirone is a city built on ceramics. Perched on a ridge in the hills of south-east Sicily, it has been making pottery since ancient times, and the tradition is everywhere: majolica tiles on balconies, bridges and church domes, pottery shops lining the streets and a museum devoted to the craft. Its most famous sight is the Scalinata di Santa Maria del Monte, a staircase of well over a hundred steps climbing from the lower town to a church at the top, each riser decorated with hand-painted tiles in different patterns and colours. In late July, for the feast of Saint James, the staircase is lit with thousands of oil lamps arranged in designs, a magical sight.

The town was largely rebuilt after the great earthquake of 1693, which devastated south-eastern Sicily, and it is one of the eight Late Baroque Towns of the Val di Noto listed by UNESCO. Churches, palaces and squares show the exuberant style of that period, with curved facades, balconies on carved brackets and grand staircases.

The countryside around Caltagirone is rolling farmland, with wheat fields, olive groves, orange orchards and prickly pears, and the hills offer wide views over central Sicily. Grammichele, a short ride east, is a curious town laid out after the same earthquake on a perfect hexagonal plan.

The riding is enjoyable, with country roads climbing and winding through the hills between towns, and generally light traffic away from the main routes. The main road between Catania and Gela passes nearby and can be busy with trucks. Sicilian roads can be challenging: potholes, broken surfaces and gravel are common on minor roads, and local driving habits require constant attention. Summers are very hot, while spring brings green fields and wildflowers and is the best time to ride.

Caltagirone is a town of over thirty-five thousand people, with fuel, shops and plenty of restaurants. Climb the staircase in the evening when the heat eases, then sit in a piazza with a granita or an arancino, the fried rice ball that every Sicilian town claims to make best, and think about how you will carry a ceramic souvenir home on a bike.
t.palazzolo acreide@37.1,14.9:
Long before the Baroque churches, there were the Greeks. In the seventh century BC, settlers from Syracuse founded a hilltop outpost here called Akrai, controlling the routes into the interior of Sicily. The remains of their town lie on the hill above modern Palazzolo Acreide: a small, beautifully preserved Greek theatre with views over the hills, stone quarries turned into burial chambers, and the Santoni, a series of rock-cut figures of the goddess Cybele, carved into a cliff face, weathered but still powerful.

The modern town below was devastated by the earthquake of 1693 and rebuilt in the exuberant late Baroque style, with grand churches, ornate balconies and elegant palaces. It is one of the eight Late Baroque Towns of the Val di Noto listed by UNESCO in 2002. The churches of San Sebastiano and San Paolo face each other in friendly rivalry, and each has its own festival; the feast of Saint Paul in late June is celebrated with fireworks, processions and crowds. The town also has a delightful house museum created by the ethnographer Antonino Uccello, displaying everyday objects of Sicilian rural life, from puppets to kitchen tools.

Palazzolo lies in the Monti Iblei, the limestone hills of south-east Sicily, a landscape of dry-stone walls, olive groves, carob trees and deep gorges. Nearby, the necropolis of Pantalica, with thousands of tombs cut into the cliffs of a gorge, is another World Heritage site, together with Syracuse, and worth a visit.

The riding here is excellent. Roads wind through the hills between towns like Noto, Modica, Ragusa and Palazzolo, with plenty of bends, climbs and views, and little traffic away from the main routes. Surfaces can be rough, with potholes and gravel common on minor roads, and local driving demands attention. Spring is the best time, when the hills are green and full of wildflowers, while summer is hot and dry.

Palazzolo Acreide has over eight thousand inhabitants, with fuel, shops and restaurants. Try the local sausages, seasoned with fennel and wild herbs, or a plate of ricotta, fresh from the sheep's milk farms of the Iblei, and finish with a cannolo or a granita in the main square.
t.roskilde cathedral@55.6,12.1:
Roskilde Cathedral is where Denmark keeps its kings. Since the fifteenth century, almost every Danish monarch has been buried here, and the chapels and crypts hold around forty kings and queens, from medieval stone tombs to ornate baroque sarcophagi and modern designs. The cathedral itself, begun in the late twelfth century under Bishop Absalon, the warrior-churchman who also founded Copenhagen, was one of the first big brick Gothic churches in Scandinavia, and it set the style for church building across the region. UNESCO listed it in 1995. Inside, look for the clock with the figure of St George slaying the dragon, which strikes the hour, and the pillar where royal visitors have marked their height.

The town of Roskilde sits at the southern end of a long fjord, and it was an important Viking centre. In the 1960s, archaeologists raised five Viking ships from the fjord, deliberately sunk around the eleventh century to block the channel against raiders. They are now displayed in the Viking Ship Museum on the waterfront, together with reconstructions that you can sometimes see sailing. Today Roskilde is also famous for its huge music festival, held every summer on the edge of town.

As for the riding, Zealand is flat, green and windy, and the roads around Roskilde are good, straight and well marked, but not very exciting. The coastal roads along the fjord and north toward Frederikssund are the most scenic, with views over the water, fields and woods. Traffic can be heavy around Copenhagen, especially at rush hour, and Danish drivers are generally disciplined, but watch for cyclists everywhere; they have their own lanes and right of way. The weather is changeable, with rain and wind possible at any time of year.

Roskilde, with forty-four thousand inhabitants, has everything you need: fuel, supermarkets, cafés and restaurants. Try smørrebrød, open sandwiches on rye bread with toppings such as herring, roast beef or shrimp, or a hot dog from a pølsevogn, the classic Danish sausage wagon. A cinnamon pastry and a strong coffee in one of the cafés near the cathedral will warm you on a cold day.
t.stevns klint@55.3,12.4:
Stevns Klint is a white cliff of chalk and limestone, some fifteen kilometres long, on the east coast of Zealand, south of Copenhagen, and it holds one of the most important records of a global catastrophe. About sixty-six million years ago, an asteroid struck the Earth near what is now the Yucatán Peninsula in Mexico, causing a mass extinction that wiped out the dinosaurs and much of life on Earth. In the cliff, a thin, dark layer of clay, called the fish clay, marks that moment, and it contains high levels of iridium, a metal rare on Earth but common in asteroids. This layer was a key piece of evidence for the impact theory, and the cliff was listed by UNESCO in 2014.

The cliff is also beautiful. Its layers of white chalk and yellowish limestone rise above a narrow beach of stones and fossils, and you can walk along the top or down on the shore. At Højerup, an old church stands right at the edge, and in 1928 part of the cliff collapsed, taking the chancel into the sea. The church has been reinforced and is a popular stop. Further north, the Cold War fortress of Stevnsfort, built inside the cliff to guard the entrance to the Baltic, is now a museum, with tunnels, guns and missiles.

The riding is gentle and flat, with straight roads through farmland and villages, and views of the sea. The wind can be strong, especially along the coast, and the weather changes quickly. Traffic is light, but watch for cyclists and tractors. The roads along the coast are narrow in places, and some have cobbles or gravel near the villages. Rødvig, a small harbour town nearby, has a few cafés and a beach.

Store Heddinge, five kilometres away, is a small town with a supermarket and a few shops, but for fuel and more services, head to Køge, about twenty-six kilometres north. Try smørrebrød, open sandwiches on rye bread, or fresh fish from the harbour at Rødvig. On a sunny day, a picnic on the cliff top, looking out over the Baltic, is hard to beat.
t.villa romana del casale@37.4,14.3:
Somewhere in the fourth century AD, a very rich Roman, perhaps a senator or an imperial official, built a country villa in the hills of central Sicily and covered its floors with mosaics. The Villa Romana del Casale, just outside Piazza Armerina, has some of the finest and most extensive Roman floor mosaics anywhere, around 3,500 square metres, inscribed on the UNESCO list in 1997. Buried by a landslide in the Middle Ages, the villa was rediscovered and excavated mainly in the twentieth century, and the mosaics were preserved remarkably well.

The scenes are extraordinary. The great hunt corridor, sixty metres long, shows wild animals being captured in Africa and India and shipped to Rome for the games. The famous bikini girls are young women exercising in what look like two-piece costumes. There are scenes of mythology, fishing, children playing and daily life, all rendered with lively detail. Walkways let you look down onto the floors without touching them. Arrive early to avoid tour groups and the midday heat.

Piazza Armerina itself is a hilltop town of medieval and Baroque buildings, crowned by a large cathedral, and it is worth a walk. In August, the Palio dei Normanni recalls the Norman conquest of Sicily with a medieval pageant. The town has fuel, shops and restaurants serving Sicilian classics, from arancini to pasta alla norma and cannoli.

The riding in central Sicily is surprisingly good. The roads through the interior are winding, hilly and often quiet, passing through wheat fields, olive groves and hill towns, with views toward Etna on clear days. Surfaces can be rough, with potholes and repairs, and some roads have been damaged by landslides, so stay alert. From here, the rides lead south-east to the Baroque towns of the Val di Noto, Caltagirone with its ceramic staircase, and Militello, all part of another UNESCO listing. Spring is the ideal time, when the hills are green and covered in wildflowers.
t.ragusa@36.9,14.7:
In 1693 a terrible earthquake destroyed much of south-eastern Sicily, and the towns of the Val di Noto were rebuilt in the baroque style of the time, creating a group of towns of extraordinary beauty, now a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Ragusa is one of them, a town divided into two parts: Ragusa Superiore, the newer town on the ridge, built after the earthquake, and Ragusa Ibla, the old town on a lower hill, rebuilt on its medieval street plan.

Ragusa Ibla is the jewel, a maze of narrow streets, stairways and squares, with baroque churches and palaces at every turn. The cathedral of San Giorgio, designed by Rosario Gagliardi, rises at the top of a flight of steps, its façade a masterpiece of Sicilian baroque. Between the two parts of the town, long staircases and winding roads climb up and down the slopes, offering views over the rooftops and the valley. The town has been used as a setting for the television series Inspector Montalbano.

The riding around Ragusa is delightful. The Hyblaean plateau is a landscape of limestone hills, dry stone walls, carob trees and farms, cut by deep gorges, the cave, and the roads wind over the plateau and down into the valleys, with tight bends and views. The road from Ragusa to Modica, the neighbouring baroque town, crosses a deep valley with spectacular bridges. The coast, with beaches and fishing villages, is a short ride south. Summer is hot, and spring and autumn are the best seasons. Surfaces vary, and some roads are rough.

Ragusa has fuel, shops and restaurants, and parking in Ibla can be tricky, so park on the edge and walk in. Modica, eight kilometres away, is famous for its chocolate, made with an old cold-working technique that gives it a grainy texture. The local food includes scaccia, a folded flatbread filled with tomato and cheese, and caciocavallo ragusano, a local cheese. In the evening, the passeggiata in Ibla, with families strolling through the illuminated streets, is a lovely way to end the day.
t.scicli@36.8,14.7:
In January 1693 an earthquake flattened much of south-eastern Sicily, and the towns that rose from the rubble were rebuilt in a confident, theatrical late baroque style. Scicli is one of the eight towns of the Val di Noto listed by UNESCO for that reason, and it may be the most charming. It sits at the meeting of three limestone gorges, with a rocky hill above crowned by the ruins of the old church of San Matteo, and a centre of honey-coloured churches and palaces whose balconies are held up by carved grotesque faces, horses, sirens and monsters.

Television fans will recognise it. The town hall and the Via Mormino Penna, a street lined with baroque churches and palaces, appeared in the series Inspector Montalbano as the police station of the fictional town of Vigata. The streets are quiet and elegant, especially in the evening when the stone glows and the locals take their passeggiata. The coast is a few kilometres away, with sandy beaches at Donnalucata and Cava d'Aliga, and the countryside around is a patchwork of dry-stone walls, carob trees and greenhouses.

The riding in the Ragusa area is a pleasure. The roads wind through the plateau between dry-stone walls, then plunge into the gorges with tight bends and climb out again. The surface is mostly good but can be dusty, and in summer the heat is intense. Traffic is light except in the towns and along the coast in August. The light is wonderful, especially in spring and autumn, and the countryside smells of wild herbs and orange blossom. Watch out for farm vehicles and stray dogs, and for parked cars on narrow town streets.

Scicli has fuel, shops and plenty of bars and restaurants. Sicilian food here includes cavati pasta with pork ragù, scacce, folded flatbreads filled with tomato and cheese, and sweets like cannoli and almond biscuits. Modica, nearby, is famous for its chocolate, made with a cold process that leaves it grainy and intense. Park near the centre and walk the Via Mormino Penna, then climb to the hill of San Matteo for the view over the rooftops and the gorges, especially at sunset, when the town turns gold.
t.j gersborg dyrehave and j gersborg hegn@:
Danish kings loved to hunt, and in the late seventeenth century they laid out forests north of Copenhagen in a geometric pattern of straight paths radiating from central points, designed for par force hunting, in which riders and hounds chased a stag until it was exhausted. Jægersborg Dyrehave, the deer park, and Jægersborg Hegn are included in UNESCO's inscription of the par force hunting landscape in North Zealand, together with forests further north. The star-shaped network of rides is still visible, with numbered stone posts at the intersections that helped the hunters find their way.

The deer park is a beautiful mix of open grassland, ancient oaks and beech woods, home to large herds of red, fallow and sika deer, which wander freely and can be approached quite closely. In the middle of the park, on a hill, stands the Eremitage, a small baroque hunting lodge where the king and his guests dined after the hunt. At the edge of the park, Bakken, said to be the oldest amusement park in the world, has entertained visitors since the sixteenth century with rides, games and beer halls. The park is a favourite place for Copenhageners to walk, cycle and picnic.

The park itself is closed to motor traffic, so you will be on foot or in a horse-drawn carriage inside. The riding around it is pleasant. The Strandvejen, the coastal road north from Copenhagen to Helsingør, runs along the Øresund with views of the sea and Sweden, past villas, harbours and beaches, though it is busy on summer weekends. Inland, the roads through the forests and lakes of North Zealand are gentle and scenic. Watch for cyclists, who are numerous and have their own lanes. Weather is changeable, with wind and rain.

Klampenborg, Kongens Lyngby and the surrounding towns have fuel, shops and restaurants. Danish food includes smørrebrød, open sandwiches, frikadeller, meatballs, and pastries, and Bakken has traditional restaurants. Helsingør, at the end of the coast road, has Kronborg castle, the setting of Hamlet. Park the bike at Klampenborg, walk into the deer park, and climb to the Eremitage; the view over the meadows with the deer grazing is lovely, especially on an autumn morning, when the stags are rutting and their roars echo through the woods.
t.kronborg castle@56.0,12.6:
Hamlet never lived at Kronborg, but Shakespeare put him there, and the castle has been Elsinore in the imagination of the world ever since. It stands on a point of land at Helsingør where the Øresund narrows to about four kilometres, with Sweden clearly visible across the water, and for centuries it controlled one of the most important shipping lanes in Europe. King Frederik II built the castle in its Renaissance form in the 1570s and 1580s, and every ship passing through the strait had to stop and pay the Sound Dues, a toll that made the Danish crown rich for over four hundred years until it was abolished in 1857. Kronborg was inscribed on the UNESCO list in 2000.

The castle burned in 1629 and was rebuilt by Christian IV, then later used as a barracks. Today its great hall, chapel and royal apartments are open to visitors, along with the dark casemates below, where the statue of Holger Danske, the legendary hero said to wake when Denmark is in danger, sits asleep with his arms folded. Every summer, performances of Hamlet are staged in the courtyard, and actors from around the world have played the prince here. The Maritime Museum of Denmark, built into an old dry dock next to the castle, is a striking piece of modern architecture.

The riding around Helsingør is pleasant rather than thrilling. The coast road south toward Copenhagen, known as the Strandvejen, runs along the Øresund past fishing villages, beaches and grand villas, with views of the water and Sweden. It is busy, slow and full of cyclists, but the scenery is lovely. Inland, North Zealand has forests, lakes and the royal hunting grounds of Gribskov and Jægersborg, part of a UNESCO-listed par force hunting landscape, with quiet roads through beech woods. The ferry to Helsingborg takes only about twenty minutes, making a quick trip to Sweden easy.

Helsingør is a working town of about thirty-five thousand people with a filling station, somewhere to eat and supermarkets. Try smørrebrød, the Danish open sandwich, or fresh fish from the harbour. Walk around the castle ramparts, look across the strait to Sweden, and imagine the ships lining up to pay their dues. Then take a coffee by the harbour and watch the ferries cross back and forth.
t.store dyrehave@55.9,12.4:
North of Copenhagen the royal family once hunted on a scale that reshaped the landscape, and Store Dyrehave, the Great Deer Park, near Hillerød, is a piece of that design. The forest is cut by straight rides, long avenues that radiate like the spokes of a wheel, so that horsemen and hounds could follow a stag at speed without losing sight of it. This kind of hunting, called par force, was fashionable at European courts in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, and the Danish kings built an entire landscape for it, now recognised by UNESCO as the Par Force Hunting Landscape in North Zealand.

Close by stands Frederiksborg Castle, built in the early seventeenth century by Christian IV on three small islands in a lake, a red-brick Renaissance palace with copper roofs and towers. It houses the Museum of National History and is among the grandest buildings in Denmark. The deer park itself is a mixture of beech woodland, heath and meadow, and you will see deer, wild boar and many birds, and the forest is pleasant in every season. Beech leaves in spring are a luminous green, and in autumn they turn copper and gold.

For a rider, Zealand is gentle and rewarding at a calm pace. Roads in the forest are narrow and well surfaced, with moderate bends and cyclists, and the speed limits are strictly observed and enforced, with cameras on main roads, so ride at the limit. Some forest tracks are closed to motor vehicles, and signs are clear, so respect them. The best seasons are May, when the forest is fresh, and October, when the colours peak, though summer weekends bring many visitors.

Hillerød has fuel, supermarkets, restaurants and the castle, and Lillerød, a few kilometres from the park, also has services. Danish food is simple and excellent, with open sandwiches called smørrebrød, pastries known as wienerbrød and strong coffee, and a cafe by the castle lake is a pleasant place to rest. Leave the bike at the edge and walk the avenues for a while, when the light slants through the trees and the only sound is leaves.
t.cefalu cathedral@38.0,14.0:
Cefalù is where Sicily squeezes a medieval town between a rock and a beach. The Rocca, a limestone crag, rises a steep couple of hundred metres straight behind the old centre, and the cathedral sits at its foot, a heavy, golden-grey Norman building with two square towers that you can see from the coastal highway long before you reach the town. According to tradition King Roger II promised to build it after surviving a storm at sea, and work began in 1131. Whatever the truth of the vow, the church is a statement of power by a Norman king who ruled Sicily and wanted it to look Mediterranean, not merely northern.

Inside, the apse holds the great mosaic of Christ Pantocrator, a huge, stern, gold figure with an open book, made by Byzantine craftsmen. Cefalù and the Norman buildings of Palermo are listed together by UNESCO as Arab-Norman Palermo and the Cathedral Churches of Cefalù and Monreale, a reminder that this island blended Latin, Greek and Arab cultures in a way that nowhere else in Europe quite did.

The riding to get here is a pleasure when you pick the right roads. The coast road, the SS113, follows the Tyrrhenian shore with sea views but plenty of towns and traffic, and the fast motorway behind it saves time. If you want fun, turn inland into the Madonie mountains, where roads climb through oak, ash and beech to villages such as Castelbuono and up toward Piano Battaglia, with hairpins, short straights and cool air even in July. Surfaces vary, and a few stretches have patches and loose gravel, so keep a bit of margin.

Cefalù itself has about eleven thousand people, so fuel, parking and plenty of restaurants are easy, and Lascari next door is quieter. Summer brings crowds to the beach and old lanes, so come in May, June or October, when the sea is warm enough for a quick swim and the evening light turns the cathedral honey-coloured. Eat granita with a brioche in the morning, and finish the day on the seafront with fish and a glass of local white wine.
t.modica@36.9,14.8:
Modica was destroyed in 1693, rebuilt in a hurry, and the result is one of the most dramatic baroque towns in Europe. A great earthquake that January killed tens of thousands across south-eastern Sicily, and the towns of the Val di Noto rose again in a new style, with curved facades, carved balconies and grotesque stone faces looking down from the corners. UNESCO listed eight of them together in 2002, and Modica is one of the finest. It occupies two steep ridges and the gorge between them, and the houses climb up the sides in layers, so that a walk through the streets is mostly a matter of steps.

The church of San Giorgio stands at the top of a long flight of steps, a tall facade of golden limestone with a belfry rising from the middle, and the effect from the bottom of the stairs is theatrical. The cathedral of San Pietro, in the lower town, has its own staircase decorated with statues of the apostles. Modica is also famous for chocolate. The local method, passed down from the Spanish rulers who brought cacao from the Americas, grinds the beans cold with sugar, leaving a grainy, crumbly texture that is quite unlike the smooth bars of the north, and shops along the main street offer bars flavoured with chilli, cinnamon or orange. A local pastry, mpanatigghi, is filled with chocolate and spiced meat, and you should try one at least once.

The riding in the Iblei hills around the town is remarkable. The plateau is a landscape of dry stone walls, carob trees and honey-coloured limestone, with narrow lanes that wind between small fields and drop into steep valleys. Ragusa, eight kilometres away, has its own baroque old town, Ibla, and Scicli, a short ride south, was the setting for the TV detective Montalbano and has a fine baroque street. Surfaces vary, with potholes, loose gravel and occasional goats, and Sicilian drivers overtake with confidence. Spring is lovely, with wildflowers, and autumn is warm. Summer afternoons are extremely hot.

Modica has forty thousand people, so fuel and food are everywhere, and traffic in the lower town is thick. Park outside the old centre and walk. A granita with brioche for breakfast and a plate of pasta with ricotta for lunch make a proper day. The evening light on the golden stone is the best reward.
t.medina of sousse@35.8,10.6:
Sousse is a city that has been busy for nearly three thousand years, under the Phoenicians, the Romans and the Arabs, and its old town, the medina, still has the crowded, enclosed feel of a place built behind walls. It stands on the Tunisian coast, in the region called the Sahel, a belt of olive groves and white towns between the sea and the dry interior. Sousse was Hadrumetum in Roman times, and later became an important port, and it was ringed by walls in the ninth century, parts of which still stand.

The medina is a World Heritage site, and a good walk takes in its highlights. The Ribat, a fortified monastery built in the late eighth century, has a tall watchtower that gives a sweeping view over the rooftops and the harbour, and the Great Mosque, from the ninth century, is plain and austere, like a fortress for the faith. In between, the souks sell leather, brass, spices and sponges, and the shopkeepers will invite you to tea. Early morning is the best time, when the alleys are quiet and the light falls at an angle onto the whitewashed walls.

The riding in the Sahel is flat, open and sunny, with olive groves in all directions. The coastal road is fast and busy, and traffic in Sousse itself is chaotic, with mopeds, taxis and horse carts. Heading south, the road leads to El Jem, about forty kilometres away, where one of the best-preserved Roman amphitheatres in the world rises from a small town. In summer, the heat is fierce, and the best seasons are spring and autumn, when the temperature is pleasant and the olive harvest begins.

Fuel is easy to find in Sousse and Hammam Sousse, and there are plenty of cafes and restaurants. Try brik, a thin pastry filled with egg and tuna, and lablabi, a spicy chickpea soup eaten for breakfast, and finish with mint tea and a pastry. Leave the bike in a secure car park outside the medina walls and explore on foot, as the lanes are too narrow for anything wider than a donkey.
t.medina of tunis@36.8,10.2:
Tunis begins in the narrow lanes. The medina, the old walled city, lies on a low ridge between the salt lake and the Sebkha of Ariana, and the main street runs uphill from the Bab el Bahr, the Sea Gate, towards the Zitouna Mosque, the Mosque of the Olive Tree. The mosque's origins go back to the late seventh century, soon after the Arabs founded Tunis, and the city grew around it. Its great period came under the Hafsid dynasty in the thirteenth to sixteenth centuries, when Tunis was a wealthy capital with libraries, schools and merchants trading across the Mediterranean. Later came the Ottomans and the beys, who added palaces and fountains.

The medina has about seven hundred monuments by the usual count, packed into a maze that was designed for walking and for staying cool. Houses turn blank walls to the street and open onto inner courtyards with tiles and jasmine. The souks are organised by trade, so you pass through leatherworkers, goldsmiths, perfume sellers, and the chechia makers who make the red felt caps worn across North Africa. The covered lanes keep out the sun, and the sound and smell change every few metres from incense to leather to frying dough.

On a motorcycle, the approach is simple: do not take the bike into it. The medina is largely pedestrian and the surrounding streets are a lively tangle of traffic, with horn-heavy driving, trams and light rail, and a casual attitude to lanes. Park somewhere you can watch, near the gates at the edge, and go in on foot. Be ready for firm bargaining in the souks, which is part of the game and is best treated with good humour.

Beyond the city, Tunisia rewards riders. The roads north to the Ichkeul wetlands and west to the Roman city of Dougga run through olive groves, wheat fields and low hills, with fine, usually well-surfaced asphalt, sudden dust and the occasional animal. Spring, with green fields and wildflowers, and autumn, with softer light, are best. Summer inland can be punishing.

Tunis is a large city of nearly seven hundred thousand people, so fuel, food and everything else is easy. Drink a strong mint tea with pine nuts, eat a brik, the crisp pastry parcel with an egg inside, and give yourself an afternoon to get lost on purpose.
t.m ns klint@55.0,12.6:
The chalk cliffs of Møn rise out of the Baltic in a long white wall, with beech woods growing on top, and it is one of the few places in Denmark where the land stands up and makes an impression. At its highest the cliff is about 120 metres, and it runs for around six kilometres along the island's eastern coast. The chalk was laid down on the sea floor in the Cretaceous period, about 70 million years ago, from the skeletons of tiny marine organisms, and glaciers in the last Ice Age pushed it up and folded it into the shape you see.

The beech forest on the top, Klinteskoven, is old, with tall, grey-trunked trees, and in May the fresh green leaves against the white chalk are glorious. Orchids grow in the woods, and peregrine falcons nest on the cliffs. A long flight of wooden steps leads down to the beach, which is covered with white pebbles and flints, and fossils such as sea urchins and belemnites are easy to find, though you should not dig into the cliff, which is unstable. The Geocenter Møns Klint near the car park explains the geology and the story of the ice.

The ride across Zealand and onto Møn is relaxed. The island is reached by the Dronning Alexandrine Bridge from Zealand, and the roads then run through small farms, thatched villages and white churches with frescoes. The terrain is gentle and the roads are narrow, with long views, and traffic is moderate except on summer weekends. Wind off the Baltic can be brisk, and rain showers come and go quickly, so a waterproof is a good idea. Early summer and September are the nicest times.

Stege, about 17 km away, is a small old town of about 3,900 people with remains of a medieval town wall, and it has a supermarket, fuel stations and a few cafés. Beyond it there is little, so fill up there. Out near the cliffs there is a café at the visitor centre. Danish summer evenings are long, and the sun sets over the Baltic late, so it is easy to stay for the light. The chalk glows warm in the evening, and a stroll along the beach below it is a good way to end the day.
t.the par force hunting landscape in north:
Par force hunting sounds like a French affectation, and it was. The kings of Denmark in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries imported the style from the French court, in which riders on horseback and packs of hounds chased a stag until it was exhausted. To make it work, they needed a landscape designed for speed, and in North Zealand the royal foresters cut long, straight rides through the woods, many of them meeting at star-shaped crossings, so that the hunters could see the quarry and keep control of the chase. The pattern is still visible in the forests of Gribskov and Store Dyrehave, and UNESCO listed the landscape in 2015.

The heart of it is the area around Hillerød, where the great red-brick Frederiksborg Castle stands on three small islands in a lake. It was built by Christian IV in the early seventeenth century and now houses the Museum of National History. Nearby are Fredensborg Palace, still used by the royal family, and Esrum Lake, the largest in the region, with the remains of a medieval monastery at Esrum. The forests are mostly beech, with big, smooth-barked trees, and the rides are used by walkers, cyclists and riders on horseback.

The riding is gentle and varied. Roads run through the forests, past lakes and through small villages, with long, straight sections and the occasional bend, and the surface is generally good. Speed limits are low in the woods, and cameras and police checks are common in Denmark, so keep to them. Be careful at dawn and dusk, as deer cross the road without warning. Spring, with the beech leaf unfolding, and autumn, with the copper colours, are the best seasons.

Hillerød, with about 31,000 people just four kilometres away, is the logical place for fuel, food and a bed, and Lillerød has more shops to the south. Copenhagen is about 35 km to the south-east, so the area makes an easy day out from the capital. Try smørrebrød, the open sandwich on dark rye bread, at a café in town, or a cinnamon pastry from a bakery. Walk a short stretch of a ride, look down the line and imagine the sound of hooves and horns, which stirred this forest a few centuries ago.
t.ta hagrat@35.9,14.4:
Ta' Hagrat stands on a low ridge near the village of Mgarr in the north of Malta, and it ranks among the oldest buildings anywhere. The temple was built in the Neolithic period, around 3600 to 3200 BC, centuries before Stonehenge and the pyramids, and its limestone walls and paved forecourt still show the shape of a small sanctuary. A short distance away lies the site of Skorba, another early settlement. Together they belong to the group of Megalithic Temples of Malta, which are among the oldest free-standing monuments on earth.

The builders were farming people who had no metal tools and no wheeled carts, yet they raised rooms with curving walls, trilithon doorways and carved altars, and covered the interiors with spirals and animal figures. No one knows exactly what they believed, but the famous plump figurines found on the islands suggest a cult of fertility and the dead. The stone, a soft golden limestone, glows in the late afternoon and weathers into honeycomb patterns.

Malta is a tiny, crowded island with a dense network of narrow roads, and riding there is an adventure of its own. Traffic drives on the left, a legacy of British rule, and local drivers are quick and assertive. Surfaces are often rough and patched, with potholes, and walled lanes can be blind. Around Mgarr the country is more rural, with terraced fields, prickly pear, and carob trees, and Mgarr is known for its strawberries in spring. From here the road leads quickly to the coast and the Gozo ferry at Cirkewwa.

Mgarr is a village of a few thousand, and Mellieha, four kilometres off, has fuel, supermarkets and cafes. Malta's food is a blend of Italian and Arab influences, with pastizzi, rabbit stew and fresh fish. The summer sun is fierce, so bring water and sun protection, and come in spring or autumn when the island is green or gold and the light is soft. Check opening times before visiting the temple.
t.skorba@35.9,14.4:
Under a field near the village of Mġarr, in the north-west of Malta, lie the layers of a farming settlement that is older than the island's famous temples. Skorba was excavated in the 1960s by the archaeologist David Trump, who found the remains of houses from about 4500 BC, built by the island's first farmers, and above them the foundations of two small temples from the later centuries, when Malta's builders began to put up great buildings of stone. It is part of the group of Megalithic Temples of Malta that UNESCO lists as among the oldest free-standing monuments in the world.

The site is small, tended by Heritage Malta, with a low wall around it, and nothing to compare with the bigger temples at Ħaġar Qim or Ġgantija. What it offers is a chance to see how the story started: a village of farmers growing wheat and barley, keeping sheep and goats, and slowly developing the ideas that led to temple building. Look for the signs of the earlier huts, and the curved walls of the temples, with the characteristic trefoil plan.

Malta is small, crowded and busy, and riding here has its own rules. Traffic drives on the left, a legacy of British rule, and the roads can be congested and potholed, with little patience from other drivers. In the north-west, the roads are quieter, running between stone-walled fields and prickly pear, with views of the sea and the island of Gozo. Golden Bay and Għajn Tuffieħa are nearby, with sandy beaches that fill in summer. The cliffs between them are good for a walk.

Fuel is easy to find. Mellieħa, five kilometres away, has six thousand people and several stations, and Imġarr, a village of three thousand, has bakeries and bars. Try a pastizz, a flaky pastry filled with ricotta or peas, and a glass of Kinnie, a bitter-sweet orange drink that is the island's own.

Valletta, the capital, is on the same ride, and is a different kind of monument, a baroque city built by the Knights of St John after the Great Siege of 1565. Spring and autumn are the best times to visit, while summer is very hot.
t.agar qim@35.8,14.4:
Ħaġar Qim stands on a windswept ridge at the southern end of Malta, with the sea below and a small rocky island, Filfla, on the horizon. The temple was built around 3600 to 3200 BC, which makes it older than Stonehenge and the pyramids, and it is built of huge blocks of coralline limestone, some of them several metres high. The tallest single stone, in the facade, is about five metres, and the whole structure is laid out in a pattern of curving chambers, like a clover leaf. Inside are altars, carved holes and doorways that hint at ceremonies we can only guess at.

A walk down the hill leads to Mnajdra, a second temple complex a few hundred metres away and closer to the sea, which is aligned with the sun so that at the equinoxes and solstices the light enters in special ways. The two sites together make one of the most atmospheric places in Malta. A giant canopy now covers Ħaġar Qim to protect the stone from the weather, and there is a visitor centre with a museum and a cafe. Tickets are required, and opening times vary by season.

The road here runs through a landscape of stone-walled fields, carob trees and cactus, with a feeling of space that is rare on the island. The surface is mixed, with potholes and patches, and traffic keeps to the left. Nearby, the cliffs at Dingli rise to the highest point in Malta, a little over two hundred and fifty metres, and a road along the top gives views over the sea. Wied iż-Żurrieq, a narrow cove, is the starting point for boat trips to the Blue Grotto, a sea cave of luminous blue water.

Qrendi is a small village with two and a half thousand people, and Żurrieq has more than nine thousand, and between them they have fuel, bakeries and bars. Try the rabbit stew, the national dish, and a plate of fresh fish at one of the cove restaurants.

The best time is spring or autumn, when the stone is warm but not scorching. Summer can be fiercely hot, with little shade.
t.swakopmund@-22.7,14.5:
Swakopmund is a German seaside town that someone dropped into the Namib Desert, and it is still a little startled to be there. Palm-lined streets, half-timbered houses, a lighthouse and a pier would suit the Baltic, yet the sand dunes begin at the edge of town and the sea is the cold, grey Atlantic, chilled by the Benguela Current. The German colonial administration founded it in 1892 as a landing point, since the lagoon harbour at Walvis Bay lay in British hands, and the old buildings, bakeries and the Kaffee und Kuchen habit are what remains.

The climate shapes everything. Sea fog rolls in on many mornings and can sit over the town until noon, while ten kilometres inland the sky is blue and the desert is hot. That sharp edge between cold coast and dry interior produces a strange light, and is the reason the dune belt south toward Walvis Bay is so photogenic. Locals pursue sandboarding, quad biking and fishing, and the oysters from Walvis Bay are among the best things you will eat in Namibia.

Riding north from here is one of the strangest roads in Africa. The coastal highway to Henties Bay is made of compacted salt, pale and hard, running between the surf and the desert, and it is oddly smooth and slippery when damp with fog. Wind-sculpted dunes lie to the right and wrecked trawlers and driftwood to the left. The road is mostly straight, so the challenge is concentration, not bends. Fog can cut visibility fast, and wind can throw sand across the carriageway, so ride with your lights on and keep your distance from lorries.

Swakopmund is the main service town on this coast, so fuel, repairs, supermarkets and hotels are all here, and it is smart to fill up before heading north, where pumps are spread out. Walvis Bay, thirty-odd kilometres to the south, is bigger still. Bring layers even in summer, since the sea breeze is chilly, and try German-style cakes and strong coffee while the fog burns off.
t.henties bay@-22.1,14.3:
Henties Bay is a fishing town with a sandy main street and a very honest purpose: it is where Namibians come to cast a line into the surf. It lies about seventy kilometres north of Swakopmund, where the dry bed of the Omaruru river reaches the Atlantic, and its name is said to come from a man called Hentie van der Merwe, who found a freshwater spring here in the 1920s while fishing. Rock lobster, kabeljou and steenbras are the catch, and anglers line the beach at dawn with rods like a row of antennas.

Behind the town the land is stony desert, as barren as a lunar plain, with low hills and, on a clear day, the faint outline of the Brandberg massif far inland. In front, the coast runs north into the Skeleton Coast, whose name comes from the bones of whales and the wrecks of ships that drifted ashore through the fog and surf. A track and a salt road continue to the Cape Cross seal reserve, where tens of thousands of Cape fur seals crowd the rocks, noisy, pungent and fascinating. The smell reaches you before the sight does.

For riders, Henties Bay marks a transition. The salt road from Swakopmund ends here, and beyond lies a grittier gravel route toward the seal colony and the park gate at Ugab. Fog can close in suddenly, wind blows in strong afternoon gusts, and the temperature feels cold on a bike. Mornings are usually clearer. Gravel surfaces need care with tyres, and loose stones thrown up by passing trucks are a hazard. Keep your speed measured, particularly where the road is slick with sea mist.

The town has fuel, a supermarket, a few simple restaurants and guesthouses, and it is the last dependable place for supplies before the long empty miles, so fill the tank and the water bottle here. Park entry to the Skeleton Coast itself requires permits, and the northern stretches are strictly regulated, so check beforehand.
t.amphitheatre of el jem@35.3,10.7:
El Jem is a small Tunisian town with a very large building. Rising out of the flat plain of the Sahel, the amphitheatre of Thysdrus, as the Romans called the place, is one of the biggest ever built, a three-tiered oval of pale limestone more than a hundred and thirty metres long, and it was designed to hold some thirty-five thousand spectators. Construction began in the early third century, probably under the rule of the wealthy local landowners who grew rich on olive oil, and it was never fully finished, because the African governor who encouraged it was killed in a revolt in 238.

The amphitheatre stands almost whole, and you can walk through the passages beneath the arena where animals and gladiators waited, climb the tiers for a view over the plain, and see the arches that frame the sky. Little stands between you and the ancient world. The building has played a part in films, including Gladiator and Monty Python's Life of Brian, and each summer a music festival fills the stone seats. Nearby, a museum shows beautiful Roman mosaics found in the town's villas, with scenes of the seasons, the gods and the beasts of the arena.

For motorcyclists, El Jem is an easy stop on the main road between Sousse and Sfax, with flat, straight highways and olive trees to the horizon. The amphitheatre is in the middle of town, so parking is easy, and locals will offer to watch your bike for a small tip. Traffic on the main road includes heavy lorries and shared taxis that stop abruptly. Summer heat is severe, and midday visits to the exposed stone can be exhausting, so go early or late.

El Jem has about twenty thousand people, with fuel stations and cafés along the main street. Kairouan, one of Islam's holiest cities, with its great ninth-century mosque, is a short day's ride inland to the west, and the sea resorts of the Sahel are close to the east.

Aim for early morning, when the stone is cool and the coach parties are still at breakfast.
t.ecosystem and relict cultural landscape:
In central Gabon, where the rainforest breaks up into patches of open savanna, the Ogooué river bends through a landscape that has been a meeting place for about as long as people have crossed Africa. The long official name belongs to the Ecosystem and Relict Cultural Landscape of Lopé-Okanda, a UNESCO mixed site listed in 2007 for both its nature and its human story. The forest here is not a solid green wall. It shifts between thick canopy and grassy clearings, giving animals an unusually rich mix of habitats.

That mix is the reason the park is so good for wildlife. Lopé holds one of the largest populations of mandrills in the world, with troops sometimes reaching into the hundreds, the males painted in startling blue and scarlet. Forest elephants, buffalo, gorillas and chimpanzees live in the trees and clearings too, and the Ogooué has hippos in places. The air is humid, scented with damp earth and flowers, and the dawn chorus of birds can be remarkable.

The human story is carved in the rocks. At sites in the park, hundreds of petroglyphs were left by ancient peoples, and archaeologists have found evidence of iron-working and trade. The valley is thought to have been a corridor for the Bantu migrations that spread across central and southern Africa over the last couple of thousand years. In other words, the savanna and river here were a crossroads long before there was a road.

Do not expect smooth riding. The main route from Libreville toward the interior is paved for long stretches, but the quality varies and the rainy seasons, roughly from October to December and from February to May, bring flooding and potholes. The Trans-Gabon railway, which carries the manganese and timber, passes through the area, and the station at Lopé is a notable point in the park. Fuel is limited in this part of the country, so fill up in the larger towns on the way and carry a reserve. Villages offer simple food, and lodges near the park can arrange guides for walks and drives. The driest months, roughly June to August, are the best for wildlife and the easiest for travel.
t.ugab@-21.0,13.7:
The Ugab is a river that rarely runs, and its dry bed is the reason there is a gate here at all. On the C34, the gravel and salt road that runs along the Namibian coast, the Ugab River Gate marks a southern entrance to the Skeleton Coast National Park, a long, narrow strip of desert, fog and shipwreck that stretches north toward Angola. The name comes from the whale and seal bones that once littered the beach, and from the ships that ran onto the rocks in the thick fog caused by the cold Benguela current meeting hot desert air. The Portuguese sailors called it the Sands of Hell, and local people called it the land God made in anger.

The landscape is stark and strange. Gravel plains stretch to the horizon, broken by dark rocky ridges and the dry courses of rivers whose hidden water supports a surprising amount of life. Desert-adapted elephants and lions have been recorded along some of the dry riverbeds, and the coast is home to Cape fur seals, jackals and hyenas. In the mornings, fog rolls in from the ocean and condenses on the plants, which many desert species rely on for water. The smell of the sea, rotten kelp and salty air, hangs over everything.

Riding here needs preparation. The C34 is generally a graded salt road, hard and smooth in good conditions but slippery and sometimes corrugated, and it can be soft with sand in places. Fog can reduce visibility to a few metres, and the wind often blows hard from the south-west. Entry to the park requires a permit, obtained from the tourism authority, and the gates have set hours, so check the rules in advance. The nearest fuel to the south is at Henties Bay, a fishing and holiday town on the coast, and farther north are small rest camps, so carry spare fuel and plenty of water.

The best seasons are the cooler months, from about May to September, though it is rarely warm on the coast. Take warm layers, spare tyres and a satellite messenger if you can, and travel in company. The silence at dusk, with the surf booming in the distance, is unforgettable.
t.gribskov@56.0,12.3:
Gribskov is the second largest forest in Denmark, a broad expanse of beech and spruce on the north Zealand plain. Walking or riding here, the first impression is of light. Beech trees in spring have a green so fresh and bright that it is almost unreal, and in autumn they turn bronze and gold, and the forest floor is carpeted with leaves. The ground is gently rolling, with small lakes and bogs hidden between the trees, and red deer and roe deer live in the woods.

The forest was once a royal hunting ground, and the kings of Denmark came here for deer and boar. Close by, Esrum Lake is the biggest lake on Zealand, and on its shore stands Esrum Abbey, founded by Cistercian monks in 1151 and later turned into a royal hunting lodge. Nødebo, the village at the edge, has a small church and a well-known folk high school, and the whole area has a quiet, cultivated feel, with farms, thatched houses and lines of old beech along the roads. The Danes have a strong love of forests, and the practice of wandering freely among the trees is part of daily life.

The riding is easy and relaxed. Roads through and around the forest are narrow, smooth and tree-lined, with gentle bends and occasional dips, and the speed limits are low and strictly enforced. Cameras and police checks are common, and the penalties are steep, so keep to the signs. Cyclists are everywhere, and in summer the roads fill with families on bikes, so go gently. Deer cross the road at dusk, and a collision with one is serious.

Hillerød, a town of about thirty-one thousand people four kilometres away, has fuel stations, shops and cafés, and its castle, Frederiksborg, is among the finest Renaissance buildings in Scandinavia, standing on three small islands in a lake. Nødebo has a small shop and a tavern. Take your lunch and eat it by the lake. The best seasons are May, when the beech buds open, and October, when the colours burn. Denmark's weather is changeable, so carry a rain jacket, and wear layers in all seasons.
t.tolvkarlevej and h jager@55.9,12.3:
Hillerød is the town where the Danish kings built their most ambitious castle, and the roads around it carry some of the best light in northern Zealand. Frederiksborg Castle stands on three small islands in a lake, a red-brick and sandstone Renaissance palace with towers, spires and a copper roof turned green. King Christian IV, who rebuilt it in the early seventeenth century, was a builder of grand projects and a lover of show, and he made Frederiksborg a stage for royal life. Today it houses the Museum of National History, and its gardens in the baroque style stretch away in terraces.

The two labels of this pin, Tolvkarlevej and Højager, are road and place names in the countryside near the town, and they hint at the older layer of local life: farm tracks, hedge lines and small fields that once belonged to estate and village. I cannot vouch for the stories behind the names, but the land itself is plain to see, a gentle glacial landscape of low hills, beech woods and meadows, dotted with farms and lakes. The ride from here turns toward Roskilde, where the cathedral, a brick Gothic building begun in the twelfth century, holds the tombs of Danish monarchs and is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

Danish roads suit a relaxed rider. They are smooth, well signed and usually quiet, with gentle bends and frequent roundabouts, and the speed limits are low, commonly eighty on country roads and fifty in villages. Police and automated cameras enforce them strictly, and fines are steep, so keep to the limits. Cyclists have their own lanes, and drivers are polite, but the weather changes quickly, and a clear morning can turn to drizzle by noon.

Hillerød is a town of about thirty-one thousand people with fuel stations, shops and cafés, and it makes a convenient base for exploring the north of Zealand. Try a smørrebrød, an open sandwich on dark rye bread with toppings of herring, roast beef or egg and shrimp, or a pastry from a bakery, which Danes do very well. May and June are lovely, when the beeches are fresh and the evenings are long, and September has a golden light. Winter is dark, damp and cold.
t.copenhagen@55.7,12.6:
Copenhagen is a city that runs on bicycles, and a motorcyclist arriving here should take the hint and ride softly. Cycle lanes carry thousands of commuters at rush hour, and a car door or a turning van can ruin everybody's day, so patience and constant mirror checks are the rule. In return, the city is compact, handsome and unhurried, with copper-green spires, canals and handsome old warehouses along the harbour, where the bright houses of Nyhavn, once home to Hans Christian Andersen, are crowded with tourists on summer evenings. A short stroll away, Tivoli Gardens, opened in 1843, remains one of the oldest amusement parks in the world and glows with lights after dark.

The Little Mermaid sits on her rock on the waterfront, smaller than most people expect, while across the harbour Christianshavn, a quarter of canals and leaning houses, leads to Christiania, a self-governing alternative community founded in 1971. Frederiksberg has a garden and a hill with views. Eating is a pleasure: smørrebrød, open sandwiches of rye bread with herring, roast beef or egg and shrimp, are the classic lunch, while the New Nordic cooking movement has made the city a destination for serious food.

The riding beyond is a different sort of pleasure. Denmark is low and gentle, and the best roads are quiet back lanes through beech woods and fields, with the sea always close. North of the city the coast road, Strandvejen, runs past elegant villas, small harbours and the deer park of Dyrehaven, where wild fallow deer roam among ancient oaks. Further west, Roskilde, about thirty kilometres away, was the capital of the Danes in the Viking age, and its cathedral, built mainly in brick from the twelfth century, holds the tombs of Danish monarchs and is a World Heritage site. The nearby Viking Ship Museum displays five ships sunk in the fjord around the eleventh century.

Fuel is no problem anywhere, and in Denmark there are many automated stations, which usually accept cards. The weather can be wet and windy in any season, and a good rain suit is worth more than any clever gadget. Speed cameras are widespread and fines are steep, so stay within the limits. Use bike racks and secure parking, since theft is a risk, and give extra space to cyclists in the cycle-lane crossings.
t.hardanger fjord and waterfalls photo pul:
The western shore of the Oslofjord, south of Drammen, is a gentle, forgotten coast of small farms, birch woods and rocky inlets, and the pin sits in the middle of it, between Sande, Hvittingfoss and the old town of Holmestrand. Vestfold, the county it belongs to, is one of the oldest settled places in Norway. In the ninth century the kings who ruled here were buried with ships, and the Oseberg ship, one of the most beautiful Viking vessels ever found, was dug from a burial mound near Tønsberg in 1904. The Gokstad ship, another great find, came from Sandefjord. Both are now in museums in Oslo.

Holmestrand, with about six thousand people, claims to be the smallest city in Norway, and is a pretty little place of old wooden houses and a harbour, tucked beneath a steep cliff. Its location, on the main line from Oslo, means that the railway runs through a long tunnel under the town. Hvittingfoss, a little inland, is a village built around a waterfall on the Lågen river, where old industrial buildings stand beside the rapids. Sande, to the south, is the main local centre, with shops and services.

The label refers to Hardanger Fjord and its waterfalls, which are on the west coast of Norway, and the pin is a different kind of place: a calm, rural fjord landscape without the mountains. The riding is easy, with flowing roads through woods and farmland, little traffic and few steep climbs. Surfaces are good, and the curves gentle, so it is a good ride for a relaxed evening. The ferry across the fjord from Moss to Horten is an alternative way to travel, with views of the water and the old naval harbour.

The stop is marked for swimming, and there are rocky bays and small beaches along the fjord where Norwegians swim in summer, though the water is cold even in July. Fuel and food are easy at Holmestrand, and Sande has supermarkets and a petrol station. Local cafés serve fish soup, shrimp sandwiches and cakes, and in summer many small farms sell strawberries and vegetables.

Give yourself time to wander. The fjord is quiet in the evening, with a glassy surface that reflects the sky, and the smell of salt and pine is strong. It is a gentle place, and a good introduction to the Norwegian coast.
t.kulsviervej and byskellet@55.9,12.4:
North Zealand is the part of Denmark where the kings went to hunt, and the roads around Hillerød still have the air of a royal estate. The label here points to a couple of residential lanes on the edge of town, but the real draw is what surrounds them: Frederiksborg Castle, a vast Renaissance palace of red brick and sandstone on three small islands in a lake, built mainly for Christian IV in the early 1600s, and the forest and lake country that stretches north toward Fredensborg and Esrum. Hillerød has about thirty thousand people, so fuel, food and a station for trains to Copenhagen are all here.

The landscape is gently rolling, shaped by the ice age, with beech forests that glow green in May and copper in October. The roads are narrow, well surfaced and very Danish: tidy, signposted, with careful speed limits and camera enforcement that you should take seriously. Corners are smooth and flowing rather than technical, and the dense woodland makes a cool tunnel on hot days. Traffic gets heavy near the capital at commuting hours, but the lakeside lanes around Nødebo and Fredensborg are pleasant on weekdays and Sunday mornings alike.

Fredensborg Palace, on the shore of Lake Esrum, is the spring and autumn residence of the royal family, and its Italianate gardens are open to the public in summer. The word fredens-borg means peace castle, and it was built in the early 1700s to celebrate the end of a war with Sweden. Nearby, Esrum Abbey, founded by Cistercian monks in the twelfth century, adds a quiet medieval layer to the story. Danish pastry, smørrebrød and strong coffee are available in every town, and the lakeside cafes in summer are a reward for a morning's riding.

The practical advice is to respect the speed limits, fill your tank in Hillerød before leaving, and ride early or late to avoid the commuter and tourist traffic. In summer the forest is full of cyclists and walkers, and in winter the road can be icy in the shade long after the open fields are clear. The air smells of beech leaves and lake water, and the sky is huge and changeable. There is a great deal of history packed into a very small space here, and none of it is shouted at you.
t.mnajdra@35.8,14.4:
Mnajdra stands on the south coast of Malta, on a bare limestone cliff above the sea, and it is among the oldest buildings in the world. The temples date from the fourth millennium BC, earlier than Stonehenge or the pyramids, and were built by farmers using stone tools. Haġar Qim, a short walk uphill, belongs to the same complex. The nearest towns are Qrendi, a village of a couple of thousand, and Żurrieq and Siġġiewi a little further.

The ride in is a lesson in Maltese geography. Narrow roads run between dry-stone walls and prickly pear, with rough tarmac, sharp bends and frequent patches of grit. Traffic on the island drives on the left, and in the villages it moves slowly and unpredictably. Away from the coast the land is a patchwork of tiny fields, and the sea shows up suddenly, a hard blue line, as you come over the last rise. Wind off the Mediterranean can be strong at the cliff edge.

What makes Mnajdra special is its alignment. The southern temple faces the rising sun, and at the equinoxes and solstices the light enters through the doorway in precise ways, hitting particular stones. Whoever built it was watching the sky closely, and the careful curves of the walls and trilithon doorways show real skill. Below the site you can see Filfla, a small uninhabited rock island that was once used for target practice and is now a bird sanctuary.

Fuel is available in Siġġiewi, Żurrieq and across the island, since nothing on Malta is far from a station. The site has a visitor centre, with shade provided by a large tent-like structure, and there is a cafe nearby. Summer heat is serious, so go early or late. In winter the cliffs can be windswept and wet, but the place is empty and more atmospheric. Bring a layer, and give yourself time to stand quietly and look at the horizon.
t.tarxien@35.9,14.5:
Tarxien is part of the sprawl south of Valletta, where Malta's towns have grown into each other, and it is hard to tell where Fgura ends and Tarxien begins. Together they hold more than twenty thousand people, plus Santa Luċija close by. The reason a rider comes here is under the houses: the Tarxien Temples, a Neolithic complex dating from about 3600 to 2500 BC, one of the great prehistoric sites of the Mediterranean.

The temples are famous for their carvings. Spirals, animals and processions of goats and pigs are cut into the stone, and there was once a statue of a huge seated figure, of which only the lower half, in a skirt, remains in place, with a copy; the original is in the National Museum of Archaeology in Valletta. Excavations began in 1913, when a farmer's plough kept hitting large stones. The site now has a protective canopy, which gives shade and keeps the weather off the limestone.

The riding in this part of Malta is slow and urban. Roads are narrow, one-way streets abound, and drivers do as they please, so patience is essential. Parking is limited, but a bike can usually squeeze into a corner. Beyond the built-up area, the road to the Marsaxlokk fishing harbour, a few kilometres south, is a pleasant run, with colourful luzzu boats painted with an eye on the bow and a Sunday fish market.

Petrol stations turn up in Fgura and around Paola and Żabbar, and so is food. Try pastizzi, the flaky pastries filled with ricotta or peas, from a corner shop, and ftira, the island's bread, filled with tuna and olives. The heat from June to September is heavy, so stick to mornings. Winter brings occasional rain and wind but it is cool and quiet. Malta is small enough that you can see most of it in a weekend, so there is no need to hurry.
t.elarmekora@-0.1,11.1:
Elarmékora is a name to look for on a map of central Gabon, and most people will not find it. It belongs to the Lopé-Okanda landscape, a UNESCO World Heritage site where the equatorial rainforest breaks into patches of open savanna along the Ogooué River. This odd mosaic is a relic of ancient climate swings, when the forest shrank and grassland spread, and the people who lived here left a record of it in iron-working sites and rock engravings dated to thousands of years ago.

The hill itself is known for engraved rocks, carved with circles, lines and shapes whose meaning is lost. Nearby valleys held Bantu-speaking farmers whose ancestors moved across this region over the course of millennia, carrying ironworking with them, and the passage left a mark on the languages of much of Africa. It is a place that rewards slow looking, and a local guide is a very good idea.

The surroundings are rich in wildlife. Lopé National Park is home to forest elephants, buffalo, red river hogs and one of the largest groups of mandrills in the world, the big baboons with blue and red faces that gather in troops of hundreds. Gorillas and chimpanzees live in the forest, and birds fill the canopy with noise. Rain falls in two seasons, with the longest dry period from June to August, which is the best time for travel.

Roads are a mix of tarmac and laterite, with long gaps between settlements, and the railway that cuts through the area is the main artery of the interior. Fuel is hard to find away from the main towns, so carry extra and plan stops with care. Heat and humidity are high all year, and rain can turn red tracks to slick mud. Cash is needed for everything, and lodging is simple, often a basic guesthouse or a lodge run for park visitors. Move slowly, be friendly at checkpoints, and take advice from locals.
t.mount iboundji@-1.2,11.8:
Iboundji is a name that carries over a large, quiet area of central Gabon, a country that is more than eighty percent forest. The mountain of that name rises from the rainforest of the Ogooué-Lolo region as an isolated massif, a green dome among low ridges, and for those who live nearby it has long been a landmark and a place of local stories. The pin falls on the forested slopes, far from any big town, and there is little here for a casual visitor except space and silence.

The country around is cut by rivers that run toward the great Ogooué, the main waterway of Gabon, and by streams that are brown with tannin. The forest holds elephants, gorillas, chimpanzees, buffalo and countless birds and butterflies, and it grows tall and dense, with a canopy that shuts out most of the light. Mist often clings to the mountain in the early morning. The smell is wet earth, rotting leaves and flowers, and it is a place that rewards patience.

For motorcyclists, roads in this region are mostly laterite tracks that run between villages, with a few stretches of asphalt on the main routes. They can be dusty and bumpy in the dry season, and slippery or impassable after heavy rain. Koulamoutou and Lastoursville, the main towns of the area, are the nearest places with services, and both are some distance away. Bridges can be rough and ferries are sometimes needed, so ask locally about conditions before setting out.

Fuel is the main issue. Between towns there may be no pump at all, so carry a spare and fill at every chance. Food in the villages is simple, often cassava, plantain and fish or bushmeat, and lodging may be a guesthouse or a room with a family. Respect local customs, ask before photographing, and keep your documents handy for checkpoints. The best time for travel is the long dry season from June to August, when the roads are firmest and the forest more open.
t.vladivostok@43.1,131.9:
Vladivostok means Lord of the East, and the city lives up to the name. It spreads over steep hills around the Golden Horn Bay, a deep natural harbour that the Russian navy chose in 1860, and it is the end of the Trans-Siberian Railway, 9,289 kilometres from Moscow. The hills are cut by narrow streets that run up and down at crazy angles, and cable cars, trams and a funicular have long helped residents cope. On a clear day the bay is blue and busy with warships, ferries and tankers.

The city has a distinct feel from the rest of Russia. It is closer to Seoul, Tokyo and Beijing than to Moscow, and nearly every second car on the road is a right-hand-drive Japanese import, a result of decades of used-car trade. Pacific seafood is fresh and cheap, with crab, scallops and sea urchin in the markets. The Russky Island bridge, opened in 2012 for the APEC summit, has a cable-stayed span of 1,104 metres, the longest in the world, and it carries the road across the Eastern Bosphorus to the island's beaches and forts.

Riding here is a mix of city and coast. Roads on Russky Island run past old military batteries, bays with pale sand and views across the water, and traffic is light outside summer weekends. South along the coast toward Nakhodka, the highway runs through hills and forests of oak and Korean pine, with views of bays and fishing villages. Fog is common in summer, when the monsoon brings damp air from the sea, and typhoons can arrive in late summer. Autumn is the best season, dry and clear. The forests of Primorye also hold the Amur tiger, though few people ever see one.

Vladivostok has almost six hundred thousand people, so fuel, food and repairs are easy, and Russky has basics. Traffic in the city is heavy and drivers are quick, so stay alert. Foreign riders should check current conditions and requirements before planning travel.
t.walvis bay@-23.0,14.5:
Walvis Bay is where the Namib Desert meets the Atlantic, and the pin lands on the edge of town, beside a lagoon that is one of the most important wetlands in southern Africa. Flamingos, both greater and lesser, gather here in their thousands, along with pelicans, terns and waders, and the pink line of birds against the grey water is a sight that makes even a hurried rider slow down. The Benguela current, cold and rich, brings fish and fog, and the town is often wrapped in mist while the desert behind is sunny.

For many years the port was a South African enclave inside Namibian territory, and it was handed over only in March 1994, after independence. Today it is Namibia's main harbour, with cranes, salt works, fish factories and a pleasant waterfront. Swakopmund, a German-flavoured resort town, lies thirty kilometres north along a road that runs between sea and dunes, and Dune 7, a huge golden dune, is a short ride away. Pelican Point, a long sandspit across the bay, is home to a colony of seals.

The Gamsberg Pass route heads inland from here, and it is a very different kind of riding. The roads go east into the desert, through the gravel plains and the deep canyon of the Kuiseb river, and up onto the Khomas Hochland, the high plateau, passing the Gamsberg, a flat-topped mountain of about 2,350 metres. Much of the road is gravel, with corrugations, sand patches and loose stones, and it demands lower tyre pressures, steady speed and respect. Rain is rare, but when it falls, dry riverbeds can flood suddenly. Temperatures swing from cool mornings to hot afternoons, and the sky at night is brilliant.

Fuel is available in Walvis Bay, which has several stations, and it is essential to fill up completely and carry extra, since stations inland are far apart and may be closed. Carry water, spare tubes and a tyre pump, and tell someone your route. Oysters from the lagoon, grilled fish and German-style pastries are good in the town.

Watch the flamingos for ten minutes before you go. The calm of the lagoon is a good start for a long, hard road.
t.telemark@59.8,10.4:
Røyken is a small town on the shore of the Oslofjord's long western arm, and the pin lands near it, with Blakstad close by and Asker, a town of sixty thousand, seven kilometres to the north. It is the edge of the Oslo region, a wooded landscape of low hills, farms, inlets and small boats, with the Hurum peninsula to the south and the Drammensfjord to the west. After the Telemark canal roads, this is the way home.

The riding is gentle and varied. Narrow roads run through spruce and birch forest, with bends, rises and views over water, and the surface is generally good, with patched sections. Traffic is moderate, building at commuter hours on the main roads towards Oslo. In summer, the lanes are busy with cyclists, and in winter, ice can linger on shaded roads. Early autumn, with gold leaves and still water, is the best time.

The fjord has a strong story. At the narrows near Drøbak, a short way to the south-east, the old fortress of Oscarsborg sank the German cruiser Blücher on the night of 8 to 9 April 1940, delaying the invasion force and giving the king and the government time to leave Oslo. The Hurum peninsula has the old village of Holmsbu, where painters gathered in the early twentieth century, and many old wooden houses with white trim. Asker has a museum of local history and a long coastline of sheltered coves.

Fuel and food are easy in Asker, which has stations, supermarkets and many cafes, and Røyken has smaller services. Norwegian bakeries sell excellent cinnamon rolls and open sandwiches, and a coffee with a waffle is a typical afternoon treat. The commuter train runs from Asker to Oslo in about twenty minutes.

If the weather is calm, sit by the water for a while. The fjord at dusk is quiet, with the smell of seaweed and wet pine.
t.aurlandsfjellet snow road@59.6,11.3:
Askim is an industrial town of twelve thousand on the Glomma, in Indre Østfold, the part of Norway that lies south-east of Oslo and looks more like Sweden than the postcards: wide farmland, patches of spruce, red barns, church spires, and a broad slow river. The town grew around the falls and the mills, with textile and rubber factories that gave employment to generations, and the Viking brand of rubber boots was made here, which tells you something about the climate. Mysen, a few minutes away, has a handsome old church and a quiet centre.

You are here to fill the tank and begin, and Askim does that well, with several petrol stations and a good range of shops. The first part of the ride goes out into the rolling farmland of Østfold, along roads that wind between fields and woodlots with gentle gradients and a surface that is mostly good. Morning traffic from the commuter belt can be heavy, so leave before seven or after nine. The mood is rural, and the pace is slow, which suits a warm-up.

The Glomma, Norway's longest river, runs for more than six hundred kilometres from the mountains down to the sea at Fredrikstad, and for centuries it was a transport route for timber floated downstream to the mills. The river is part of the landscape of this region, and little parks and picnic spots along the bank give a view of the water and of cormorants and herons. Anglers fish here for pike and trout, and in spring the river runs high with snowmelt.
