Eat at a bakery in the centre of town before you go. Norwegian pastries, the cinnamon buns, the cardamom ones and the waffles, are a better bet than the petrol station sandwich. In winter this part of Norway gets cold and icy, with studded tyres on cars and short days, so this is a ride for the warmer months from May to September. Check the weather before you leave, because the clouds roll in off the Skagerrak.
The name on the map promises a mountain, but the ground here is the soft, low country on the east shore of the Oslofjord, near Larkollen, where the coast is a mix of rocky headlands, small beaches and farmland rolling down to the sea. The highest points are only a few tens of metres above the water. What the area has instead is light and air: a wide view across the fjord toward Jeløya and the towns of the western shore, and the kind of long summer evening where the sun hangs low and orange over the water until almost eleven o'clock.

Larkollen is a seaside village that fills with holidaymakers in July and has a little camping, a beach and a long tradition of Oslo families coming out for summer. A short ride away, Moss is the real town of the district, with the car ferry that crosses the fjord to Horten in about half an hour, a handy shortcut if your route turns west toward Vestfold. The ferry runs frequently and carries motorcycles easily, and it is a pleasure to stand on the deck with the wind in your face.

Riding here is gentle. The roads are narrow country lanes with the occasional bend through trees and past old farms, quiet in the early morning and busier on warm weekend afternoons when everyone heads for the beach. The surface is good, speed limits are low and cameras are common, so there is no reason to rush. Fuel is easy at Moss, and at the larger stations on the main road, so you will not be stuck.

History sits close to the surface in this region. The Rygge area was a military airbase and is now a civilian airport, and further along the coast, medieval farms and burial mounds hint at the importance of the fjord as a Viking highway. Walk down to the shore at Larkollen, where the water is clear and cold, and notice the smooth rock the glaciers left behind.
t.aurlandsfjellet snow road scenic road@59:
Wooded hills, small lakes and the quiet farmland of Vestfold's northern edge make up this stretch, close to Sande and Hvittingfoss, where the land rises behind the Drammensfjord and then rolls westward toward the Numedalslågen river. The Lågen is one of Norway's great salmon rivers, running down from the Hardangervidda plateau, and at Hvittingfoss it tumbles over a waterfall that has been harnessed for power since the early industrial age. The name means white falls, and in spring flood the white is no exaggeration.

The roads here are a pleasant tangle of local routes with modest climbs and descents, hardwood and spruce forest coming right to the verge, and occasional glimpses of water between the trees. The surface changes from fresh tarmac to older patches where frost has broken it, and the bends are mostly tight enough to be interesting without needing great speed. In autumn the birch and aspen turn gold and cover the surface in wet leaves, so grip drops and braking distances grow. This is the kind of road best enjoyed at a reasonable pace, with a few stops.

There are not many services on the back roads, so rely on the larger towns for fuel. Sande and the surrounding district have petrol stations, with Kongsberg and Drammen offering more choice, and a grocery shop in a village will usually sell the sort of sandwich and coffee that keeps a rider going. Norwegian shops often close early on Saturdays and stay shut on Sundays, so plan your supplies ahead.

Look for old farm buildings with turf roofs, a few mounds from the Viking period and the local churches, many of them white-painted wood from the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries. The air here has a resin and wet-earth smell that is worth noticing. Late spring, when the leaves are fresh and the rivers are high, and early autumn, when the light turns low and clear, are the best seasons for this stretch.
t.rondane scenic route@59.5,10.9:
Rygge and Råde are neighbouring municipalities on the east shore of the Oslofjord, a gentle district of farmland and woodland about an hour south of Oslo. The dominant presence is the airfield at Rygge, once a Norwegian air force base and now a civil airport, and the lake of Vansjø, a long, shallow, weedy lake that is a popular place for paddling, fishing and swimming on warm days. The nearest real town for services is Moss, a port and industrial town that sits on the fjord a short distance away.

This is a practical place to start. Karlshus is a small settlement, and the filling station options are in Råde and in Moss, so fill the tank before you ride out into the countryside. Norwegian fuel prices are high, so it is worth being sensible and carrying a spare bottle or at least planning stops, though in this part of the country you are never far from a pump. Morning commuter traffic towards Oslo on the E6 is dense, so use the local roads and head south or west instead.

The roads out of here are quiet and flat, running between fields of grain, patches of oak and birch, and the occasional red farm. It is easy riding with few demanding bends, a good warm-up for the day. You may see herons at the ditches and flocks of geese in the fields in autumn, and in spring the cranes pass overhead. The Østfold coast has more oak woodland than most of Norway, which gives it a distinctly southern feel.

History is close by. The Oslofjord was a Viking highway, and the region holds many burial mounds, rune stones and old farmsteads. In the nineteenth century Moss was known for its ironworks and for the Convention of Moss in 1814, the agreement that brought Norway into a union with Sweden after Denmark gave it up. That is a fairly important date in Norwegian history, since the country got its own constitution that same year.
This corner of Vestfold lies just north of Tønsberg, between the villages of Sem and Barkåker, in country that has been farmed since the Viking Age. Tønsberg itself claims to be the oldest town in Norway, with a founding date traditionally given as 871, and the claim is taken seriously locally, with a ruined hilltop castle, Slottsfjellet, and a medieval history that includes kings, bishops and merchants. The land around it is gently rolling, with oak and beech woodland, fields of grain and clusters of old farms.

The most remarkable thing here is underground. In 1904 a farmer digging into a burial mound at Oseberg, a few kilometres away, uncovered a Viking ship, a beautifully carved vessel from the ninth century that had been used for the burial of two women. A few years earlier, in 1880, the Gokstad ship had been found near Sandefjord, and both are now displayed in the Viking Ship Museum in Oslo. The Oseberg farm is still there and the mound is visible, though the finds themselves are in the capital.

Riding in this district is calm and unhurried. Narrow roads wind among farms and woodland with a mixture of short climbs and bends, the surface is usually good and the traffic is local. You will pass old white-painted churches, large manor houses with their fields, and the odd view across to the fjord. Jarlsberg manor, which gave its name to the well-known cheese, lies close by, and the cheese is sold in local shops. Take a block home if you have space in the panniers.

Fuel is easy at Tønsberg, a city of some fifty thousand people, with several large stations and plenty of food. Local bakeries and cafes in Sem and Barkåker are worth trying for a coffee and a cinnamon bun. The best time to ride here is late spring or early summer, when the oak leaves are fresh and the days are long, but autumn, when the beech turns copper, is a close second.
t.trollstigen and geiranger expedition hig:
Rivers shape this country, and the biggest of them is the Glomma, Norway's longest, which flows for more than six hundred kilometres from the mountains near Roros to the Oslofjord. Near Fetsund, where the river widens and slows before it enters Lake Oyeren, the Glomma has a long history as a timber road. For centuries, logs from the forests in the north were floated down the river, and at Fetsund, they were sorted and gathered in a system of floating booms, called lenser, before being sent to the sawmills. The last log drive ended in the 1980s, and the booms are now preserved as a museum, one of the best industrial heritage sites in the country.

The high point here is modest, a forested rise in the hills of Enebakk and Aursmoen, but in this flat region even a hundred metres of height gives a view. The woods are spruce and pine, with birch and aspen, and small lakes lie in the hollows. Many are popular for swimming and fishing, and the forests have a network of tracks and trails used by walkers, cyclists and, in winter, skiers. The air smells of resin and moss, and in summer there are blueberries and chanterelles.

The roads through the district are quiet, with winding lanes through the forest, passing farms and lakes, and short climbs and descents. The surface is generally good, though patched in places, and traffic is light. Watch for elk, especially at dusk, and for cyclists. Flateby, Fetsund and Aursmoen have fuel and shops, and Fetsund, with over six thousand people, is the biggest, at eleven kilometres. There are cafes by the old log booms, and a stop for coffee and a waffle is a pleasant reward.

Seasons matter. Spring brings fresh green and the sound of birds, and the rivers run high with snowmelt. Summer is warm and long, with light until late. Autumn turns the forest gold and red, and winter covers the land in snow, with roads that may be icy, so studded tyres are used by cars and bikes are better kept in the garage. In the evening, the light on the river is soft, and the quiet is deep, broken only by the call of a loon or the splash of a fish.
t.trollstigen and photo pull off@59.6,10.9:
The Oslofjord lies just to the west of this stop, and the land between is a patchwork of farms, forest and low hills, the district called Follo, south of the capital. Around As and Vestby, the fields are large and open, with red barns and white farmhouses, and the road runs between them in long, easy bends. On a clear day, the fjord glints in the distance, and the hills on its far side stand blue on the horizon. It is a gentle landscape, and a good place to stop and take a picture.

As has the Norwegian University of Life Sciences, a successor to the agricultural college founded here in 1859, and the town has the feel of a place devoted to farming, forestry and research. Students ride bicycles in all weather, and experimental fields and orchards surround the campus. Vestby, a little farther west, lies close to the fjord, and a track leads down to the shore and its small beaches. Between them, the E6 motorway carries traffic south toward Sweden, but the older roads are quiet.

A short way north-west, the narrows of the fjord at Drobak have a place in history. On the night of 8 to 9 April 1940, as German warships headed up the fjord toward Oslo, the old fortress of Oscarsborg opened fire on the heavy cruiser Blucher and sank her, delaying the invasion long enough for the king and government to escape. A visit to the fort, reached by boat from Drobak, is a very good way to understand the event. The town itself is charming, with wooden houses, small shops and a year-round Christmas shop.

Fuel and food are easy here. As has about eight thousand people and Vestby over five thousand, with stations, supermarkets and cafes, and smaller places like Tomter are also served. The roads are good, and traffic is light outside commuting hours, with speed limits strictly enforced and cameras on many roads. Be careful of farm vehicles and cyclists, and watch for deer at dusk. In spring, the fruit trees blossom, and in autumn, the fields turn gold, and the evening light is warm. The ride back to Oslo is short, and an evening stop at a cafe by the fjord is a pleasant end.
Drammen is where the Oslo traffic gives up and the real Norway starts to loosen its collar. The town sits at the mouth of the Drammenselva, the river that drains a huge slice of the interior down to the fjord, and for a few centuries it lived off what floated down it: timber, cut in the mountains, driven along the river and sawn on the banks. You can still read that history in the wide quays, the old merchant streets of Bragernes on the north bank and Strømsø on the south, and the sheer practical heft of the place. It is a proper city of ninety thousand people, so everything you need is here, fuel included, and nobody will look at you oddly for pulling in with a helmet under your arm.

As a riding stop it is a good one precisely because it is easy. Come in from the east on the E18 and you cross the river on one of its big bridges, with the water going by wide and brown-green below. If you have twenty minutes to spare, go up the hill behind Bragernes by the Spiralen, a road that corkscrews up through the mountain inside a tunnel and pops you out at a lookout above the town. It is a slightly absurd piece of engineering and a pleasant little diversion, with the whole fjord laid out beneath you on a clear day.

For food, the riverside around Bragernes torget and the pedestrian streets nearby have more cafes and bakeries than you can sensibly sample, and the pattern in Norway holds here too: order the daily lunch plate if there is one, drink the strong coffee, and expect to pay for the privilege. Skoger, a few kilometres away, is only a village of a thousand souls, so treat Drammen as the place to eat and fill the tank before the long run west.

Think of it as the last comfortable hour of the day. From here the roads begin to climb into the hills and lakes of Buskerud and Telemark, the villages get smaller, and the next big pump may be a good while off. Eat properly, check the weather, and get going before the afternoon traffic builds on the E18.
t.aurlandsfjellet@59.6,11.3:
Askim is a river town in Østfold, the southeast corner of Norway, and the point sits close enough to it and to Mysen that one coffee stop could serve both. The name on the label belongs to the high mountain road far to the west, but the place on the map is low, green, farm country, and a good deal more peaceful than the label suggests.

Askim, with around twelve thousand people, grew along the Glomma, Norway's longest river, which here flows broad and slow towards the Oslofjord. For much of the twentieth century the town was famous for its rubber factory, and Viking boots made in Askim were on the feet of fishermen, farmers and soldiers around the country. Mysen, a little smaller, is the centre of the inner Østfold area, with a railway line and a typical Norwegian mix of timber houses and modern shopping. Around both, the land is a patchwork of grain fields, woodland and small lakes.

The roads are quiet and easy. You can ride long, gentle straights between farms, with rolling hills and the occasional blind crest where a tractor may be waiting. The surface is generally good, and the E18 passes close by if you need to make time. In spring there is often gravel from winter treatments on the edges, and in autumn wet leaves can make shaded bends slippery. Elk are a real hazard at dawn and dusk, so keep your eyes on the verges.

Fuel is no trouble, as Askim has several stations and supermarkets, and Mysen has more. It is the sort of place where you can buy a pastry and a coffee without a fuss and sit on a bench by the river. Prices are Norwegian, so expect everything to cost more than at home.

If you have time, find a spot beside the Glomma and watch it pass. In late summer the water is warm, the fields are golden and the light is long, and you realise the south of Norway has an agricultural side that most visitors never see. It is a gentle contrast to the dramatic passes the ride is named after.
t.lysefjord and suleskar@59.8,10.6:
The name on this stop points toward the fjords of the far south-west, but the coordinates land on the Oslofjord, on the east shore a short way south of the capital. That makes it a different kind of place altogether, and a rather good one. The Oslofjord here is a long, sheltered arm of sea with forested slopes, pale cliffs of rounded granite, small boatyards and a ceaseless traffic of ferries, sailing boats and weekend motorboats. The closest bigger town is Drøbak, about ten kilometres on, with the Nesodden peninsula and its ferry link to Oslo just across the water.

Drøbak is the place to know. It is a small harbour town of about eleven thousand with wooden houses in white and ochre, a reputation as a sort of Christmas village and an unusually important role in Norwegian history. In April 1940, the narrow channel just off the town, Drøbaksundet, was guarded by the old Oscarsborg fortress on its islet. The invading German heavy cruiser Blücher came up the fjord in the dark and was hit by shells from the fortress and by torpedoes, then sank. It bought the king, the government and the gold reserve the time they needed to get out of Oslo. You can see the fortress from the shore, and you can take a boat out to it in the warmer months.

As a fuel gate this works well: the town has stations, shops and a harbour front full of cafes, and you are never far from either on this side of the fjord. The riding on the Fv152 and the smaller roads is more pleasant than thrilling, with short rolling bends through spruce and farmland and the occasional flash of blue water between trees. It is best on a weekday morning, before the commuter traffic into Oslo thickens, or in the evening when the light comes in low across the water.

Pack a layer even in summer. The fjord can throw up a cold breeze the moment the sun dips, and shaded sections of road take a long time to dry after rain, so be gentle on the first corner you cannot see round.
t.lysefjord and suleskar high point@59.7,1:
Here the land narrows between two arms of water, and you find yourself on the Hurum peninsula, or just beside it, on forested ground that falls toward the Oslofjord on one side and the Drammensfjord on the other. Røyken is the nearest village of any size, with about three thousand people, and the real shape of the place is wooded ridges, small farms, ponds, and little dead-end roads leading down to boat sheds. The name attached to this stop suggests a high mountain pass far away, but the truth is much gentler: a rolling low ridge where a viewpoint of any kind is something you earn by the occasional gap in the trees.

What makes this corner of Norway interesting is under the surface. The whole district lies on the Oslo Rift, a down-faulted trough that opened about three hundred million years ago, filled with lava, and then cooled into a patchwork of dark volcanic rocks and pale limestone. Geologists have loved it for more than a century, and the fossil-rich shales on the nearby shores have drawn collectors and students for just as long. For the rider, the practical effect is that the hills are low and rounded and the road keeps turning, because the ground itself is full of folds.

Riding here is relaxed and intimate. Surfaces are mostly good, bends are short and well signed, and the traffic is local: tractors, cyclists, people towing boats toward a ramp. Early autumn is lovely, when the oak and birch colour up and the fjord turns steely. Early summer smells of cut grass and resin. In winter these roads are salted and slick, and best left alone.

For fuel, the nearest real choice is Drammen, about eleven kilometres away, and Røyken itself usually has a station and a supermarket for sandwiches and drinks. If you need a swim, the shoreline of both fjords has public bathing spots, though the water remains bracing until well into July. A quiet spot to pull in, drink something hot from the flask and let the engine tick as it cools is never hard to find.
t.lysefjord and suleskar@59.8,11.4:
Setskog and the forests around Aurskog make a kind of Norwegian interior that tourists never reach: miles of spruce and pine, small farms along the ridges, and a network of narrow roads that wind between lakes and marshes. The closest villages are Aursmoen and Bjørkelangen, each about ten kilometres off, and the bigger town of Fetsund lies further west, near where the Glomma river runs out into Øyeren. This is a place to eat and to rest, not to be dazzled, and the food stop it hosts is the kind where the menu is short and the portions are not.

Fetsund is worth a few words, because it is the doorway to something unusual. The river Glomma, Norway's longest, meets the lake Øyeren here, and the delta it has built in the northern end of the lake is the largest inland river delta in northern Europe, a flat expanse of reeds, sandbanks and shallow channels that thousands of migrating birds use each spring and autumn. At Fetsund itself, an old timber-sorting station called the Lenser preserves the story of how logs were floated down the river, caught in booms and sorted by owner's mark. It is a simple and touching piece of industrial history, and a good reason to come out this way.

The roads in the forest are narrow, often patched and occasionally bumpy, so take them at an easy pace. The bends are mostly gentle, though crests and corners hide gravel in spring, and farm traffic is common. Elk are plentiful and nobody should treat that warning as decoration. Late September, when the leaves turn and the air has a clean cold edge, is the best time, though evenings in summer come close.

Fill the tank in Fetsund or at the bigger stations on the main road, since smaller villages can have unmanned pumps or none at all. For food, small bakeries and grocery counters in Aursmoen and Bjørkelangen will do you well. In summer, carry mosquito repellent, because the marshes breed them with great enthusiasm.
t.lysefjord@59.8,10.6:
The Oslofjord narrows here, and the town to know is Drøbak, about ten kilometres away on the eastern shore. The coordinates sit at the water's edge near Fagerstrand on the Nesodden peninsula, looking across to the Åros side, where the fjord begins to squeeze through the Drøbak Narrows. It is a long way from the real Lysefjord in Rogaland, but it has its own claim to a place in history.

On the night of 8 to 9 April 1940, the German heavy cruiser Blücher led an invasion fleet up the Oslofjord towards the capital. At Oscarsborg, a small island fortress in the narrows, old guns and torpedoes sank her, and the delay gave the Norwegian king, government and gold reserves time to leave Oslo. That is why the little fortress is treated with reverence. The fortress is open to visitors in summer, reached by a short boat from Drøbak, and the wreck of the ship is still on the bottom.

Drøbak itself is a delight, with a few thousand inhabitants in a tight huddle of white wooden houses, narrow lanes and a small harbour. It has long marketed itself as the Christmas town, and a year-round Christmas shop runs there, which sounds kitsch but is charming in the right mood. Walk along the waterfront, have a waffle, and look out at the island fortress, which sits in the water like a stone ship.

For riding, the roads down the east side of the fjord are good, with moderate bends, wooded hills and views of the water. They are not demanding, but they are pleasant, particularly outside rush hour, and a ride along the old road through the little villages is better than the motorway. Speed cameras are plentiful. The area is popular with cyclists on weekends, so give them room.

Fuel is available in Drøbak and in Nesoddtangen, though the larger choice is in Ski or Asker. Cafes at Drøbak are good for lunch, and the evenings in summer are long and light.

Visit on a calm morning in June or September, when the fjord is a sheet of silver and the traffic is light, and look for the island at the narrowest point.
t.gothenburg@57.7,12.0:
Sweden's second city has the manners of a harbour town and the weather to match. Gothenburg sits where the Göta älv river reaches the Kattegat, and the old canals, the cranes of the shipyards and the trams that clatter along the avenues all point to a place built on trade. Founded in the early seventeenth century by King Gustav II Adolf, who invited Dutch engineers to lay out the canals, it has always faced west, toward the sea and the rest of the world rather than toward Stockholm. It is also the home of Volvo, which is why the roads leading out of town are some of the best maintained in the country.

Start the day with coffee and a cinnamon bun, because fika is a serious matter here. Haga, with its wooden houses and cafes, is the usual choice, and the fish church, Feskekôrka, which is a fish market in a building that looks like a Gothic cathedral, is a short walk. Seafood is the thing to try, especially the prawns, the mussels and the shrimp sandwiches. In the evening the Götaplatsen square near the art museum fills with people, and the harbour front has plenty of places to eat.

Leaving town, the riding changes quickly. Within half an hour the E6 and the smaller coastal roads cut through granite outcrops, pine woods and flat farmland, with glimpses of the sea. South of the city the roads run through the Halland coast, past fishing villages and beaches, with gentle bends and a lot of long straights. Speed cameras are common, fines are heavy, and Swedish drivers stick to limits, so you should too. In summer the evenings last until almost midnight, and the light on the water is something you remember.

For practical purposes, Gothenburg has everything: fuel on every ring road, bike shops, hotels in every price range, and ferries to the car-free islands of the southern archipelago. Rain is possible in any month and wind off the sea can be strong, so pack a waterproof layer. The best season is late May to September, with June and early July the finest.
t.grimeton radio station@57.1,12.4:
Six steel towers, each one about a hundred and twenty-seven metres tall, stand in a flat Halland field south of Varberg, and from a distance they look like a fence for giants. This is Grimeton, a long-wave transmitter built in the early 1920s so that Sweden could talk to America without relying on cables that others controlled. Inside the long brick hall sits an Alexanderson alternator, a huge spinning machine that makes the signal, with no valves and no transistors, and it still works. On a couple of days a year, including Christmas Eve, the station fires up and sends a message in Morse code, a ritual that draws enthusiasts from across Europe. UNESCO listed it in 2004, and it is unusual among heritage sites in being an old machine you can hear.

The countryside is Halland at its most ordinary and most pleasant: low fields, hedged lanes, farmhouses painted red or white, and pockets of beech forest. Riding here is relaxed. Roads are good, gradients barely exist, and bends are gentle, with the sea a few kilometres to the west. Coastal Route 158 and the small lanes toward Tvååker give you a quiet way in, and traffic is mostly local. Elk do roam this part of Sweden, so be careful at dawn and dusk, particularly in autumn.

Visits to the hall are usually done on a guided tour, and the museum explains how the station worked, with the generators, the operators' rooms and the old telegraph equipment. Check opening times before you ride out, as the season is shorter than you might expect, and the long winters mean limited access. A small cafe usually serves coffee and cinnamon buns, which is really all you need.

For fuel and a proper meal, head the eight kilometres into Varberg, a seaside town of about thirty-four thousand people with a medieval fortress on the harbour, a sea-bathing tradition that goes back to the nineteenth century, and a cold-water bath house on the rocks. Tvååker is smaller but has basic services. The best months are June to August, with long warm evenings, though spring and early autumn are quieter and cheaper.
t.zawiya de sidi sahib@35.7,10.1:
Kairouan was founded in 670 by an Arab general named Uqba ibn Nafi, who reportedly chose a dry plain far from the sea so that his army could not be attacked from ships, and over the centuries it became the fourth holy city of Islam, after Mecca, Medina and Jerusalem. The zawiya of Sidi Sahib, usually called the Barber's Mosque, is one of the places where that reputation shows. It is a mausoleum complex built around the tomb of Abu Zama al-Balawi, who is said to have been a companion of the Prophet and to have carried three hairs of his beard, which is how the barber nickname came about.

You walk in through a long passage into a series of courtyards, with a tiled arcade and carved plaster, and then rooms covered in glazed tiles with floral and geometric patterns in blue, green and yellow. The decoration mostly dates from the seventeenth century, long after the original burial, when Ottoman-era craftsmen refined the place. It is unusually colourful for Kairouan, whose famous Great Mosque is austere and sandy in tone. Visitors are usually welcome outside prayer times, but dress with covered arms and legs, and expect to take off your shoes. Early morning, before the tour buses, is calm and cool.

Kairouan lies on an open plain in central Tunisia, and the ride in from the coast or from Tunis crosses flat steppe with olive trees, sheep and the occasional prickly pear hedge. The roads are generally good but busy with trucks and shared taxis, and the climate is harsh: scorching in summer, sometimes surprisingly cold on winter mornings, and with dust whenever the wind blows from the south. Spring, March to May, is the best time, when the fields are briefly green and wildflowers cover the verges.

The city has more than a hundred thousand people, so you will find fuel and hotels without trouble. Do not leave without trying makroud, a date-filled semolina pastry fried in oil and soaked in honey, sold in the shops along the medina's main street. The city is also known for carpets, and the sellers will tell you so before you reach the doorway, so be ready for good-humoured bargaining.
t.tunis@36.8,10.2:
Tunis does not hurry to impress you. It sits between a salt lagoon and the Gulf of Tunis, with a wide boulevard, Avenue Habib Bourguiba, running through the French-built part of the city and the old medina rising behind it. The medina's maze of covered souks climbs to the Zitouna Mosque, which dates from the eighth century and anchors the whole quarter. Cafes spill onto the pavements, men play cards and drink coffee, and the smell of grilled meat, jasmine and spices rolls out of the alleys. About seven hundred thousand people live in the city proper, with several million more in the larger area.

Traffic is lively and a bit chaotic. Lane markings are suggestions, roundabouts are tests of nerve, and cars stop wherever they find a gap. As a rider, you should stay alert, keep your speed under control and be ready for pedestrians crossing between lanes. The best time to leave the city is early in the morning, when the sun is low and the main roads are clear. The route out to the north-east leads along the coast, toward Carthage and Sidi Bou Said, on the road that follows the lagoon and the sea.

History is thick on the ground. The Phoenicians founded Carthage around the ninth century BC, and for centuries the city rivalled Rome until the Romans destroyed it in 146 BC. The Bardo Museum, in a former palace, holds one of the best collections of Roman mosaics in the world, and is worth a morning if the weather is poor. French influence remains in the cuisine, the language and the architecture of the avenues, and the mix of Arabic and French in conversation is a pleasure to listen to.

For practical needs, the capital has everything: fuel at stations on every major road, workshops, hotels at all prices and good food. Try a brik, a fried pastry with an egg in the middle, or a bowl of lablabi, a chickpea soup eaten at breakfast. Spring and autumn are comfortable, while July and August can be brutally hot and humid.
t.land of the roman houses of amilcar@36.9:
The ground around Carthage is one huge archaeological layer cake. Phoenician traders arrived about the ninth century BC, a Punic city grew up and dominated the western Mediterranean, and in 146 BC the Romans finished it off after a long series of wars. A century later they decided to build a new city on the same hill, and it grew into one of the richest in the Roman world, the capital of the province of Africa. The Amilcar district, a residential area on the coast just north of the main ruins, is where some of the wealthy Romans built their villas, with views of the sea and gardens running down to the shore.

What survives is mostly foundations, mosaic floors and fragments of walls, scattered between modern houses and gardens. Carthage today is a leafy suburb of Tunis, with villas behind walls covered in bougainvillea, a presidential palace and the sort of quiet streets where cats sit in the sun. You need patience to read the site, and a bit of imagination, but the mosaics, with their geometric patterns and hunting scenes, are the real prize. Many of the best pieces are in the Bardo Museum in Tunis, so a visit there fills in what you see in the ground.

The riding here is slow and gentle. The roads are narrow and often lined with parked cars, and the TGM commuter train runs along the shore, with stops at Carthage and Sidi Bou Said. Traffic builds in the afternoon, and weekends bring families to the beaches, so go early or after the rush. Surfaces are generally good, but there are speed bumps and patches of loose sand near the sea. Keep a bit of change for parking attendants, who appear everywhere.

Carthage, with nearly sixteen thousand people, and the larger town of La Marsa a couple of kilometres up the coast, have fuel, cafes and shops. A stop for tea with pine nuts at a terrace in Sidi Bou Said, only a few minutes away, goes well with a morning of ruins. Spring is wonderful, with clear air and flowers in the gardens.
t.basilica of saint cyprien@36.9,10.3:
Cyprian was bishop of Carthage in the middle of the third century, a former orator who converted late in life and became one of the great voices of the early African church. He argued about how to treat Christians who had given way under persecution, he stayed with his flock during a plague, and in 258 the Roman authorities beheaded him for refusing to sacrifice to the gods. The Christians of Carthage never forgot him. Over the centuries churches were built in his honour around the city, and the basilica of Saint Cyprien is associated with that memory, though what remains on the ground is modest, mostly traces of walls and columns that you need a guide or a good map to interpret.

That is the honest part, and it is worth saying that Carthage rewards slow looking rather than grand monuments. The Antonine Baths, the Punic harbours, the Roman theatre, the hill of Byrsa with its museum and the cathedral of Saint-Louis, built in the French colonial period, all lie within a short distance, and the early Christian sites fit among them. North Africa produced Tertullian, Cyprian and later Augustine, and without them the history of Latin Christianity would look different.

On the bike, the neighbourhood is a pleasure for its calm. The roads are shaded by eucalyptus and pine, sea air blows up from the gulf, and you pass villas with painted gates and gardens. Sidi Bou Said, with its blue and white houses on the cliff, sits less than a kilometre away, and the tourist traffic there can be heavy on weekends, so consider walking up the hill from the train station rather than riding. Surfaces are usually fine, though speed humps appear without warning and rainwater collects in dips after storms.

Fuel and food are no trouble. Carthage and La Marsa have petrol stations, bakeries and cafes where you can try bambalouni, the fried doughnuts rolled in sugar that people eat by the sea. Spring and early summer are comfortable, with the light at its best an hour before sunset, while August is hot and busy.
t.la medina et ses faubourgs@35.7,10.1:
Kairouan's medina is a walled city that still behaves like one. Its limewashed alleys wind between houses with blue doors, studded with nails in geometric patterns, and the main street leads past a mix of carpet shops, sweet-sellers and workshops where men hammer copper and sew leather. The walls, mostly rebuilt in the eighteenth century, enclose a place that has been important since the seventh century, and UNESCO listed the old city in 1988. The faubourgs, or suburbs, spread outward from the walls, with the cemeteries, the Aghlabid water basins and a number of tombs and zawiyas.

The Great Mosque, named for Uqba ibn Nafi, is the heart of the medina. Its courtyard is huge and paved in stone, with a sundial and a cistern system, and its minaret, one of the oldest in the Islamic world, rises in three tapering stages. Non-Muslims can usually visit the courtyard but not the prayer hall, so ask politely and respect the signs. Nearby, the Bir Barouta, a well said to be linked to Mecca, has a camel that walks in circles to raise the water, which is a bit of a show, though the well itself is old and revered.

The riding here is not the point. Kairouan sits on a flat steppe, and the roads in and out are straight, hot and busy with lorries, shared taxis and carts. What makes the journey worthwhile is the way the landscape opens, with olive groves, sheep, low walls and distant hills, and the sense of an old inland capital in the middle of nowhere. Park outside the walls and explore on foot, because the alleys are narrow and the sun can be fierce at midday. Leave valuables out of sight and expect a few friendly offers from guides.

The city has fuel and food in all directions, with simple restaurants serving couscous, grilled lamb and brik, and teahouses where you can sit with a glass of mint tea. October to May is the comfortable season, and the early morning light on the walls is lovely.
t.le grand bassin des aghlabites@35.7,10.1:
Water is the thing you cannot take for granted in central Tunisia, and the Aghlabid emirs, who ruled from Kairouan in the ninth century, solved the problem with engineering. They built a series of reservoirs outside the city, fed by a channel that brought rainwater down from the hills to the west. The Great Basin is a huge round pool, about a hundred and twenty metres across, with thick buttressed walls and a small central pavilion, and it looks more like a stage than a tank. Next to it, a smaller settling basin allowed silt to drop out before the water flowed in.

Standing at the rim, you can imagine how important this was. Kairouan has hardly any natural water, and the basins supplied the city and its gardens when the desert wind blew. They fell out of use over the centuries, were restored in the nineteenth century, and now sit among dusty lots and modern houses, a bit sad but still impressive. The water is often low in summer, green and still, with birds on the surface and children fishing nearby, and the stone walls give the place a calm, almost sculptural look.

Getting here is easy, a short ride from the old city walls through streets of low houses. The tarmac is fine, but watch for potholes at the edges and for goats wandering across the road. A tour bus or two will usually be parked nearby, and small stalls sell postcards and carved souvenirs. Visit in the late afternoon when the low sun lights up the stone, and keep sun protection handy, as shade is scarce.

Kairouan, with its hundred and twenty thousand people, has everything for riders, from petrol stations on the main roads to hotels in converted houses. The next stage of the ride heads east toward El Jem, about sixty kilometres of flat road through olive groves, where the Roman amphitheatre rises dramatically out of the plain. Plan spring or autumn, and expect a hot, dry wind from the south in summer.
t.le petit bassin des aghlabites@35.7,10.1:
The smaller of Kairouan's two Aghlabid pools has none of the drama of its bigger neighbour, and that is part of why you should stop. It is a polygonal settling tank, about thirty-seven metres across, built in the ninth century to catch the first rush of rainwater and let the mud sink before the clean water moved on to the main reservoir. Engineering of this kind is usually invisible, and here you can see how it worked: the channel entering at one side, the stepped sides, the tower in the middle that once held an observation platform.

The surroundings are modest. A fence runs along the edge, a few trees give a bit of shade, and the pool sits among streets of low concrete houses, with kids kicking a ball on a patch of dust nearby. After rain, the water turns the colour of tea. During long dry spells it shrinks to a puddle, and you can walk around the dry bottom to see the stone floor. Most visitors spend ten minutes here, and ride on to the larger basin or into the medina.

The roads around the basins are quiet, with narrow tarmac, patchy edges and the occasional donkey cart. In a city of this size, traffic is mostly shared taxis and small vans, which stop without warning, so give them space. Come in the morning, before the sun gets harsh, and plan to leave by midday in summer, as temperatures can reach forty degrees. Wear a hat, carry water, and keep your phone camera ready for the late light, which is soft and golden.

Kairouan itself is a good base. Fuel stations line the main approaches, food is cheap, and many guesthouses in the medina occupy old merchant houses with courtyards. The famous Great Mosque is a short ride away, along with the Barber's Mosque and the carpet workshops. From here the road east to El Jem is flat and fast, with olive trees stretching to the horizon, and the amphitheatre waiting at the end like a surprise.
t.springerville@34.1,-109.3:
Springerville sits on a high volcanic plain in the White Mountains of eastern Arizona, a few feet under seven thousand feet above the sea, and anyone who thinks of Arizona as flat desert is in for a surprise. The air is thin and cool, the hills are dotted with ponderosa pine and juniper, and the town lies on grassland at the foot of a huge volcanic field. Springerville and its neighbour Eagar form a ranching and mountain-resort community of about six thousand people together, with the old cattle-country feel, a few motels and cafes, and a view of Escudilla Mountain's dark bulk.

For riders, this is the northern end of the Coronado Trail, US 191, which runs south for about 120 miles to Clifton through the Apache-Sitgreaves National Forest. It is known for its curves, famously several hundred of them, and for its drops and climbs through conifer forest, aspen and open meadows, with long stretches where you see no other vehicle. The road follows an old route said to have been taken by Francisco Vázquez de Coronado's expedition in 1540, though historians question the details. Weather changes fast, and on the highest sections, snow is possible well into spring and again from October.

Services are the thing to plan. Springerville and Eagar have fuel, groceries and places to eat, but between the two towns and Clifton the supply is thin, with lodges and small stores at Alpine and a seasonal lodge at Hannagan Meadow. Fill the tank before leaving, check your tyres and bring warm layers, since afternoon storms in July and August can bring lightning, hail and sudden cold. Elk, deer and cattle wander across the road, particularly at dusk.

Nearby, the Casa Malpais archaeological site preserves the remains of a Mogollon pueblo, built on a basalt ridge by people who lived here about seven hundred years ago, and there are fine views of the White Mountains from the road. Try the local green chile in a diner, with eggs or a burger. The best months are June to September, and early October for aspen colour.
t.jonkoping@57.8,14.2:
Jönköping lies at the very southern tip of Lake Vättern, squeezed between the water and the high ground, and that position made the city. Vättern is Sweden's second-largest lake, long, narrow and extremely deep, with water so clear that it is used for drinking, and the shoreline here, with its harbor, parks and promenades, is the best place to see it. The city has a lively waterfront and a long, steep main street climbing from the lake into the hills.

Industry shaped the place. In 1845 the Lundström brothers set up a match factory here, and Jönköping became famous for the safety match, a Swedish invention, with the product shipped across the world. A museum in the old factory tells the story. In neighboring Huskvarna, the Husqvarna company has made weapons since 1689 and later bicycles and motorcycles, a name that will mean something to any rider, and a museum there recounts that history. The two towns, now part of the same municipality, sit on either side of a river that powered the factories.

For riders, the lake drive is the pleasure. The road along the eastern shore, heading north through Gränna and on toward Vadstena, follow the water with gentle curves and views across the lake to the opposite hills. Gränna, about thirty kilometers north, is famed for polkagris, red-and-white peppermint candy sticks, sold in small shops, and as the birthplace of the balloonist Andrée, who set off for the North Pole in 1897 on an expedition that ended in tragedy. The surface is excellent, speeds are limited and cameras are common, so keep to the limits.

Jönköping has fuel, supermarkets, restaurants and hotels, and it is the natural stop for supplies before the lake loop. The best months are June to August, with long, light evenings, and September, with softer light. Summer weekends can be busy at the waterfront. Winter is cold and dark, and ice and snow make riding impractical. Sweden's elk and deer are a hazard at dawn and dusk, particularly on the quieter roads, so slow down where the forest meets the verge.
t.amal@59.1,12.7:
Åmål will always be the town from a film title that foreign distributors found hard to print. Lukas Moodysson's 1998 drama about two teenage girls, released in English as Show Me Love, was called Fucking Åmål at home, and the town, which had a rough time of it at first, has since embraced its fame with a certain dry humor. The film is a fair picture of what it feels like to be young in a small place, which is not a bad reason to take a look at it.

Åmål is a lakeside town on the western shore of Vänern, the biggest lake in Sweden and in all of Western Europe, a vast, island-strewn sheet of fresh water that behaves like a sea. The town received its charter in 1643, and its small center of wooden houses, painted in ochre, red and cream, lines the harbor, with a long, low bridge and a promenade. The mood is quiet, with fishermen on the quay and sailboats moored.

Behind the town lies Dalsland, a region of forest, rock and thousands of small lakes. The Dalsland Canal, built in the 1860s to link the lakes with Vänern, is the main sight, with a remarkable aqueduct at Håverud, where the canal flows in a steel trough over a waterfall while a road and railway cross beside it. For riders, the roads through Dalsland are gentle and winding, with pine forest, red wooden farmhouses and flashes of water, and traffic is light. The surface is smooth, speeds are strictly controlled, and cameras are common, so keep an eye on the signs.

Åmål has fuel, supermarkets and several restaurants, and it is the main service town for the area. Säffle, across the water, is another fuel stop. The best months are June to August, with long evenings, and the light at midsummer lingers past ten. September brings quiet roads and the first color. Winter closes the season. In the forest stretches, elk are a real danger, particularly at dawn and dusk, and a collision with one can be fatal, so slow down at the first sign of warning triangles.
t.cefalu@38.0,14.0:
Cefalù lies on the northern coast of Sicily, under a great rock called La Rocca that rises almost 270 metres straight behind the town. The old centre is a tight tangle of lanes between the sea and the cliff, with a sandy beach beside the harbour and fishermen's boats pulled up on the shingle. The population is about eleven thousand, and the town has all the services a rider needs, from fuel to supermarkets, with the next village, Lascari, a few kilometres east. It makes a very good start for the climb into the Madonie mountains.

Its great monument is the cathedral, begun in 1131 by the Norman king Roger II, who is said to have vowed to build it after surviving a storm at sea. The two square towers and the golden mosaics inside, especially the huge Christ Pantocrator in the apse, are among the finest Byzantine-style works in the Norman kingdom of Sicily. Together with the cathedrals of Palermo and Monreale, it is part of a UNESCO World Heritage listing. Beyond the town, the Rocca has the remains of a medieval castle and a path that leads to the top for a superb view.

For the ride, the point is to get out of town early, because the coast road can be busy and the mountains are cooler and quieter. The road south climbs through Gratteri and the foothills into the Madonie Regional Park, with hairpins, beech woods and stone villages. The surface in Sicily can be rough, with potholes and patched asphalt, and local drivers are quick and sometimes erratic, so keep your distance. The best seasons are spring, when the hills are green and the wildflowers are out, and autumn, when the heat has gone.

Cefalù has plenty of places to eat, and the local cooking uses fish, capers, olives and wild fennel. Start the day with a granita and a brioche, or a cappuccino at a table on the square by the cathedral. Fill the tank here before you head into the hills, since the villages in the park are small and pumps are not frequent. The sea behind you gets smaller with each bend, and the mountains rise ahead.
t.castelbuono@37.9,14.1:
Castelbuono is the main town of the Madonie, the range that rises behind the northern coast of Sicily, and it wears its history on its sleeve. A big square castle stands at the heart of the town, built in the fourteenth century by the Ventimiglia family, who were the powerful lords of this part of Sicily and ruled the surrounding country for generations. Inside the castle, a chapel dedicated to Sant'Anna, richly decorated with white stucco, holds a relic that is carried through the town in procession each year, and a small museum shows the story of the family and the region.

The town has a reputation for food as much as history. It is one of the few places in the world where manna is still harvested, a sweet sap tapped from the trunks of the flowering ash trees, which dries into white sticks used in confectionery and, traditionally, as a gentle remedy. It is a very old craft, handed down in families, and the town celebrates it in pastry and ice cream. The cakes and sweets of Castelbuono are sold in shops all along the main street, and it is hard to walk through the town without being tempted.

The Madonie are the high mountains of the region, with peaks of nearly two thousand metres and forests of oak, beech and holly. Much of the range is a regional park, protecting rare plants and wildlife, including golden eagles and wild cats. The roads climbing into the mountains from Castelbuono are some of the best riding in northern Sicily: narrow, twisting and quiet, with views of the coast far below. The surface is variable, with some very smooth stretches and others that are broken by frost and landslides, so look well ahead. In summer it is hot on the plain and pleasantly cool on the high ground.

Castelbuono has all the services you need. There are fuel stations on the approach roads, supermarkets, restaurants and cafes around the main square, and a few hotels and agriturismi in the surrounding countryside. A plate of pasta with local sausage and wild fennel, or a slice of sfincione, the thick Sicilian pizza, is a fine pause. The town is lively in the evening, with the local people out for a passeggiata, the traditional stroll before dinner.

Come in spring, when the hills are green and the wildflowers are out, or in autumn, when the beech woods turn gold and the air is fresh.
t.piano battaglia@37.9,14.0:
Piano Battaglia is the roof garden of Sicily's northern mountains, a high, open basin at about fifteen hundred metres where the road runs out of village and into the clouds. The Madonie rise around it in bare limestone ridges, with Pizzo Carbonara at nearly two thousand metres the highest of them, and the whole area feels more like the Apennines than a Mediterranean island. In winter, snow falls here, and there is a small ski area with a couple of lifts, one of the few in Sicily outside Etna. In summer, the plateau is a grassy open space dotted with cattle and walkers.

The ride up from Castelbuono or from the villages on the northern side, Isnello and Collesano, is a pleasure of a particular kind. The road climbs through terraces of olive and almond, then through oak woods, and finally through open beech forest, with a series of bends and a handful of hairpins that give good views down to the coast. The surface can be patchy and in places rough from frost, and there are sometimes loose stones and the odd cow on the tarmac, so keep a careful pace. In misty weather the visibility is poor and the temperature drops quickly. The road may be closed in heavy snow, and chains or winter tyres are necessary in cold months.

Nature is the great attraction. The Madonie park is home to a rare tree, the Sicilian fir, which grows only here in the world and has been reduced to a few dozen mature trees in a valley nearby. It is a survivor from the Ice Age, and conservation efforts are trying to bring it back. In spring the meadows are covered with wild orchids, peonies and cyclamens, and in autumn the beech woods turn from green to gold. Birds of prey, including golden eagles and buzzards, are common above the ridges.

There are a few small restaurants and refuges around the plain, serving hearty mountain food, such as grilled sausages, cheese and ricotta, but opening hours are seasonal and unreliable, so it is wise to bring something. Castelbuono, about nine kilometres away by straight line and much more by road, is the nearest large town with stations and supermarkets, so fill before you go up.

Weather is the main variable. Wind and fog can arrive without notice, and the air is much cooler than on the coast, so bring a layer even in July.
t.petralia soprana@37.8,14.1:
Petralia Soprana is the highest town in the Madonie, perched at around 1,100 metres on a rocky spur, and it has the reputation of being one of the finest hill towns in Sicily. Its twin, Petralia Sottana, lies just under two kilometres away, a little lower and larger, with about twice the population. Soprana is the smaller and older of the two, and it keeps a medieval layout of steep stepped lanes, small piazzas and stone houses with wrought-iron balconies. Its Norman history is deeper than most: Count Roger I is said to have made it a base in the eleventh century during the conquest of the island from the Arabs.

From the main square, Piazza del Popolo, you can look across the whole range, and on clear days toward the cone of Etna in the east. Churches are plentiful, including the Chiesa Madre with a carved wooden crucifix and the church of Santa Maria di Loreto, which has a terrace with a long view. It is a town to walk slowly, in part because the streets are steep and in part because there is little to do but look. In the summer there are festivals, and in winter the town can see snow, since the Madonie are the snowiest mountains in Sicily.

The ride up from the coast is a delight in its own way. The road climbs through cork oak, then chestnut and beech, and you pass from the dry Mediterranean scrub of the coast to cool upland woods. The Madonie are a regional park, home to the rare Nebrodi fir, the Abies nebrodensis, of which only a tiny number survive in the wild. The surface is variable, with some very good stretches and others broken, and sheep, cows and dogs wander on to the road without warning. Mist can come down suddenly in the forests, and in winter ice is a real hazard.

Fuel is thin on the ground in the hills, so take it in Cefalù or at Petralia Sottana, the larger of the two. In both towns, you can find simple trattorias serving local sausage, ricotta, mushrooms and pasta with wild greens, the kind of food that suits a cool mountain evening. The late afternoon light on the stone is lovely, and a coffee on the terrace is the proper way to end the ride.
t.pinos altos@32.9,-108.2:
Pinos Altos means tall pines, and the little old mining town above Silver City lives up to the name. It sits at about 2,000 metres in the Gila National Forest, in a cool bowl of ponderosa pine and oak, and the main street has the unhurried, slightly crooked look of a place that has seen a gold rush and decided to stay on. The first strike was made here in 1860, drawing prospectors and a ragged frontier population, and for a while it was a hard, violent camp, fought over by miners and the Apache, on whose land they were digging.

Today Pinos Altos is a gentle spot, with a few dozen residents, an old opera house and a saloon, a historic log building that houses a museum, and a couple of galleries and cafes. The old wooden storefronts, the dusty road and the pines overhead make it an easy place to pause. A short way along, the mountains rise toward the Gila Wilderness, the first area in the world to be officially protected as wilderness, set aside in 1924 largely through the efforts of Aldo Leopold, a forester and pioneering conservationist.

The road north is the start of the Trail of the Mountain Spirits Scenic Byway. New Mexico Highway 15 climbs from Pinos Altos in a narrow, winding ribbon through the forest, with many tight bends, blind corners and steep sections, and it is a motorcyclist's delight. It takes a couple of hours to cover the forty-odd miles to the Gila Cliff Dwellings, and the signs advise against trailers and large vehicles. The surface is good but narrow, with few barriers. Fog is possible, and snow can close the road in winter, but spring and autumn are glorious, with crisp air and clear skies.

Silver City, about twelve kilometres south, has fuel, supermarkets, motels and good coffee, so fill up there before heading north. Pinos Altos has a restaurant and a few small shops, but petrol is not reliable. There are no more services on the road, and the nearest stations beyond are on the far side of the mountains. Bring water, a layer and a good map. The night sky here is among the darkest in the country, and the stars are worth staying up for.
t.lake roberts@33.0,-108.2:
Lake Roberts is a small reservoir in a pine-and-juniper valley in the Gila National Forest, at about 2,000 metres, and it has the quiet, slightly secret air of a place that most travellers drive straight past. The lake is under a hundred acres, edged with reeds and ponderosa pine, with a campground and a small marina on one side and rounded hills on the other, and it is popular with anglers after trout and bass. Mornings are still, with mist rising off the water, and evenings bring elk and deer to the shore.

The valley sits in the heart of the Mimbres country, home of the Mimbres people, ancestors of the Pueblo, who from about the ninth to the twelfth century made some of the most beautiful pottery in the Southwest, black-on-white bowls painted with fish, birds and human figures. The designs are so lively that museums around the world collect them. To the north, the Gila Wilderness stretches into the Mogollon Mountains, and the Gila Cliff Dwellings, built by the Mogollon people in the thirteenth century, lie a long and winding ride beyond.

The roads are the reason to ride here. New Mexico Highways 35 and 15 form part of the Trail of the Mountain Spirits, a loop of tight, twisting mountain road through the national forest. The bends are constant, the surface decent but narrow, and the traffic very light. Hazards include loose gravel, the odd cow and deer on the road, and sudden storms in summer. Autumn is the best time, with golden cottonwoods in the creek bottoms, and spring is cool and fresh. In winter, snow and ice can make the higher roads treacherous.

There are no major services at the lake. A small store near the water sells basics and sometimes drinks and snacks, and the campground has toilets and water in season, but fuel is another matter. Silver City, about thirty kilometres south, has everything, and it is the place to fill the tank. Bring food, water and warm clothes, and tell someone your plans, because mobile coverage is poor. The stars are brilliant, the silence is deep, and nobody is in a hurry.
t.gila cliff dwellings@33.2,-108.3:
The last miles to the Gila Cliff Dwellings are the reason the Trail of the Mountain Spirits has its reputation. From Silver City the road climbs through the old mining village of Pinos Altos and then settles into a long, tight conversation with the mountains: pine, juniper, a ridge, a drop, another ridge. It is slow going, and nobody who rides it fast enjoys it. Count on a couple of hours for the last stretch, and be glad of every turnout, because the corners come in strings and the surface is the sort of patched asphalt that rewards a rider who looks well ahead.

The destination sits in the Gila Wilderness, a huge roadless block of southwestern New Mexico that was set aside as wilderness in the 1920s, one of the first places anywhere to be protected that way. The dwellings themselves are small rooms tucked into natural caves high in a canyon wall above the Gila River's forks. People of the Mogollon culture built them in the late thirteenth century, using timbers that can be dated to within a season or two, and they lived here only a short time before moving on. The cave rooms are reached on foot by a short loop trail from the parking area, with a creek crossing and a climb up a stairway of stone. Bring boots you can walk in, not racing leathers, and expect the whole visit to take an hour or more.

What stays with you is the quiet. The canyon walls are a pale volcanic tuff, pocked and stained, and the river runs clear over cobbles under sycamores and cottonwoods. Mule deer wander the picnic ground without much interest in visitors, and in the evening there is a smell of warm pine and dust. Hot springs are scattered through this country, a reminder of how recently, in geological terms, it was all volcanoes.

Plan your fuel before you leave the highway. There is nothing for the bike out here, and the nearest town of any size is Silver City, back down the road you came on. Take water, because the visitor area is small and remote, and give yourself daylight both ways. The mountain road in the dark, with elk and deer about, is not the ride you came for. Late spring and autumn are the kindest seasons; midsummer brings monsoon storms in the afternoons, and winter can leave ice in the shaded corners.
t.russky island@43.0,131.8:
Russky Island is Vladivostok's offshore backyard, a hilly knuckle of land separated from the mainland by the narrow Eastern Bosphorus strait. For a century it was a military fortress, closed and ringed with batteries and barracks, and many of the forts and bunkers still stand in the woods and along the shore, grey and overgrown. Then, in the run-up to the 2012 APEC summit, the island was suddenly opened up with new roads, a university campus and a bridge that made headlines around the world.

That bridge is the first thing to ride. The Russky Bridge is a cable-stayed span with a central section of 1,104 metres, the longest of its type in the world, and crossing it on a bike is a small event in itself, with the strait far below and the Vladivostok skyline behind you. Wind can be strong on the deck, so keep both hands steady. Once across, the roads wind among hills, past quiet bays and fort ruins, with a surface that is usually good near the campus and rougher on the secondary tracks. There is little traffic on weekdays, though Saturday afternoons draw city families to the beaches.

Fuel and food are available but limited, with a few stations and cafes around the main settlements, and Vladivostok itself, eleven kilometres away, is the place for serious supplies. The nearest village, Russkiy, has some five thousand people, and Popova a handful more. Take water and something to eat if you plan to explore the quieter coastal tracks, since you may find yourself on a headland with a view of the Sea of Japan and nothing to buy.

The island's nature is surprisingly rich for such a small place. Oak and lime woods, wild grape and Manchurian walnut grow on the hillsides, and the air smells of salt and warm leaves in summer. Fog rolls in from the sea in early summer and can swallow the bridge, so choose a clear day. Autumn is the best season, with warm days, clear light and deep colours, before the winter wind arrives. A loop around the island is a pleasant half day, and the sunset over the strait is reward enough.
t.shkotovo@43.3,132.4:
Shkotovo is a town of about five thousand people in the south of Primorsky Krai, set among the low wooded hills that sit between the Ussuri Bay and the interior. It lies in the belt of country between Vladivostok and Nakhodka, the two big ports of the south coast, and the countryside around it is typical of the region: oak and birch woods mixed with Manchurian walnut and wild grape, fields in the valleys, and occasional views of the sea from the ridges. It gives the first hint that the Russian Far East is closer to Korea and Manchuria than to Moscow, in both climate and character.

As a ride, this is gentle, flowing country. The roads curve through the hills with easy gradients, a mostly good surface, and a steady flow of lorries heading to the ports, so keep an eye on your mirrors and be patient on the climbs. Summer here is warm and humid, with monsoon fog and heavy rain, particularly in July and August. Autumn is the best time, with dry, clear weather and brilliant colour in the forest, while spring can be foggy and cold. A waterproof jacket should be standard kit.

With its size, Shkotovo has fuel, shops and cafes, and nearby Smolyaninovo, with more than six thousand people, adds further options. The big cities on either side, Vladivostok and Nakhodka, have everything else. There is no reason to linger, but a bowl of hot soup and a coffee make a good break. Ask for local honey, which comes from the region's forests and is among the best in the country, and for smoked fish or crab, depending on the season.

The wider area has more going on than the road suggests. The Sikhote-Alin mountains lie to the north and east, and they are the home of the Amur tiger, one of the rarest big cats on earth, along with bears and sika deer. You will not see them from a motorcycle, but the forest behind the town is part of their world, and it explains the empty look of the hills. Take it slowly, watch for animals at dusk, and enjoy a road that feels like the start of something bigger.
t.lazo@43.4,133.9:
Lazo is a small village of about three and a half thousand people, set between the Sikhote-Alin hills and the Sea of Japan in the south of Primorsky Krai. It is named for Sergei Lazo, a Civil War figure remembered across the Russian Far East, and the same name is carried by the district and by the nature reserve that covers a large part of the mountain land behind. If you want one word for the setting, it is green: dense mixed forest, rivers running clear and fast to the coast, and a sea that on some days looks almost tropical under a hazy sky.

The coastal road that brings you here is quiet and has a character of its own. The surface varies between good asphalt and patched sections, the bends are moderate, and the gradients are gentle, so it is a relaxed ride rather than a technical one. Fog and rain are the usual hazards, especially in summer when the monsoon pushes damp air in off the sea, and a cold, wet morning can turn into a hot, bright afternoon. Autumn is the best season, with dry weather, clear light and the forest turning every shade of red and gold. Spring comes late and can be cold.

Fuel is available in the village, though you should not expect much choice or late hours, and the nearest big town is far away, so fill up before heading in. Shops stock the basics, and a couple of cafes serve plain Russian dishes: soup, dumplings, fried fish, and the strong tea that appears automatically. In season, ask about local seafood, as this coast has plenty of it, and sellers by the roadside offer fresh and dried fish in summer.

The reserve itself is worth thinking about even if you only pass its edge. It protects one of the richest tracts of temperate forest in the world, a place where northern spruce and southern vines grow side by side, and where the Amur tiger, the Himalayan bear and the sika deer all live. The odds of seeing any of them from the road are slim, but footprints in the mud or a rustle in the undergrowth remind you that the forest is full. Keep your speed down at dusk, when deer step out without warning, and keep your eyes up.
t.preobrazheniye@42.9,133.9:
Preobrazheniye is a fishing port of around nine thousand people on a bay of the same name along the rugged southern coast of Primorsky Krai. The name means transfiguration, taken from the church feast, and fits better than you might expect, because the place changes character with the weather. On a clear morning the bay is blue and sharp, with fishing boats in rows and hills rising behind. On a foggy day it becomes a smudge of grey with the smell of salt and diesel, and the horn of a ship somewhere in the murk.

Its life has always depended on the sea. The town grew up around a fishing fleet and fish processing, and you can still see the working harbour, the cold stores and the lorries lined up to load. That makes it a useful place to stop on a coastal ride: with its size, it has fuel, shops, a market and a number of cafes, so you can top up the tank and eat properly before moving on. Seafood is the thing to try, and whatever the catch of the week is, from salted and smoked fish to crab and scallops, will probably be better here than anywhere inland.

The riding is the typical Primorye mix: roads that twist between forested hills and the shoreline, good asphalt in some sections and patched or worn in others, with heavy trucks to be watched on the corners. Summer brings humidity, rain and fog that can cut visibility, while autumn is clear and crisp. Winters are cold, with north winds, and snow can linger in shaded places. The sea is cold for most of the year, but warms enough in August for swimming from the beaches nearby.

If you have time, walk down to the harbour and watch the unloading. Coastal Primorye is a place of hard, honest work, and the ports like this one hold the memory of a century of fishing and Soviet-era industry. The hills behind are covered with oak and Korean pine, and the air has a faint tang of seaweed and woodsmoke. Fill up your tank and water, eat something fresh, and keep an eye on the weather before going on.
t.slavyanka@42.9,131.4:
Slavyanka is a bay-side town of nearly fifteen thousand people in the far southwest of Primorsky Krai, in the district of Khasan, close to the borders with China and North Korea. It sits on the shore of Slavyanka Bay, part of Peter the Great Gulf, and the water in front of it is wide and calm with steep, wooded hills at its back. For decades it was a naval and fishing community with a ship repair yard, and the layout still follows that story, with the harbour at the centre and the streets climbing the slopes.

Because of its size, this is the proper service stop for the Gamov Peninsula road. There are fuel stations, shops, a market and several cafes, and it is the best place to fill the tank, buy water and get your bearings before the quieter villages further south. Do not expect anything fancy, but the food is generous, the tea is hot, and the staff are used to people arriving in motorcycle gear. Beyond here, supplies get thin, so fill up before you go on.

The road in from the north curves along the coast and over low hills, with long views across the gulf. The surface is usually decent but can be broken by frost damage and heavy trucks, and bends are moderate with the occasional blind crest. Summer fog is common, rolling in from the sea and clearing again by afternoon, and during July and August heavy rain can make the road greasy. Late summer and early autumn are the best period, with warm water, clear air and fewer clouds.

Remember that you are in a border district. The frontier lies not far to the southwest, and officials expect travellers to carry passports and to follow the rules for restricted areas, so check what applies before heading into the more remote peninsulas. The landscape is the reward: oak woods, bays with pale sand, and small islands visible offshore, many of them part of the marine reserve in the gulf. The local people eat a lot of seafood, and you can often find fresh scallop, crab and sea cabbage in the market stalls if you arrive early and have a cool bag.
t.andreevka primorye@42.6,131.1:
Andreevka is a coastal village in the Khasan district, the far southwestern corner of the Russian Far East, only a few kilometres from the port settlement of Zarubino. In summer it fills with holidaymakers from Vladivostok and the surrounding towns, drawn by sandy beaches, shallow bays and a sea that actually becomes warm enough to swim in during August. Outside the season, it is quiet, with shuttered holiday cabins and the sound of the surf.

It lies on the Gamov Peninsula road, and it is a gentle place to ride to. The route follows the shoreline and the edge of hills covered in oak, birch and Manchurian walnut, with curves that suit a relaxed pace rather than a racing line. The surface is mostly good, though worn near the villages, and traffic is light except at weekends in high summer, when cars crowd the beaches. Fog is common in early summer, and the weather can switch from bright sun to drizzle in an hour. The best conditions come in September, when the water remains warm, the air is clear and the holiday crowds have gone.

Services are modest. Zarubino, with about three and a half thousand people, is the nearest place with shops and fuel, and Slavyanka, more than thirty kilometres back, is the place for anything bigger. Local cafes serve fish, soup and dumplings in the summer, but opening hours are unpredictable outside the high season, so carry some food and water. Do not treat the village as a place to count on late supplies, and fill the tank in Slavyanka on the way in.

What makes this stretch of coast special is the wildlife offshore and inland. The waters of the gulf are part of a marine reserve with sea birds, seals and rich underwater life, and the forests nearby shelter some of the last Far Eastern leopards in the world, a rare cat that survives only in this part of the Russian-Chinese-Korean border zone. You will not meet one from the saddle, but the sense of living on the edge of a very special ecosystem adds weight to the view. Because the area lies near the frontier, carry your passport and keep your route simple.
t.gamov peninsula@42.6,131.2:
The Gamov Peninsula pushes out into the Sea of Japan as the southern cap of Peter the Great Gulf, a rugged wedge of hills, bays and cliffs on the far southwestern edge of Primorsky Krai. Its tip, Cape Gamov, has a lighthouse and a view over open water, and the shore is cut by small coves where the sea is clear and cold. The peninsula is part of the Khasan district, one of the most remote parts of the Russian Far East, and it has a wild, windblown feel quite different from the busy streets of Vladivostok, many hours to the north.

The road in passes through Zarubino, a port settlement some thirteen kilometres short of the cape, and then runs out along the spine of the hills. Expect a narrow surface, with broken asphalt in places, gravel in others, and tight bends where it follows the shoreline. Gradients are short and steep, there are blind corners, and fog can drop without warning, so ride carefully and keep your lights on. In summer the air is damp and warm, in autumn dry and clear, and in winter the wind is bitter. September is the sweet spot, with warm sea and fewer people.

There are no real facilities at the end of the road. Fuel and food should be bought in Zarubino or Slavyanka, the latter more than thirty-eight kilometres back, and you should carry water, a small repair kit and some extra layers. Mobile coverage is patchy, and help may take a while to arrive if something goes wrong. Because this is a border region, you must also check the rules on access to coastal and frontier zones before setting out, and carry your passport everywhere.

What draws people here is the sea and the forest. Offshore lies the Far Eastern Marine Reserve, one of the richest areas of cold-water marine life in the region, with scallops, sea cucumbers, seals and a spectacular variety of seabirds. Inland, the oak and mixed forests hold deer, bears and, rarely, tigers and leopards. The smell of salt and pine, the sound of waves on the rocks, and the lighthouse standing against a wide sky are what you remember. Come on a calm evening, pull on a jumper, and watch the light fade over the water.
t.ussuriysk@43.8,132.0:
Ussuriysk is the big agricultural and railway town of southern Primorsky Krai, with about 157,000 people and a long history of being the place where roads, railways and fields meet. It began in the 1860s as a settlement called Nikolskoye, grew with the arrival of the Trans-Siberian line and Chinese Eastern Railway branches, and took its present name in the middle of the twentieth century. The streets still carry an old provincial character, with brick merchant buildings, tree-lined avenues and a cathedral that is easy to spot from afar.

For a rider heading north into the Sikhote-Alin, this is the final stop for everything you might need. Fuel stations are abundant, supermarkets and markets sell everything from rice to spare chains, and cafes serve a wide mix of Russian, Korean and Chinese dishes, reflecting the history of the Far East. A few hours here can make a long journey easier: change oil if you must, check your tyres, buy water, and eat properly. The traffic can be heavy and the road surface in town patchy, so allow time and watch for potholes.

North and east of the city, the road enters hills and forest. The scenery changes quickly from flat farmland to wooded ridges, and the climb into the Sikhote-Alin brings cooler air and the first real corners of the day. Surface conditions vary, with good asphalt on main routes and worn sections on the older roads. Summer is warm and humid, with fog and thunderstorms, while September and early October bring the best weather, with dry days and strong colours in the trees. Winters are cold and snowy, with icy roads and short days, so the season for riding is limited.

The countryside around Ussuriysk is where the Russian Far East begins to feel different from Siberia. Fields of soya and rice, Korean villages with their own traditions and a climate shaped by the monsoon mean that gardens are lush in a way you would not expect so far north.
