The region takes its name from the Ussuri River and from the taiga that once covered the whole area, home to the Amur tiger. The town is also known for its markets, and a walk through one is the quickest way to taste the mix of cultures that make up Primorye today.
t.megalithic temples of malta@36.0,14.3:
Before there were pyramids in Egypt, or Stonehenge on its plain, people on a small Mediterranean island were building enormous stone temples, and some of them are still standing. The group at Ġgantija, on the island of Gozo, goes back to roughly 3600 BC, which makes it among the oldest free-standing monuments in the world. The walls are made of huge limestone blocks, some weighing several tonnes, and they curve into rounded chambers like the lobes of a clover leaf. Local legend said they were built by a giantess, and the name comes from the word for giant.

The temples are part of the larger group of Maltese megalithic sites that UNESCO listed in 1980. Little is known about the people who built them, but they left behind carved spirals, altars, and the famous broad-hipped figurines, and they evidently had a sophisticated society on an island with little more than farming and fishing to support it. Today the site sits on a ridge above the village of Xagħra, with views over the fields of Gozo toward the sea.

Getting here with a motorcycle means the ferry from Ċirkewwa on Malta's north coast to Mġarr on Gozo, a short crossing that is part of the fun. Traffic drives on the left, as in Britain, and the roads are narrow, patched and busy with minibuses and tourist cars, with potholes in places and lots of tight village squares. Gozo is much quieter than Malta, and the small hill roads around Victoria, the citadel town, and out to the coast at Dwejra and Ramla Bay are a pleasure at an easy pace. Summer is hot and crowded, so spring and autumn are better, with clear light and fewer queues at the ferry.

Fuel is easy enough in Victoria, only a few kilometres away, and Xagħra and Xewkija have small shops and cafes. Try the local bread with olive oil and tomato, or the sheep's cheese called gbejniet, in a village bar, and ask about the rock salt pans along the northern coast. The famous Azure Window at Dwejra collapsed in a storm in 2017, but the coast there is still dramatic.
t.m ns klint@55.0,12.5:
Møns Klint is where the Baltic suddenly gets dramatic. Over a stretch of some six kilometres on the east coast of the island of Møn, chalk cliffs laid down in the late Cretaceous rise straight out of the sea, white and crumbling and streaked with grey flint, to a height of about a hundred metres and more. The highest point of the cliffs is the Dronningestolen, the Queen's Chair, reaching more than a hundred and twenty metres above the beach. Beech woods grow right to the edge, and in the green light under the trees the contrast with the chalk is a surprise.

The chalk was pushed up and tilted by the weight of the ice sheets in the last glaciation, and the layers are folded in a way that geologists love. Fossils turn up on the beach after storms, including sea urchins and the occasional shark tooth, and the woodland above is rich in orchids, which bloom in early summer. A visitor centre called GeoCenter Møns Klint tells the story. A long staircase leads down to the beach, and it is hard work on the way back up, so allow time, and take care of the loose chalk at the foot of the cliff, which does fall.

The ride to the cliffs is part of the pleasure. Møn is reached from Zealand over a long bridge, and the roads across the island are narrow, quiet and bordered by hedgerows, whitewashed churches with frescoes, and the occasional thatched farm. Cornering is gentle, the surface good, and the speed limits sensible. In July and August the cliffs get their crowds, so late afternoon, when the day-trippers leave and the light lies low across the sea, is the best time to arrive.

Stege, thirteen kilometres west, is the island's small town and has petrol, supermarkets and a few cafés beside the old town ramparts. Nothing is sold at the cliffs beyond a kiosk and the centre, so fill the tank before you come. Vordingborg, on the mainland side, is the nearest larger town. If the weather is wet, the cliffs turn a soapy grey and the beach path gets slippery, which is a bad bet; a clear spring day, with beech leaves just out, is hard to beat.
t.archaeological area of agrigento@37.3,13:
The Valley of the Temples is not really a valley at all, but a long ridge running parallel to the Sicilian south coast, with the sea shining a few kilometres to the south and modern Agrigento climbing the hill behind. The Greeks called their city Akragas. It was founded around 580 BC by settlers from Gela and became one of the great cities of the Greek west, rich enough that the philosopher Empedocles, who lived here, is said to have remarked that the citizens built as if they would live forever and ate as if they would die tomorrow.

What survives is staggering. The Temple of Concordia, from the fifth century BC, is among the best-preserved Greek temples anywhere, mainly because it was later turned into a church. The Temple of Juno stands on the ridge's eastern end with a fine view over the olive and almond trees, and the fallen Temple of Olympian Zeus still lies in huge broken pieces that give a sense of its scale. A giant stone figure, a telamon, lies on its back on the grass. In February the almond trees bloom and the town holds its almond-blossom festival, which is the most beautiful time to be here, with white flowers around the golden stone.

Riding to the site is easy enough from Agrigento, though the town's streets are steep and busy. The road along the ridge, the scenic Via dei Templi, is a gentle ribbon with views to the sea. To get here from the interior you will probably take the SS640 or SS115, both solid roads through sun-baked, yellow-brown hill country that suddenly drops toward the coast. In July and August the heat is serious, so try to arrive in the early morning or just before closing, when the stone turns honey-coloured.

Agrigento is a proper town of thirty thousand, so you will find fuel, restaurants and cafes without trouble. Try the local almond pastries, and the sweet-and-savoury Sicilian staples: caponata, pasta with sardines, and cannoli whose ricotta tastes remarkably unlike anything outside the island. The writer Luigi Pirandello was born just outside town, and his house is a modest place of pilgrimage for anyone who likes the theatre of the absurd.

From here the long routes lead east, toward Ragusa and the Roman mosaics of Villa del Casale, across a Sicilian interior that is emptier and wilder than most visitors expect.
t.trelleborg@55.4,11.3:
In the late tenth century, on the western coast of Zealand, King Harald Bluetooth built a fortress that must have looked to its neighbours like a statement written in earth. Trelleborg is a perfect circle, about a hundred and thirty metres across, ringed by a high rampart with four gates facing the compass points, and inside, sixteen long houses are arranged in four neat blocks around a central crossing, like a plan drawn with a compass and ruler. Archaeologists dated the timbers to around the 980s, and the same geometry turns up at other Danish fortresses, at Fyrkat in Jutland and Aggersborg by the Limfjord, which suggests a royal building programme under a single mind.

The purpose is debated. It may have been a base for a standing army, or a place to gather men and ships for campaigns, or a show of the king's power at the Great Belt crossing, which was an essential route. What is clear is that the fort was used for a short time, perhaps a few decades, and then abandoned. The visitor centre has a reconstructed longhouse with a turf roof and a museum of Viking Age finds, and the ramparts have been reconstructed so that you can walk the full circle. The site is part of the UNESCO listing of the Viking-Age Ring Fortresses of Denmark.

The country around is soft and green. Zealand's southwest is low farmland, with fields of barley and rapeseed, small woods and lakes, and the Great Belt on the horizon. The roads are quiet and straight, with the occasional turn at a farm or a village, and not a hill in sight, so the pleasures are the sky, the wind and the cycle paths. Summer is the best season, and weather can come in fast from the west. Speed limits are strictly enforced in Denmark, with fixed cameras and patrols, and fines are heavy.

Forlev, two kilometres away, is a small village, and Slagelse, six kilometres off, is the larger town, with fuel stations, supermarkets, a museum and a historic centre with a medieval church. Skælskør and Korsør are the nearby harbour towns, and the Great Belt Bridge, on the east side, is a long toll crossing for motorbikes. Try a smørrebrød open sandwich, and in the afternoon a kanelsnegl, a cinnamon pastry. The site is open daily in summer with a modest fee, and the wind on the rampart is often strong, so bring a windproof layer.
t.gr nholtvangen north of gr nholt vang@56:
North Zealand is the part of Denmark where kings went to relax. The coast road runs up the Øresund from Copenhagen to Helsingør, past beach villas and harbours, and inland, behind the first ridge, lies a quieter country of beech woods, lakes and rolling fields around Fredensborg and Lake Esrum. Grønholtvangen is a stretch of open land and woodland north of Grønholt Vang, a name that suggests an old common, in a landscape that was shaped by royal hunting and by the great beech forest of Gribskov, one of the largest in Denmark. The ride belongs to Kronborg Castle, the Renaissance fortress at Helsingør that Shakespeare turned into Elsinore, the home of Hamlet.

Fredensborg, two kilometres away, has its own royal connection. Its palace, begun in the early eighteenth century and inspired by Italian villas, is used by the Danish royal family in spring and autumn, and the palace gardens are open to the public in summer. On the shore of Lake Esrum, a few kilometres north, stand the ruins of a Cistercian abbey, founded in the twelfth century, with a monastery garden and a small museum. The lake is clear and long, with forests along its banks, and boat trips run in summer.

For motorcyclists, the area is a quiet pleasure. The roads are narrow and smooth, with gentle curves between hedgerows and beech trunks, and the traffic is light apart from Sunday drivers heading for the coast. The landscape is gentle, with hills only a few dozen metres high, so this is not a ride for dramatic bends but for smooth surfaces and green tunnels. Danish speed limits are strictly applied, and automatic cameras and mobile patrols are common. Weather comes in from the west and changes quickly, with showers and sunshine in the same hour. The best months are May, June and September.

Fredensborg is a town of about eight thousand people, and you will find fuel, bakeries, cafés and a supermarket, with larger stations in Hillerød and Helsingør. Try a cheese and rye bread sandwich, a Danish pastry in the bakery, and a cup of strong coffee. Parking near the palace is easy, and the nearest signage for the lake is clear. Respect the signs about camping and fires in the Gribskov woods, which are protected. Carry a waterproof layer for the sudden showers.
t.city of valletta@35.9,14.5:
Valletta is a city drawn with a ruler. After the Great Siege of 1565, when the Knights of St John and the Maltese held out through a summer against the Ottoman fleet, Grand Master Jean de Valette decided to build a fortress city on the narrow peninsula between two deep harbours, and the foundation stone went down in 1566. The streets run in a straight grid, which was unusual for the time, and the steep ones end in steps and views of the sea. Within a couple of generations it was one of the finest baroque cities in Europe, and it is still compact enough to walk end to end in half an hour.

The jewel is St John's Co-Cathedral, plain outside and overwhelming inside, with every wall and floor covered in gilded carving and inlaid marble tombs of the knights. In the oratory hangs Caravaggio's Beheading of Saint John, the largest painting he ever made, which he painted while a fugitive in Malta and which carries his only known signature, written in the blood of the saint. Upper Barrakka Gardens look over the Grand Harbour, where a noon gun is still fired, and the view of the fortified harbour across the water is quite something.

Malta drives on the left, a legacy of British rule that lasted until 1964, and the island is small enough that riders find themselves in a different corner within an hour. Valletta itself is crowded and parking is a puzzle, so I would leave the bike outside the gate in Floriana, where the bus terminal and the larger car parks are, and walk in. The streets are steep and sometimes slippery with polished stone, so take care in the wet. Fuel is not a problem on such a small island, and Floriana and the surrounding urban area have several stations.

The best riding on the island lies elsewhere, along the west coast and out to the Dingli cliffs, but the sea approach is worth a thought. Many riders reach Malta from Sicily by ferry, arriving by the Grand Harbour below the bastions, which is a fine entrance for a motorcycle trip.

Come out of season if you can, in spring or autumn, when the limestone is warm but not oven-hot and the cruise ships are fewer.
t.cape cross@-21.8,14.0:
You smell Cape Cross before you see it. A cold wind off the Atlantic carries a thick, rank, fishy odour across the coastal desert of Namibia, and then the beach appears, packed with brown bodies, and the noise arrives: a continual barking, bleating and groaning from tens of thousands of Cape fur seals. The colony is one of the largest on the African coast, and in the pupping season, around November and December, the rocks and shingle are crowded with newborns. Black-backed jackals patrol the edges, hoping for a weak pup, and the Benguela current, cold and rich in fish, is the reason for the whole noisy business.

The cape has a place in European history too. In 1486 the Portuguese navigator Diogo Cao landed here on his voyage south and planted a stone cross, one of the padroes that the Portuguese used to claim the coast. The original was taken to Germany in the nineteenth century, and a replica now stands near the site, while a second copy, put up by the Germans, stands beside it. The place has a lonely feel, with fog banks drifting in from the sea and the grey surf breaking on the rocks.

The road to the cape is part of the pleasure. From Swakopmund, the C34 runs north along the coast, a salt road built on a hard crust of gypsum and salt that is smooth, pale and often damp with fog, so the surface can be slippery and the visibility short. The desert on one side, the ocean on the other, and little else except the rusting hulks of old wrecks and the fishermen's cabins of Henties Bay. The wind is strong, and cold, even in summer, so bring layers. The road is mostly straight, but a headwind and the monotony can tire you, and trucks carrying salt and mining equipment use it.

Fuel needs planning. Swakopmund, about a hundred and twenty kilometres south, and Henties Bay, about sixty kilometres, are the last proper stations, and there is nothing at the reserve itself except a small gate and a shop. A small entry fee is charged at the entrance. Fill the tank at Henties Bay, take water and a warm layer, and arrive by mid-morning, because the afternoon wind can be fierce. The fog usually lifts by late morning, and the light on the seals can be wonderful, though the smell, I warn you, stays in your jacket for days.
t.path@55.9,12.3:
Hillerod is a town north-west of Copenhagen with a palace that looks as if it were built for a fairy tale. Frederiksborg Castle sits on three small islands in a lake, a red-brick Renaissance building with copper-green spires, towers and gables, reflected in the water. It was built for King Christian IV in the early seventeenth century and became the site where Danish kings were crowned for generations. Today it houses the Museum of National History, with portraits and rooms full of Danish history.

The town has about thirty thousand people, and it makes a good base for exploring North Zealand, a region of lakes, beech forests and gentle hills. The landscape around Hillerod is the Danish idea of wild, which is to say soft and green, with woods of tall beech trees, small lakes and meadows. Gribskov, a large forest to the north, is one of the biggest in Denmark, and in spring, its floor is covered with anemones.

The ride from here connects to Borgring, a Viking-age ring fortress found in 2014 near Koge, south of Copenhagen, one of a small family of circular forts built around the year 980 in the reign of Harald Bluetooth. The ring fortresses, including Trelleborg and Fyrkat, are among the most intriguing sites of Viking Denmark, and Borgring has been the subject of excavations that have revealed its gates and ramparts. A path on the ground is something you can follow in several places in this region.

The roads in Zealand are smooth, flat and straightforward, with speed limits that are lower than in much of Europe and enforced by cameras. The countryside is dotted with farms, thatched cottages and white churches, and the light is soft and changing. Wind is almost constant, and rain can arrive without warning. Fuel is easy to find in Hillerod, at several stations, and the town has bakeries, cafes and restaurants. Denmark is expensive, so be ready for high prices. Summer evenings are long, and the best time for riding is late spring to early autumn.
t.gr nholtvangen south of gr nholt vang@55:
North of Copenhagen the Danish landscape turns into a mixture of beech woods, lakes and open meadows, a fragment of what the whole country looked like before the farmers took over. Grønholt Vang belongs to that world, a patch of countryside near Hillerød and Fredensborg in north Zealand, where woodland and open ground sit side by side. The word vang is old Danish for a field or open ground, and it hints at the pattern.

This is royal country. Fredensborg Palace, a few kilometres away, has been a summer residence of the Danish royal family since the eighteenth century, and the hunting forests nearby were once reserved for the king's sport. The great Frederiksborg Castle at Hillerød, a Renaissance palace on three islands in a lake, is close, and the whole area has a feeling of old estates and managed woodland. Lake Esrum, the second largest in Denmark, lies to the north and is worth a detour.

The roads in north Zealand are among the most civilised in Denmark. They wind through beech forests, along lake shores and between fields, with gentle bends and a good surface, and they are quiet outside the commuting hours. Speed limits are low and enforced, with cameras on the main roads, so take it easy and enjoy the scenery. The country is flat to gently rolling, and in autumn the beech leaves turn a golden copper that is hard to beat.

This particular spot is on the ride that links the area with the Viking ring fortress at Trelleborg, on the other side of Zealand. Nødebo is a small village with a few shops, while Fredensborg, with about eight thousand people, and Hillerød, with over thirty thousand, offer fuel, supermarkets and restaurants. Danish bakeries are a pleasure, and a pastry and a coffee are a good way to start the day.

Come in spring, when the beech leaves are fresh and the woodland floor is carpeted with wood anemones, or in October for the colour. Midsummer evenings are long and light.
t.ridestien in gr nholt vang@56.0,12.4:
A ridestien is a bridle path, and in Denmark they are taken seriously. Grønholt Vang, in the woodland and open country of north Zealand, has a network of them, and the one marked here runs through trees and along the edge of open ground a few kilometres from Fredensborg and Hillerød. The paths are meant for riders on horseback, so a motorcycle has no business on them, but they are a clue to the character of the area: an old landscape of forest and estate, now shared by walkers, cyclists and horse riders.

The surroundings carry a lot of Danish royal history. North Zealand was the king's hunting country for centuries, and the grand palaces of Fredensborg and Frederiksborg, along with the hunting park of Jægersborg Dyrehave to the south, are part of the same story. The Dyrehave, the deer park, was laid out in the seventeenth century for royal hunts and is now a place for Copenhagen families to walk at weekends, with red and fallow deer in the open ground and the little Hermitage hunting lodge on its hill.

Riding on the roads around Grønholt Vang is relaxed and polite. They wind through beech woods and past farms and lakes, with easy bends and a good surface, and Danish drivers keep to the speed limit, which is a good example to follow. In autumn the beech trees turn gold and copper, and the light through the leaves is warm. In spring, the first leaves are the freshest green.

The nearest villages, Nødebo and Fredensborg, have basic services, and Hillerød, a town of over thirty thousand, has fuel, supermarkets and restaurants. Danish bakeries sell excellent pastries and rye bread, and a cup of coffee and a cinnamon swirl is a good start to the morning. Drivers will be sharing the roads with horses in places, so slow down where you see riders and give them plenty of room.

This stop is linked on the ride with the Jægersborg deer park and the wider Par Force Hunting Landscape, a World Heritage site that preserves the geometry of royal hunting rides. Early in the morning, with the light slanting through the trees, is the best time to be there.
t.isole eolie@38.5,14.9:
The Aeolian Islands rise from the Tyrrhenian Sea north of Sicily like the tops of a drowned mountain range, which is more or less what they are. Seven main islands, Lipari, Vulcano, Salina, Stromboli, Panarea, Filicudi and Alicudi, are the summits of volcanoes, and two of them are still active: Stromboli, which has thrown out glowing fragments every few minutes for centuries and is known as the lighthouse of the Mediterranean, and Vulcano, whose steaming crater gave every volcano its name. UNESCO listed the archipelago in 2000 for its value in the study of volcanism.

The coordinates sit on Lipari, the largest island, near Canneto on the east coast, where white cliffs of pumice tumble toward a dark pebble beach. Obsidian and pumice made the islands rich: in the Neolithic period, black volcanic glass from Lipari was one of the most valuable materials in the Mediterranean, traded across Italy and beyond for sharp blades. The castle hill in Lipari town holds a fine archaeological museum that tells this story, with Greek theatre masks, Bronze Age finds and a collection of old amphorae pulled from the sea.

Riding here is a short, sweet affair, and you must be willing to take a ferry or hydrofoil to start. Boats leave from Milazzo, on the Sicilian coast, and the larger ferries take motorbikes, although in summer you should book ahead. The roads on Lipari are narrow, with tight hairpins, sudden gradients and a rough surface in places, and the island loop, which takes under an hour to ride, offers striking views of the other islands floating on the horizon. In high summer the roads are crowded with scooters and minibuses, and parking in Lipari town is tight. Out of season the island is quiet, and the wind can be sharp.

Fuel is available on Lipari, though at island prices and in limited places, and you will find shops, restaurants and small hotels in Lipari town, with a smaller choice at Canneto. Pianoconte, in the hills above, has views over the sea. The wider choice of supermarkets and garages is on the Sicilian mainland, at places like Patti, thirty-odd kilometres away across the water, so fill the tank before you board.

Food is a joy: capers from Salina, Malvasia, a sweet golden wine from the islands, fresh fish, tuna, and granita with brioche for breakfast. Spring and early autumn are lovely, with warm seas and fewer people, while August is hot and busy.
t.al saflieni hypogeum@35.9,14.5:
Beneath a quiet residential street in Paola, a few kilometres south of Valletta, there is a labyrinth carved into the rock about five thousand years ago. The Ħal Saflieni Hypogeum is a prehistoric underground sanctuary and burial complex, cut by hand with stone and antler tools into the soft limestone on three levels, with chambers, passages and niches that descend to about ten metres. It was in use from around 3300 BC to 3000 BC, and the remains of thousands of people were found in it when workmen broke into it by accident in 1902, while digging a cistern.

What strikes visitors is that the architecture imitates the free-standing temples above ground, with curved ceilings, doorways and carved spirals painted in red ochre. In the so-called Oracle Room, a small chamber with an odd acoustic quality, a deep voice is said to boom through the whole complex. A small clay figurine of a sleeping woman, found here, is one of the best-known pieces of Maltese prehistory. The Hypogeum is part of the UNESCO listing of the Megalithic Temples of Malta, and because the microclimate inside is fragile, visitor numbers are strictly limited. Tickets sell out weeks or months ahead, and photography is forbidden, so book early and do not expect to be admitted on the day.

Riding in Malta is an adventure with a particular flavour. Traffic drives on the left, a legacy of British rule, and the roads around Valletta are busy and often congested, with buses, vans and small hatchbacks driven with great confidence. The surface is patched, drains are common, and the limestone dust and polished stone can be slick in the first rain after a dry spell. The urban sprawl blurs towns into each other, and Paola, Fgura and Santa Luċija seem to be a single built-up area. Parking is tight but easier for a bike than for a car.

Fuel, supermarkets and cafés are abundant in Fgura and Paola, with a population of eleven thousand in Fgura alone, so there is no need to plan. The nearby Tarxien Temples, a short ride away, are free-standing temples with spiral reliefs and are well worth a visit. For a snack, try pastizzi, flaky pastries filled with ricotta or mushy peas, sold from small shops for pocket change, with a cup of strong tea.

The island is hot and dry from June to September, with temperatures that make helmets uncomfortable. Spring and autumn are the best times to explore.
t.ggantija temples@36.0,14.3:
On the island of Gozo, the smaller sister of Malta, there stands a pair of temples that are older than the pyramids of Egypt and older than Stonehenge. The Ġgantija temples were built between about 3600 and 3200 BC, and the name comes from the Maltese word for giant, since islanders long believed that only a race of giants could have lifted such enormous stones. Local legend adds a giantess who carried the blocks on her head while nursing a baby, and who lived on a diet of broad beans. Some of the standing stones are over five metres tall, and the outer walls are made of massive pieces of coralline limestone, while the inner walls are finer-grained globigerina stone.

Inside the walls are a series of curved apses leading off a central passage, with altars, libations holes and carvings of spirals. It is one of the best preserved prehistoric monuments in the world, and the site is part of the UNESCO listing of the Megalithic Temples of Malta. Next to the temples a small visitor centre displays finds and models and explains what people think the buildings were used for, though the honest answer is that nobody knows for sure.

Gozo is a place for slow riding. The island is only about fourteen kilometres long, with green fields, terraced hills, small villages and stone farmhouses, and the roads are narrow, quiet and well surfaced, though busy near the ferry in summer. Reaching it requires the short car ferry from Ċirkewwa on Malta to Mġarr, which takes around twenty-five minutes and carries motorbikes. Xagħra, the nearest village, has fewer than four thousand people but supplies a shop, cafés and a petrol station nearby, and Victoria, the island's capital, has the supermarkets and the bigger garages. The huge dome of the church at Xewkija, visible for kilometres, is worth a short detour.

Food on Gozo is simple and local: gbejniet, small round cheeses made from sheep or goat milk, ftira, a flatbread pizza topped with potatoes and cheese, and sweet figs and honey. The nearby Ramla Bay has red sand and a hillside cave said by legend to be the home of Calypso, who held Odysseus captive for seven years.

Go outside high summer if possible, as the heat is intense and the island is crowded, and enjoy the quiet fields in spring, when the hillsides turn green and the wildflowers bloom.
t.sector of bib knissia basilica@36.8,10.3:
Carthage is a name that carries more weight than the site can show, because the Romans did their best to erase it. According to tradition, Phoenician settlers from Tyre founded the city in the ninth century BC, led by Queen Dido, and it grew into a naval and trading power that fought Rome in three wars. Hannibal came from here, the general who crossed the Alps with elephants. In 146 BC Rome destroyed the city after a long siege, and a century later it was refounded as a Roman colony and became one of the great cities of the western Mediterranean. The Vandals took it in 439, the Byzantines in 533, and the Arabs in 698.

The coordinates fall in the sector of the Roman and Byzantine city, and I do not know the details of the specific basilica sector at Bib Knissia, so I would rather not invent a tour of it. What I can say is how the whole area feels today: a suburb of villas, gardens, bougainvillea and scattered ruins on a low hill above the Gulf of Tunis, with archaeological sites tucked between modern houses and the presidential palace. The main ones include the Antonine Baths on the seafront, the Roman theatre, the Punic ports, the Tophet and the Byrsa hill with its museum and cathedral-turned-concert hall. The site is on the UNESCO list.

For a rider the ride here is a slow, local one. The roads around Carthage are narrow and busy, with taxis, minibuses and delivery vans moving fast and unpredictably, and surfaces are patched, with cobbles on some streets. A light rail line, the TGM, runs between Tunis and La Marsa and stops at several stations near the sites, so many visitors park the bike and use it. Summer heat can be fierce, so go early, and bring water, as shade is rare among the ruins.

Carthage is a town of fifteen thousand, and La Goulette, the port next door, is far bigger, so fuel, shops and cafés are never far away. The nearby village of Sidi Bou Saïd is a short walk or drive, and Tunis itself, with its medina, is a few kilometres away.

Spring and autumn are the best seasons. Try brik, a thin pastry filled with egg and tuna, fried until crisp, and a glass of mint tea with pine nuts, served in a café with a view of the Gulf.
t.village of sidi bou said@36.9,10.3:
Sidi Bou Saïd is a village painted in two colours, white and a deep Mediterranean blue, and rising above the Gulf of Tunis on a cliff that falls to the sea. The whitewashed houses, blue doors and window grilles, studded iron nails and bougainvillea spilling over walls are known the world over, though it was a conscious choice: in the early twentieth century a French baron and musicologist, Rodolphe d'Erlanger, who built a palace here, helped to promote a local style and then the authorities protected it by rule. The village is named after a Sufi saint, Abu Said al-Baji, who lived and taught here in the thirteenth century and whose tomb draws pilgrims.

The lanes are steep, cobbled and narrow, climbing through whitewashed arches to a small square and a café overlooking the harbour. The most famous is the Café des Nattes, where mats cover the steps and the mint tea comes with pine nuts, and in the early morning, before the tour groups arrive, it is a calm place. Vendors sell bambalouni, a ring-shaped doughnut dusted with sugar, and strings of jasmine flowers, which people tuck behind their ears. The scent of jasmine on an evening in summer is one of the great smells of Tunisia.

For a rider, the village is best as a short, slow visit. Cars are limited in the old lanes, parking is limited, and the climb is a short, steep walk from the car park near the TGM station at the bottom of the hill. The road along the coast from Carthage to La Marsa is busy but pleasant, with sea views and villas, and the traffic is chaotic, with drivers making up their own rules at junctions. The stones are slippery when wet, and sunlight in summer reflects fiercely off the white walls, so sunglasses are useful.

The village itself has around five thousand people and enough cafés and shops for a day, but for fuel and supermarkets, the larger place is Carthage, only two kilometres away, and Tunis beyond. In summer it is hot and crowded, while spring and autumn are gentle and the light is soft, perfect for photography.

Walk out to the cliff-top lighthouse at Cap Carthage if you have time, for a view across the bay to the mountains of Cap Bon.
t.telemark canal roads@59.6,11.3:
Mysen sits among the clay farmlands of eastern Østfold, in a countryside of wide fields and low wooded ridges that feels more like Sweden than the Norway of postcards. The pin lies on the edge of the town, a few kilometres from the shores of Lake Mysen, and it is marked as a food stop and a finish. Mysen has about five and a half thousand people, a handful of cafés and bakeries, and a long-standing tradition of Norwegian roadside food, which means pølse in a bun, waffles with jam and brown cheese, and strong coffee.

The old stone church at Eidsberg, a few minutes away, dates from the Middle Ages and is among the oldest in the county. The soil here is heavy marine clay, left behind when the sea covered the land after the Ice Age, and it makes some of the most fertile farmland in the country. Wheat and barley fields stretch to the horizon, and in late summer the whole district is gold. Askim, to the west, is the home of a famous rubber boot factory.

The roads in this part of Østfold are flat and straight, running between fields and through small villages, with moderate traffic and a lot of tractors in harvest season. The attraction here is not the riding but the openness. After a long ride on the winding roads of the Telemark region, the calm of the plain is welcome. Speed limits are strictly enforced, and a village's thirty zone is not a suggestion. In winter, the roads can be icy, and the sun sets early.

For a stop, Mysen is practical. Fuel and groceries are easy, and the cafés open early. A waffle with a hot drink on a cold day is a small pleasure that Norwegians take seriously. If you are finishing a day here, the railway station connects with Oslo, though the train is no help for your bike. Take your time, enjoy the quiet and look at the church, which sits on a low hill with an air of great patience.
t.atlantic road coastal bridges high point:
In the low hills north-east of Spydeberg, the land makes a modest effort to be a high point. The pin lies in the clay and forest country of Østfold, where gently rolling ridges rise a few dozen metres above the broad valley of the Glomma, Norway's longest river. Spydeberg, Askim and Flateby are the nearby towns, all small, all within a short ride. The label on this stop calls it a high point, and the view from the top of the rise looks over fields, farms and a patchwork of woodland, with Oslo's suburbs not far off.

The Glomma shaped the economy of this region. For centuries, logs from the forests of the interior were floated down the river to the sawmills near the coast, and the great timber barons of the nineteenth century built their fortunes on it. Floating continued until the 1980s, when trucks took over. The farms here grow wheat and barley, and the red barns and white farmhouses of Østfold are a classic Norwegian sight, set among old oaks.

The riding is easy. County roads follow the contours of the ridges, with long, gentle bends, and the surface is good. The traffic is local, and the speeds are low, so this is a ride for looking rather than hurrying. In May, the fields turn bright green and the apple blossom comes out. In autumn, the hills are gold and red, and the air is crisp. The weather can be wet, and in winter, ice and snow make the roads treacherous.

Fuel and food are easy at Askim, a town of twelve thousand, and Spydeberg. Cafés and bakeries in the small centres offer coffee and pastries, and a farm shop on the road may sell vegetables and honey in season. Respect private property, and keep an eye out for farm machinery on the road. If you want to make a day of it, the Glomma has quiet riverside spots for a picnic, and the sound of the water is soothing.
t.atlantic road coastal bridges scenic roa:
Øyeren is the largest inland delta in Europe, or so the Norwegians say, and the pin lies close to its western shore. The lake is a broad, shallow body of water where the Glomma river slows and spreads, and at its southern end, a vast fan of sandbanks, reed beds and channels forms a nature reserve of great importance for birds. Thousands of waders and wildfowl rest here on migration, and a viewing tower at the edge of the reserve gives a good look at them. The landscape is flat, green and wide, a restful kind of beauty.

Nearby, at Fetsund, an old log boom has been preserved as a museum, the last of its kind in Norway. The timber that floated down the Glomma was caught in the boom, sorted by owner and marked with a stamp, then released to the sawmills. The wooden walkways and sorting pens, now quiet, give a good sense of what the work involved. The village is pretty, with a little harbour and a café, and the whole place has a slow, thoughtful pace.

The road is gentle. County routes run along the edge of the lake and through farmland, with long straights and soft bends, and the surface is good. Traffic is light on weekdays, but busier on summer weekends, when families head for the water. The wind off the lake can be fresh, and in winter the shore freezes into ice. In spring and autumn, the migrating birds fill the sky, and the reeds turn gold. It is a lovely end to a ride.

Fuel and food are easy in Fetsund and Lillestrøm, which have stations, shops and cafés. If you are finishing the day here, a stroll on the boardwalks is a good way to wind down. Bring binoculars if you have them, and a jacket for the evening, when the wind picks up and the temperature drops. In midsummer, the light lasts until late, and the sunset over the water is long and slow.
t.sognefjellet high road@59.8,11.4:
Bjørkelangen is a small town in Aurskog-Høland, and it is a perfectly good place to buy fuel and a sandwich. The pin lies at its edge, and the ride that starts here heads for the great mountain roads of the west, a long day's travel away. Aurskog-Høland is a big municipality, mostly forest, with hundreds of lakes, and the town itself has about two and a half thousand people, a few shops, a bank and a bakery.

The district once had its own railway. The Urskog-Hølandsbanen, a narrow-gauge line only seventy-five centimetres wide, ran through the forests from Sørumsand to the east, carrying timber, farm produce and passengers, and it was Norway's last narrow-gauge railway to close, in 1960. A stretch has been preserved as a heritage railway, with small steam locomotives running in summer, and enthusiasts come from around the country. It is a delightful little piece of old Norway, and well worth a look.

Starting a long ride here has some advantages. The roads are quiet, the morning light is soft, and the route to the west avoids the worst of Oslo's traffic. The county roads wind through forest and farmland in easy bends, with occasional hills, and the surface is good. The first hour is a gentle warm-up, a chance to check the bike and settle into the rhythm. Note that moose are active at dawn, so keep your speed down in wooded sections.

As a fuel stop, Bjørkelangen is reliable, but the stations in smaller places may be unmanned, with card-only pumps, so carry a card that works in Norway. Groceries, coffee and snacks are available in the centre. Check the weather forecast for the mountains, since a sunny morning here can turn into rain and cold at the high passes. Pack a warm layer and gloves. From here, the mountain roads feel a long way off, but the day will pass quickly.
t.atlantic road coastal bridges photo pull:
On the morning of 9 April 1940, a German heavy cruiser named Blücher steamed up the Oslofjord toward the capital and met a pair of old guns at Oscarsborg fortress, a few kilometres north of this pin. The shells and torpedoes sank her in the narrows, the invasion force was delayed, and in those hours the King, the government and the gold reserves left Oslo. That is the story hanging over this stretch of water, and it gives the quiet shore near Tofte a weight you do not feel at first glance.

The pin lies on the Hurum peninsula, which pokes south into the fjord between the Drammensfjord and the main Oslofjord, about three kilometres from Tofte, in a landscape of forested ridges, small bays and farmland. The roads wind among the hills, and every few kilometres there is a view across the water to the opposite shore. Holmsbu, a small seaside village of white houses on the west side of the peninsula, has been an artists' colony since the late nineteenth century, and a modest gallery shows the work of painters who came for the light.

Svelvik, across the narrow strait to the north-west, is connected to Hurum by a small cable ferry, one of those quirks of Norwegian geography that make a ride feel like an expedition. The county roads on the peninsula are narrow, with tight bends and short climbs, and the surface can be patchy. Traffic is light apart from summer weekends, when Oslo families head for the beaches. The best light is in the evening, when the sun sinks behind the western hills and the fjord turns silver.

Fuel is available at Tofte and Svelvik, both small towns, and the nearest big stop is Drammen, to the north. Cafés and shops in Tofte are modest but friendly, and a picnic by the water is easy. If you stop for photographs, be careful on the narrow roads, and pull off fully. The sound of the sea, the smell of seaweed and the cry of gulls make a good stop. Bring a jacket, as the wind off the fjord can be cool even in July.
t.telemark canal roads@59.8,10.4:
Lier is where Norwegians go to buy apples, and the pin lies on its edge, near Røyken, a short ride south-west of Asker. The fields here, on the sunny slopes above the Lierdalen valley, are filled with orchards and strawberry plots, and in May the blossom covers the hills in white and pink. Roadside stalls sell fruit, jam and juice through late summer, and it is a gentle landscape of small farms and wooded ridges, a world away from the capital less than an hour's drive off.

The ride that begins here heads for Telemark, and the canal that gives the region its name is worth knowing about. The Telemark Canal, opened in 1892, links the lakes of the interior with the coast by a series of locks, rising and falling over a hundred and five kilometres. At Vrangfoss, five connected locks lift boats up a steep flight, an impressive piece of engineering. The old passenger boat Victoria, built in the nineteenth century, still makes the trip in summer, and the canal route is one of the great slow journeys of Norway.

The road from here goes through Drammen and then south-west, with a varied landscape of forest, farm and fjord. Traffic can be heavy near Oslo, so an early start helps. Further on, the county roads wind through woods and over ridges, with easy bends and moderate climbs, and the surface is good. Cameras are frequent, and speed limits low. Spring and autumn are the best seasons for the ride, with soft light and few tourists.

This is a good place for fuel and food, with Røyken and Asker offering stations, supermarkets and bakeries. Many stations are card-only, so keep a card that works. Check your tyre pressures before the long ride, and pack a rain jacket, as the weather in southern Norway can change quickly. A cinnamon bun and a coffee from a bakery are a fine start, and fruit from a roadside stall is a good snack for the road.
Drammen's party piece is a road that climbs through the inside of a mountain. The Spiralen, a tunnel that winds in a corkscrew through the hill above the town, opened in 1961 and rises about a hundred metres in a little over a kilometre and a half, bringing you out at a viewpoint and restaurant with a view across the city, the river and the fjord. For riders, it is a delightful curiosity, and the sensation of leaning around the spiral under a rock ceiling is unlike anything else in the country.

The pin lies close to the town centre, a few kilometres from the tunnel. Drammen grew up as a timber port, where the Drammenselva river, laden with logs from the forests of the interior, reaches the fjord, and the old merchants' houses and warehouses along the river are a reminder of the wealth that timber brought. In recent decades the town has been transformed, with a new riverside promenade, a modern bridge and a lively arts scene. It has about ninety thousand people, making it the biggest town in the region.

For riding, the tunnel is the highlight, but the roads around the town are also pleasant. The old road along the river climbs through forest, with moderate bends and views of the water. Traffic can be heavy in town, particularly in the morning and evening, so plan your times. Tolls apply on some roads around Drammen, and the system is automatic, so check how it works for rental or foreign vehicles before you travel.

Fuel is plentiful in Drammen, and the choice of cafés and restaurants is wide. At the top of the Spiral, the viewpoint offers coffee and a little history of the project. Ride carefully in the tunnel, where the surface can be damp and the bends are tight, and watch for pedestrians at the top. In clear weather, the view across the roofs to the fjord is fine, and in the evening the lights of the town come on, one by one.
t.sognefjellet high road scenic road@59.5,:
Moss is a small town with a big footnote. In August 1814, after Norway's brief attempt at independence, representatives of the Norwegian government and the Swedish crown met at a manor house here and signed the Convention of Moss, which allowed Norway to keep its constitution in a union with Sweden. It was a compromise that shaped the country for ninety years, and the town still bears the stamp of that moment. The pin sits close to Moss, on the east shore of the Oslofjord.

Moss is also a place of iron and water. The ironworks, founded in the early eighteenth century, once made cannon and stoves, and the old industrial buildings along the river have been turned into cafés and galleries. Jeløya, a green island just off the town, is connected by a short causeway and has beaches, woods and a small art gallery in a fine old house. Tofte and Vestby, nearby, offer more places to eat. A car ferry crosses the fjord to Horten, a convenient shortcut.

The riding along the east shore is relaxed. The old coast road, with gentle bends, passes farms and villages, with glimpses of the fjord. The surface is good, and traffic is moderate. The main hazards are the cyclists and the weekend traffic heading for the beaches. The best time is early evening, when the sun lights up the water and the sailboats return. In autumn, the light is soft and golden.

Fuel is easy in Moss, a town of over thirty thousand, with many stations, and the cafés are good. Parking at Jeløya can be busy in summer, so arrive early. Bring a swimsuit if the weather is warm, since the beaches are pleasant. The water is cold in June but warms by August. A walk on the shore at sunset, with the lights of the town reflected in the water, makes a fine end to a day.
t.sognefjellet high road high point@59.4,1:
Rygge was an air base before it was a commercial airport, and it was a commercial airport before it was nothing at all. For a few years, from 2007 to 2016, budget flights from Moss Airport Rygge took off from the runway just north of this pin, and then the airline pulled out and the runway fell quiet. The surroundings are low farmland, with big skies and long straight roads, in a part of Østfold where the highest point is a modest swell in the clay plain.

The district is a mix of farm and forest, with Lake Vansjø close by, one of the main water supplies for the region and a good place for a swim or a paddle. Karlshus and Ryggebyen are small communities with a few shops, a church and a school. The soil is rich clay, and the fields grow grain and vegetables, with large barns and farms spread across the plain. Autumn brings the harvest, and the air is full of the smell of straw and diesel.

For riding, the roads are flat, straight and quiet, with long views and few bends. The county roads link the villages, and the surface is generally good. Wind can be strong across the open land, and in winter, ice can form on the shaded stretches. The attraction here is not the road but the space, and a long day's ride can end with a feeling of calm. Speed limits are low, and cameras are frequent.

Fuel is available at Rygge and Moss, and shops in the villages sell groceries. Cafés are few, so plan your stops. The lake offers a pleasant picnic spot, with grassy banks and a view of the water. If you wish to swim, look for the public beaches, which are marked on local maps. Bring a warm layer for the evening, since the plain can be cool. The sunsets over the fields are long and soft.
t.hardanger fjord and waterfalls high poin:
Askim is a town that Norwegians associate with wellies. The rubber boot factory here, founded in the 1920s and still going under the name Viking, turned out the green and black boots that every farm, fishing boat and school playground in the country seems to own, and the town's sense of itself is tied up with the smell of vulcanised rubber. The pin lies just outside Askim, on a low rise above the Glomma river, and the label calls it a high point, which is generous. The rise is a few dozen metres at most, but the view across the river valley is good.

The Glomma is the longest river in Norway, running some six hundred kilometres from the mountains near the Swedish border to the sea at Fredrikstad, and at Askim it is broad, brown and slow, with wooded banks and the occasional island. The water has been a trade route for centuries, and in the days of timber floating, thousands of logs would come down in the spring flood, jostling in the current. Today the river is used by canoeists and anglers, and a path along the bank is popular with walkers.

Riding here is quiet and easy. County roads run along the river and over low ridges, with gentle bends and a smooth surface, and in the evenings the traffic is thin. The surrounding landscape is farmland, with red barns, white houses and fields of grain, and in autumn the oaks along the roadside turn gold. In winter, the roads can be icy, and the short days limit the riding.

For fuel and food, Askim is the best choice, a town of twelve thousand with several stations, supermarkets and cafés. Mysen and Spydeberg are close, with smaller choices. The river is cold for swimming even in July, but a paddle on a warm day is refreshing. Keep a towel and some water on the bike, and watch for farm vehicles on the narrow roads. A walk along the riverbank at dusk, as the light fades over the water, is a small reward.
t.hardanger fjord and waterfalls scenic ro:
Spydeberg is a village of three thousand people on the Glomma, and the pin lies a few kilometres to the north, among fields and woods that slope gently toward the river. It is a place where the Norwegian lowlands show their most domestic side, with red-painted barns, apple trees in the gardens and a church on a low hill that has watched the valley for centuries. The scenic road in question is a quiet county route, the sort of lane that most travellers never notice, and its charm lies in its ordinariness.

The river was the lifeblood of the district. Sawmills lined its banks, and the logs that floated down in spring were guided through channels and booms to the mills, where they were cut into planks and shipped abroad. The old mill buildings have mostly gone, but traces remain, in a stone foundation here or a rusted wheel there. The valley also produced a good deal of brick from the clay deposits along the river, and brickworks were an important industry until the mid-twentieth century.

The riding is gentle, with long, easy bends and an unhurried rhythm. Traffic is light, mostly local, and the surface is good. In the evening, when the sun sinks behind the trees, the light falls across the fields in long bars, and the whole valley glows. The road crosses the river by an old bridge in places, and the sound of water under the wheels is pleasant. In spring, the meltwater makes the river high and fast, and the banks are green.

Fuel is available at Spydeberg and Askim, and small shops offer groceries and coffee. This stop is marked as a swim and a finish, and the river offers a few quiet spots for a dip, though the water is cold and the current can be strong in spring. Choose a calm backwater, and keep an eye on the weather. Carry a towel and a warm layer, since the air cools quickly in the evening. The calm here is a good way to end a day.
t.torra bay@-20.3,13.3:
Torra Bay is a patch of gravel at the edge of the cold Atlantic, and it is one of the loneliest places a motorcyclist is likely to go. On the Skeleton Coast of northern Namibia, the Namib desert runs straight into the sea, and the shore is a line of grey waves, yellow dunes and a horizon that looks as if it has nothing behind it. The cold Benguela current, running up from the south, chills the air above it, and fog rolls in from the water most mornings, so the desert here is damp, cool and strangely quiet.

The campsite at Torra Bay is open only for a few weeks around the Christmas holidays, when Namibian families come to fish for kob and sleep in tents on the sand, and for the rest of the year it is closed. Entry to the Skeleton Coast National Park requires a permit, and you pass through a gate along the road, so plan ahead. The park is named for the whale bones and ship wrecks along the shore, where sailors were washed up, and the hulks of rusted vessels still lie on the beach in places.

The road, the C34, is a salt road, a hard-packed surface made from gravel and salt crust, which is smooth when dry and slick when damp with fog. It runs north from Swakopmund and Henties Bay, with the sea on one side and bare dunes or gravel plains on the other, and the visibility can drop in an instant. The riding is simple but demands attention, because of sand drifts, soft patches and the risk of a long fall. Carry tools, spare tubes, a tyre pump and plenty of water, and tell someone your plan.

There are no dependable services at Torra Bay. Fuel is available at Henties Bay, which is the last reliable place, and at Terrace Bay, farther north, but not everywhere or at all times, so carry extra if you can. Cape fur seals breed on the rocks, and jackals and hyenas patrol the beaches, while the dunes hold lizards and beetles that drink from the fog. Wind is constant and can blow sand across the road. In the evening, the sunset over the sea is huge, and the stars at night are among the best in the world. The silence is complete, which is both the beauty and the danger of the place.
t.hannagan meadow@33.6,-109.3:
Hannagan Meadow is a clearing in the high forest of eastern Arizona, at about nine thousand feet, and it feels more like Colorado or Montana than the desert state of popular imagination. Tall ponderosa pines, Douglas firs and aspens crowd around a wide, grassy meadow that is green in summer and white in winter, and the air smells of pine and cold earth. The road runs right past, and a small lodge and a few cabins stand at the edge of the trees.

The road is the Coronado Trail, US 191, which crosses the Mogollon Rim country from Springerville in the north to Clifton in the south, and has a reputation as one of the twistiest highways in the country. It climbs and drops through the Apache-Sitgreaves National Forests with hundreds of bends in a little over a hundred miles, and the old name, US 666, earned it the nickname of the Devil's Highway until the number was changed in 2003. The trail is named after the Spanish explorer Francisco Vázquez de Coronado, who passed through the region in 1540 while searching for the fabled cities of gold, though historians doubt that he followed this exact route.

Wildlife is abundant. Elk graze in the meadow at dawn and dusk, and their bugling in autumn is a haunting sound. Black bears, mule deer, wild turkeys and bald eagles live in the forest, and in the evening you may see animals at the road's edge, so ride carefully. The weather is changeable: snow can fall as early as October and as late as May, and storms build quickly in summer afternoons, with lightning on the high ridges. Temperatures at this height are cool even in July.

There is very little in the way of services. The lodge may offer meals and accommodation in season, but check ahead, and do not count on fuel anywhere near. Alpine, about thirty-five kilometres to the north, and Clifton, much further south, are the places to fill the tank, and the long stretch between them is the reason to carry water and a spare layer. Phone signal is patchy.

Stop and look at the meadow if elk are out, switch off the engine and wait. It is one of the quietest places on the whole road.
t.alpine arizona@33.8,-109.1:
Alpine is a mountain town that most Arizonans have never seen. It lies at about eight thousand feet in the White Mountains, a few miles from the New Mexico line, in a valley of meadows ringed by pine forest and with the long dome of Escudilla Mountain standing guard to the north. Winters are cold and snowy, summers are cool and green, and the town of a few hundred people feels like a ranching village in the northern Rockies that took a wrong turn south.

Its history is cattle and timber. Settlers came in the late nineteenth century to graze livestock on the high grasslands, and families have worked the land since, with cattle still wandering the verges and horses in the fields. Escudilla, one of the highest peaks in Arizona, inspired the conservationist Aldo Leopold, who wrote about it in his essays on the wilderness and its grizzly bear, killed in 1911, the last of its kind in the state. The mountain is now part of a wilderness area, and its rounded summit is a good landmark on a clear day.

Alpine marks the northern end of a famous road. US 191, the Coronado Trail, runs south from Springerville through the national forest to Clifton and is celebrated for hundreds of twists and turns, but the stretch near Alpine is gentler, running through open meadows and aspen groves with long views. Surfaces are mostly good, but frost heaves, loose gravel and elk on the road are all possible, so keep your speed within sight distance, especially at dawn and dusk. Weather changes rapidly, with afternoon thunderstorms in July and August, and snow from late autumn. September and early October are especially pleasant, when the aspens turn gold and the air is crisp.

Alpine has the basics a rider needs: a petrol station, a couple of small stores and cafés, a few motels and cabins, and a diner that serves big breakfasts. Eagar and Springerville, about thirty kilometres north, have larger supermarkets and more choices. South of town there is little for a long way, so fill the tank here and check your reserves. Carry water and a warm layer, and be prepared for patchy phone signal.

Stand outside in the evening and listen. At this height the sky gets dark and the stars come out in numbers that city riders never see.
t.admiral s bridge@38.1,13.4:
The Ponte dell'Ammiraglio is an old bridge that has lost its river. It was built in 1131 by George of Antioch, the admiral of the Norman king Roger II of Sicily, a Greek Christian from Syria who rose to be the most powerful man in the kingdom, and it spans the Oreto, whose course has since been diverted, leaving the bridge standing over a dry bed among modern roads. Even so, its pointed arches, built of pale stone, are a fine example of the Arab-Norman style that flourished in Sicily, and it forms part of the UNESCO listing of Arab-Norman Palermo and the cathedrals of Cefalù and Monreale, inscribed in 2015.

The setting is unglamorous, with traffic roaring around it and a small fenced area from which it is viewed, but the blend of cultures it represents is the real story of Sicily: Arab, Byzantine and Norman craftsmen working together, with Islamic geometry, Greek mosaics and Latin churches side by side. The nearby suburb of Ciaculli is known for its late mandarins, which ripen after Christmas and are prized in Sicily.

Palermo is not an easy city for riders. The traffic is dense and improvisational, with scooters, cars and pedestrians crossing in a flow, and the old streets are narrow. Take a deep breath, ride defensively and accept that the horn is a form of conversation. Outside the city, the roads climb into the hills with views over the Conca d'Oro, the golden shell of lemon and orange groves that once surrounded the city. The long run across the island to Villa Romana del Casale takes you through the high inland plateau, with wheat fields that turn from green to gold.

The villa at Piazza Armerina holds some of the finest Roman mosaics in the world, from the fourth century, including the famous scene of women in bikini-like costumes. Fuel is easy in Palermo and on the main roads, but fill the tank before heading inland. Summer heat is intense, with the scirocco wind bringing African dust, so go in spring or autumn. Eat arancini, the fried rice balls, or pasta con le sarde, and finish with a cannolo.
t.valletta@35.9,14.5:
Valletta is smaller than most people expect, a city on a peninsula, built on a grid and finished almost in one go. It is named for Jean de Valette, the Grand Master of the Knights of St John, who led the defence of Malta during the Great Siege of 1565, when an Ottoman fleet landed and fought for months before withdrawing. Afterwards the Knights decided to build a new fortified capital on the bare ridge between two deep harbours, and construction began in 1566. The streets run straight, sloping down to the water in steps, and bastions rise from the sea. The whole city is on the UNESCO list, and it was a European Capital of Culture in 2018.

The big sight is St John's Co-Cathedral, plain outside and extravagant inside, with gilded walls, a marble floor of tombstones and a pair of paintings by Caravaggio, including his huge Beheading of Saint John the Baptist. It is the only painting he is known to have signed. The Upper Barrakka Gardens look across the Grand Harbour to the Three Cities, and a salute gun fires at noon and four in the afternoon. The view of the fortifications and the harbour is one of the best in the Mediterranean.

Driving in Malta is on the left, a legacy of British rule, and the roads can be chaotic. Valletta itself is largely traffic-restricted, so park outside the gates, in Floriana, which has plenty of space. Heading out, the island is small, and roads are busy and narrow, with stone walls on both sides. Cars squeeze through tight bends and buses do not give way. The coast has quieter stretches, and the cliffs at Dingli, in the southwest, are a good place for sunset.

Fuel is easy to find in Floriana and on the main roads. Food is a mix of Sicilian, Arab and English influence, with pastizzi, savoury pastries filled with ricotta or peas, sold for small change in every street. Rabbit stew is the national dish. The ferry to Sicily runs from near Valletta to Pozzallo, and it is the route for riders heading on to the Val di Noto and its Baroque towns. Spring and autumn are the most comfortable seasons.
t.malmo@55.6,13.0:
Malmo faces Copenhagen across the water, and for most of its history it was the second city of the Danish kingdom. Skane, the southern province of Sweden, belonged to Denmark until 1658, and the old centre of Malmo, with its big square, its brick Gothic church of St Peter and its castle, still has a faintly Danish look. In the twentieth century, the city built ships and cars, and when the shipyards closed in the 1980s it fell into a slump. The comeback has been spectacular. Old docks became housing and parkland, and the Turning Torso, a twisting skyscraper by the Spanish architect Santiago Calatrava, finished in 2005, now stands as the city's emblem.

The Oresund Bridge, opened in 2000, links the city to Denmark by a road and rail connection about sixteen kilometres long, with a bridge on the Swedish side, an artificial island, and a tunnel on the Danish side. Crossing it on a motorcycle is a memorable ride, with the sea stretching out on both sides and the wind pushing at the bike. Tolls are charged, and motorcycles pay less than cars. The crossing takes ten minutes, and on the Danish side the road leads on to Copenhagen, and the chalk cliffs of Stevns Klint, a UNESCO site, further south.

Riding in Malmo itself is easy. The city is flat, with cycle lanes, and drivers are polite. Swedish law requires headlights on at all times, which motorcycles do anyway, and speed limits are enforced by cameras. Fuel is available throughout the city, and Arlov, a suburb just to the north, has stations on the main road. The countryside of Skane is open and agricultural, with large fields, white churches and old estates, and roads that run straight and gentle, with sharp wind from the Baltic or the Oresund.

The food scene is lively and international, with a large Middle Eastern community, and falafel is a local obsession, along with excellent cardamom buns. The Saluhall market, near the canal, has stalls selling everything from smoked fish to pastries. Little Torg, a cobbled square, is a nice place to sit with a coffee. The best season is from May to September, when evenings stay bright until late. Winter is dark, damp and windy.
t.kairouan@35.7,10.1:
Kairouan is the fourth holy city of Islam, after Mecca, Medina and Jerusalem, and that makes it unusual in Tunisia, which otherwise has a relaxed Mediterranean air. It was founded in 670 by the Arab general Uqba ibn Nafi as a military base in the heart of the plains, far from the coast and the Byzantine fleets, and it became the first Islamic capital of the Maghreb. The Great Mosque, also called the Mosque of Uqba, dates from that early period and was rebuilt in the ninth century. It has a huge courtyard surrounded by arcades, a three-storey minaret and a prayer hall with hundreds of columns, many taken from Roman and Byzantine ruins. The old city is a UNESCO site.

The medina, enclosed by brown walls, is a warren of lanes, with whitewashed houses and blue doors, and the carpet shops are among the best in the country. Kairouan carpets, woven from wool in rich reds and blues, are famous. The city is also known for makroudh, a pastry of semolina and dates fried in oil and soaked in honey, which is sold in every corner shop and is best eaten warm. Another sight is the Aghlabid Basins, a pair of huge circular reservoirs from the ninth century, built to store water for the city.

The landscape is dry, with steppe, olive groves and low hills, and the colour of the earth is soft brown and ochre. Around Kairouan, the road runs straight and fast across flat country, with sheep and the occasional camel by the verge. Trucks are many, and the roads are in decent condition, though sometimes uneven. Summer heat is fierce, with temperatures over forty degrees, and the best seasons for riding are spring and autumn.

The ride to El Jem, about sixty kilometres to the east, leads to one of the great monuments of the Roman world. The amphitheatre there, built in the third century, held thousands of spectators, and it still stands to its third tier, with underground chambers where the animals and gladiators waited. It is among the best-preserved Roman amphitheatres in existence, and its walls glow golden in the evening.

Kairouan has fuel stations, restaurants and a few small hotels in the old town. Sidi el Hani, nineteen kilometres away, is a small town. Try grilled lamb, and drink mint tea in a courtyard of the old city. Dress modestly, and non-Muslims can see the mosque courtyard but not usually the prayer hall.
t.nonnebakken@55.4,10.4:
Nonnebakken is a modest mound in the suburbs of Odense, easy to miss and worth finding. In the late tenth century, in the time of Harald Bluetooth, the Danish king ordered the building of a group of circular fortresses, each laid out with a ring rampart and gates facing the four directions, and the one at Nonnebakken is the Funen member of that family. Its name means the nuns' hill, which probably refers to a later medieval convent on the spot, and the earthwork lies in a residential area, so you will be walking among houses, gardens and quiet streets rather than open countryside.

The site was excavated in the 1950s, and archaeologists found the outline of the fortress, together with the post holes of houses laid out in a precise pattern. Like Fyrkat in Jutland and Trelleborg on Zealand, the fortress belongs to a period when the Danish kingdom was consolidating its power and converting to Christianity, which is why the nearby Jelling mounds, with the runestones that Harald raised, form part of the same story. There is not a great deal to see on the ground, because the original timber structures have long gone, but information boards and the shape of the ground tell the tale if you slow down.

For a rider, Funen is a good place to be. The island is Denmark's garden, with orchards, farms and thatched villages, and the roads are smooth, narrow and well maintained. Corners are gentle, with the surprise of a hill now and then, and the sea is never far away, so every few kilometres brings a view across a fjord or a bay. Enforcement of speed limits is strict. The big Great Belt Bridge, a toll crossing, lies to the east and links Funen to Zealand, and the Little Belt Bridge links it to Jutland.

Odense, with about a hundred and forty-six thousand inhabitants, is a proper city, so fuel and food are not a worry. Seden and Neder Holluf are suburbs with supermarkets and stations. The best time to visit the mound is in the morning when the city is quiet and the grass is wet with dew. In spring the local gardens are full of blossom, and in summer the long evening light lasts until almost eleven. It is a small place, but it connects you to a large story.
t.odense@55.4,10.4:
Odense is best known as the birthplace of Hans Christian Andersen, born in 1805 in a poor part of town, and his story is the thread that runs through the place. The museum dedicated to him occupies several old houses in the centre of the old quarter, with yellow walls and cobbled lanes that have been tidied to look like a fairy-tale street. The tales, which include The Little Mermaid and The Ugly Duckling, were written long after he left, but the city has made a very good job of claiming him. The town's name goes back to the Viking age, and it means Odin's shrine, which tells you how old the settlement is.

Odense is the main city of Funen, Denmark's third largest island, and the place has a lively, student-filled atmosphere, with cyclists everywhere and a long river called the Odense Å running through green parks. The Funen Village, an open-air museum of old farm buildings, is a short ride from the centre and gives a good idea of rural life in earlier centuries. The city also has a reputation for music and for being friendly and unpretentious, a quality Danes call hygge, though they would never say so about themselves.

Riding in Funen is easy and pleasant. The roads are flat to gently rolling, with a good surface and clear signs, and they pass through small villages with thatched roofs, orchards and beech woods. There are few challenging corners, but plenty of pleasant ones, and the scenery changes constantly between farmland and coast. The ride toward Christiansfeld crosses the Little Belt Bridge into Jutland, and the Moravian Church town is a neat grid of yellow brick houses founded in 1773, now a World Heritage site. Be careful with speed limits and cameras, since fines in Denmark are high.

As a city of nearly a hundred and fifty thousand people, Odense has fuel stations on every main road and many places for coffee and pastries. The morning rush hour is busy but short, and the evenings are calm. The air in the old town smells of bakeries and wet cobbles, and in summer there is music in the squares. If you start here with a full tank and a good breakfast, the island rewards you at once.
t.sognefjellet@59.8,11.4:
Sognefjellet itself is a long way from here, up in the mountains between Lom and Skjolden, and this finish point is not on it. At these coordinates you are in the forested lowlands east of Oslo, in Akershus, with Bjørkelangen, Aursmoen and Flateby around you and Fetsund, on the big river, a little way off. It is calm farm country, a patchwork of fields cut into dark spruce, with small lakes and red barns, and it is where a long mountain ride can wind down gently.

The real Sognefjellet road, riksvei 55, is worth knowing about for the contrast. It reaches about 1,434 metres and is the highest mountain road in Northern Europe, crossing a bare plateau of snow patches, black tarns and glacier-ground rock beside the Jotunheimen range. It closes in winter and opens in late spring depending on the snow, so a ride that includes it is a summer ride. Coming back down to the lowlands afterwards, you feel the air thicken and warm, and the smell changes from cold stone to resin and cut grass.

Near here the great river Glomma slows and widens toward the sea, and at Fetsund there is a museum dedicated to the log floating that once carried timber from the mountains to the mills. For centuries that river was a road made of wood, and the whole economy of this part of the country depended on it. You can still see the old booms and wooden structures, and the story of how the logs were sorted and tied is well told.

The riding in this part of the country is gentle. Roads are quiet, well surfaced, and run through woods where elk are a real hazard at dusk and dawn, so keep your speed down when the light fades. Villages are small and sleepy, and a petrol station may be a stretch of kilometres away, so fill up in Fetsund or the larger towns before you commit to the back lanes. Coffee and a bun in a local bakery is the correct conclusion.
t.zisa palace@38.1,13.3:
The Zisa is a Norman palace in Palermo that looks Arab, and that is the whole point. Begun around 1165 under King William I and finished by his son, William II, it was built as a summer pleasure house outside the city walls, set in a walled park with pools and orchards that has long since vanished. The name comes from the Arabic al-Aziz, meaning the splendid, and the building is a tall, severe block of golden stone with blind arches and a long inscription in Arabic script, designed by craftsmen from across the Mediterranean working for Christian kings. It is part of the Arab-Norman Palermo group that UNESCO listed in 2015.

Inside, the ground-floor hall is the best part. In it, a fountain used to run down a marble channel into a pool in the middle of the room, and the ceiling is a vault of honeycomb stalactites, called muqarnas, a design brought from the Islamic world. The idea was to keep the room cool, since water, shade and moving air were the original air conditioning in a Sicilian summer. Today the palace houses a museum of Islamic art, which is quiet and rewarding.

Riding in Palermo is its own adventure. Traffic is dense, drivers take liberties with lanes and signals, and the old streets are narrow, cobbled and often full of parked cars. Scooters are everywhere. A bike is more practical than a car, but you need alertness and patience, and you should avoid the central zones with restricted access. Outside the city, the road to Monreale climbs in a few bends through hillside suburbs to the cathedral with its golden mosaics, and beyond lies a beautiful countryside of olives, vineyards and stony hills.

The Zisa is about two kilometres from the centre, in a residential district, and there is parking in the streets around it. With some 650,000 people, Palermo has fuel stations on every ring road and countless cafés. Stop for a granita with a brioche, the Sicilian breakfast, or for arancine, fried rice balls with fillings of meat or butter and peas. The heat of midday is severe in summer, so go early and take shelter in the shade of the palace.
San Giovanni degli Eremiti is the church with the red domes, five of them, a cluster of small hemispheres painted the colour of a terracotta pot, and they make it one of the most recognisable buildings in Palermo. King Roger II built it in 1132, on the site of an older building that is thought to have been a mosque, and gave it to a community of monks following the rule of Saint Benedict. The domes show a clear Arab influence, and the plan is simple, with a nave, two small chapels and a square bell tower. After the Norman period it fell into ruin, and was restored in the late nineteenth century to its present form, with the domes reopened to the sky.

The best part is the cloister, a small garden of columns in pairs, with pointed arches and a tangle of vines, citrus trees, palms and roses around a well. It is a calm, scented place, hidden behind busy streets, where the noise of the city fades, and lizards sun themselves on the stones. In the garden, you can see traces of the earlier Islamic building, including a small cistern or bath. It is a place that rewards slowness.

You are close to the Norman Palace and the old centre of Palermo, in streets that are narrow, one-way and often crowded, so getting here by bike is a matter of patience. Parking near the church is limited, and the better strategy is to leave the bike in a garage or car park outside the restricted zone, then walk. Thieves target scooters and bikes, so use a strong lock and do not leave anything on the seat. The summer heat can be fierce, with a hot wind from Africa called the scirocco, and spring and autumn are more pleasant.

Palermo is a city of over 600,000 people and has fuel stations on the main roads outside the centre, and endless places to eat in the streets around. Try a sfincione, a thick, spongy Sicilian pizza with onions and breadcrumbs, from a street seller, or a cannolo filled with fresh ricotta. Prices are low and portions are generous, and the people are famously talkative. Spend an hour in the cloister before you go.
t.church of santa maria dell ammiraglio@38:
Santa Maria dell'Ammiraglio, known to everyone in Palermo as La Martorana, is a Norman church of the twelfth century that was founded in 1143 by George of Antioch, the admiral who served King Roger II. George was a Greek Christian from Syria, who had risen through the Arab administration of North Africa before moving to Sicily, and the church shows his taste, with Byzantine mosaics, Arabic inscriptions and a Norman bell tower.
