It was one of the first monuments of the Arab-Norman style, and is on the UNESCO list.

The interior is a small jewel box of gold. Christ Pantocrator looks down from the dome, surrounded by angels, and the mosaics also show the admiral himself kneeling before the Virgin Mary and Roger II being crowned by Christ, a striking portrait of how power was understood. The church was later altered in the baroque period, and some of the mosaics are lost, but the early ones are among the finest in Sicily. The name Martorana comes from a nearby convent, founded by a noblewoman, whose nuns gave the church its popular name.

The nuns also gave Sicily a sweet, frutta martorana, marzipan shaped and painted to look like real fruit, in bright colours. They are sold in pastry shops across Palermo, especially around the Day of the Dead on 2 November, when children are told that the dead leave gifts, and they look so real that people bite into them by mistake. A small bag of them makes a good gift.

The church stands on Piazza Bellini in the old centre, next to the Teatro Massimo and a street of cafés, and getting there by bike is not easy. The lanes are tight, the traffic is intense, and parking is scarce, so leave the bike in a garage and walk. Fuel stations are on the outer roads, not in the centre. The church often closes at lunchtime, and dress rules apply, with knees and shoulders covered. Come in the morning, when the light enters the dome and the golden mosaics seem to move.
t.royal palace and palatine chapel@38.1,13:
The Palazzo dei Normanni, the Norman Palace, is the oldest royal residence in Europe, and it has been continuously in use for about a thousand years. The Arabs built a fortress on this rise above Palermo, and the Norman kings of the twelfth century made it their palace, adding towers, halls and a chapel. After them it passed to the Hohenstaufen emperor Frederick II, who held a court of poets, scientists and translators here, and the early Italian lyric is said to have started in this circle. Today the Sicilian Regional Assembly meets in the building, which makes it a working parliament as well as a monument.

The Palatine Chapel, inside, is the wonder. Roger II had it built in 1130, and its walls and dome are covered with golden mosaics showing scenes from the Old and New Testaments, in a Byzantine style, while the ceiling is a carved and painted wooden honeycomb in an Arab style, with scenes of feasting and hunting. The marble floor and columns are Roman and Norman, and a mosaic of Christ looks down from the apse. It is the combination of three cultures under a single roof, Latin, Greek and Arab, that gives it its unique feel, and almost everyone falls silent when they step inside.

Getting here means threading through the old city. The palace stands at the top of the Cassaro, the old main street, beside the Porta Nuova gate, and the traffic around it is fast and chaotic, with buses, scooters and tourist coaches. Cobbles can be slick after rain. Parking a bike near the palace is hard, so leave it in a car park or garage and walk up. The rest of the city, including the market at Ballarò, is within walking distance. Beyond the walls, the hill road to Monreale starts almost at the palace gate and climbs in a few tight bends.

Fuel stations are outside the centre, on the ring road and along the main avenues, and Palermo has no lack of food. Try a panino con la milza, a sandwich of spleen, the local street food, or a slice of cassata, a sweet ricotta cake covered with marzipan and candied fruit. Queues for the chapel can be long, so arrive early, and check opening times because they vary with services.
t.monreale cathedral@38.1,13.3:
Monreale sits on the slope of Monte Caputo, a few kilometres above Palermo, and on a clear day you can see the whole Conca d'Oro basin laid out below you, with the city and its harbour at the far end. The Normans put a king's ambition up here in the 1170s: William II built a cathedral meant to rival anything in Palermo and, not incidentally, to tweak the archbishop down in the city. Inside, the walls are covered in gold mosaic, thousands of square metres of it, with a huge Christ Pantocrator filling the apse. Byzantine craftsmen did the work, and the whole story of the Bible runs around the nave like a very slow comic strip. Go in with your helmet in hand and nothing else on your mind.

The cloister next door is the quieter treat. Its paired columns, each pair carved differently, some with mosaic inlay, are a lesson in how Norman Sicily borrowed from everybody: Arab geometry, Romanesque capitals, Byzantine gold. There is a fountain in one corner shaped like a palm-column that rarely gets a photo, and it deserves one.

Getting here is the riding part. From Palermo you climb on a road that tightens into a handful of hairpins before the old town, and the traffic is the usual Sicilian negotiation, so keep your elbows in and your mirrors honest. The streets around the cathedral are narrow and steep, parking is tight, and a bike is far easier to leave than a car. Monreale is a proper town of about twenty-two thousand people, so fuel, coffee and a sandwich are all within a few minutes, and the little shops around the square sell the local bread and sweets. Come early or late; mid-morning in season the tour buses arrive together and the nave fills.

The ride from here heads inland and south toward the Roman mosaics near Piazza Armerina, a long day through wheat hills that turn from green to straw-gold as the year goes on. Spring is lovely and autumn is gentle; July on the interior roads is a hot, dry, shadeless affair. Drink water before you leave, because the best views of the gulf are the ones you stop for.
t.church of san cataldo@38.1,13.4:
San Cataldo is small, red-domed and slightly absurd, which is exactly why people love it. Three bare crimson cupolas sit on top of a square stone block, squeezed onto Piazza Bellini beside the Martorana church and a bit of Roman-era wall, in the middle of Palermo's old centre. It was built in the 1150s for Maio of Bari, an admiral and chancellor under King William I, and then promptly left unfinished when Maio was murdered a few years later. The inside has never had its mosaics, so the floor is the decoration: an inlaid marble pavement worn soft by nine centuries of feet. It is plain, and it is calm, and after the baroque excess elsewhere in the city that matters.

The church is one of the Arab-Norman monuments the city has grouped under UNESCO, and the logic is easy to see. The cubic body and the domes echo Fatimid architecture, the blind arcades are Norman, the planning is Byzantine. A cosmopolitan court built this, and it made no effort to hide it.

Now the honest bit about riding here. Palermo is a city of roughly six hundred and fifty thousand, with scooters, double parking, one-way streets that change character block by block, and a restricted traffic zone through much of the centre. The cathedral and Quattro Canti are a short walk, and a motorbike is the right tool for the job: you can slide into a space a car would circle for forty minutes. Park outside the tightest streets, lock the bike properly, and walk. Fuel is no issue, there are stations on the ring roads and the coast road toward Mondello. Eat standing up if you can: arancine, panelle in a bun, sfincione from a bakery, a granita with a brioche if it is hot.

The ride on from here crosses the island to the Roman villa at Casale, a long day that begins in this tangle and ends in quiet farmland. Leave the city before the midday heat and before the school run, and you will be on open road within the hour.
t.archaeological site@36.9,11.1:
The Cap Bon peninsula is where Tunisia stretches a thin arm toward Sicily, only about a hundred and forty kilometres of water away, and this stretch of its north-east coast is the quietest part. Close to here lies Kerkuane, the only Punic town in the Mediterranean we know to have been abandoned rather than built over. It was probably taken by Roman forces around the middle of the third century BC, in the First Punic War, and nobody came back, so what you see is a Carthaginian town frozen in a street plan: walled blocks, a grid of lanes, courtyards, wells and, remarkably, houses with their own bathrooms and hip baths.

The archaeologists were happiest about the plaster floors and the purple. Kerkuane's people made dye from murex shells, and a mound of broken shells beside the site makes that real. The place was only identified in 1952, and UNESCO listed it in 1985. There is a small museum, good for context, and a sea breeze that is welcome in summer, when the stone gives back a lot of heat.

The riding is gentle and rural. The coast road from Kélibia, eleven kilometres south, runs through olive groves, vineyards and low scrub, with the sea flashing between the pines and a surface that varies from good to patchy. Kélibia is a proper town of over forty thousand, with a hilltop fortress, a harbour full of fishing boats and a decent supply of fuel, cafes and fresh fish. El Haouaria at the tip is the other nearby base and has its own character, with falconry and a quarry coast. Do not count on fuel out in the villages between them; fill in Kélibia.

The ride goes on to Tunis and its medina, about two hours by motorway and main road, so an early start is sensible. Spring and autumn are best, when the light is clear and the maquis smells of herbs. In July and August the heat can be fierce by midday, and the afternoon wind off the sea is steady enough to push a bike around.
t.arab norman palermo and the cathedral ch:
Palermo is the city where a kingdom learned to speak three languages at once, and the Arab-Norman buildings scattered through it are the proof. When Roger II was crowned in 1130 he ruled a realm that mixed Norman knights, Greek administrators and Arab scholars, and his court employed all of them. The geographer al-Idrisi drew a famous map of the world for him, oriented with south at the top. The buildings reflect that mix: the Palatine Chapel in the Norman Palace, with its gold mosaics and painted wooden ceiling in an Islamic honeycomb style; the Zisa and Cuba pleasure palaces; and the Admiral's Bridge, a pointed-arch span over a river that has since vanished.

The group of monuments, which includes the cathedrals at Cefalù and Monreale, was listed by UNESCO in 2015. Between them they show something rarer than any single masterpiece, a society that borrowed and blended on purpose, and for a while made it work.

As a place to start a ride, Palermo is a lively, frustrating, wonderful city. Traffic is fast and improvisational, scooters thread through everything, and the one-way streets of the old centre will confuse a navigator. Cars are parked on pavements, and a motorbike is the sensible vehicle, but never leave luggage on it. The ring road and the A19 motorway are quick escape routes toward the interior, and there are plenty of fuel stations around the edge of the city. Inside the centre it is better to park and walk, ideally somewhere with a guard or a locking post.

Eat on the street: the pani ca meusa sandwich is not for everyone, but panelle and crocchette in bread are, and a cannolo made to order from a good pastry shop is a small revelation. The ride that starts from here runs toward Villa Romana del Casale, across the island's dry interior. Leave early. The light on the hills outside Palermo in the morning is gentle, and by noon in summer the same hills are an oven.
t.necropolis@37.0,11.1:
The necropolis at Kerkuane lies on the same flat, sea-fringed shelf as the Punic town, a short walk from it, and it is a different kind of visit: quieter, odder and more personal. The Carthaginians who lived here buried their dead in rock-cut tombs, some with painted plaster, with offerings of pottery and small objects. The tombs were found outside the walls, as the Punic custom was, and while the best finds have gone to museums, the site still gives a very direct sense of how close daily life and death were in this small coastal city.

The country around is the Cap Bon, the narrow peninsula that points toward Sicily. It is green by Tunisian standards: citrus groves around Nabeul, vineyards, orchards and fields of vegetables, and the smell of orange blossom in spring. Along the north-east coast the land is lower and drier, with scrub, windbreaks of cane and pine, and long beaches that are mostly empty outside August. Kélibia, twelve kilometres south, is the nearest large town, famous for its Muscat wine, its fortress above the harbour and its white sand. El Haouaria, a little further, is known for its spring falcon-handling tradition and for the ancient quarries cut into the sea cliffs, where stone for Carthage was supposedly taken out.

The roads on this coast are easy and sometimes broken at the edges, with the occasional goat, cyclist or donkey cart. They are not fast or technical, but they are friendly, and you have the sea on one side for most of the day. Fuel is available in Kélibia and in the larger villages, but do not rely on the small hamlets, and carry water in summer, when the shade is scarce.

The ride from here goes toward Tunis and its medina, so allow time for the return drive. Late afternoon light on the tombs and the sea is particularly good, and if you can combine it with a late lunch of grilled fish in Kélibia, the day will feel properly balanced.
t.palermo cathedral@38.1,13.4:
Palermo's cathedral is a building that has never settled on one identity, and that is its charm. The present church was begun in 1185 under Walter of the Mill, the English archbishop, on the site of an earlier mosque that had itself replaced a Christian church. Since then each century has added something: Gothic towers, a Catalan-style porch, a neoclassical dome in the 1700s, and a southern front that looks like a North African fortress dressed for a festival. The mixture is deliberate in neither case and somehow works in both.

Inside, the most remarkable thing is a side chapel holding the royal tombs. Roger II, the first Norman king, and Frederick II, the Holy Roman Emperor known as stupor mundi, lie in massive porphyry sarcophagi, quiet and unexplained, a few metres from the tourists. There is also a silver urn for Santa Rosalia, the city's patron, whose feast every July is a very large event. The rooftop walk gives a view across the tile roofs to the mountains behind and the sea in front.

The cathedral sits on Corso Vittorio Emanuele, the ancient street that links the harbour with the Norman Palace, and a short walk takes you to Quattro Canti, the baroque crossroads at the old city's centre, and the markets of Ballaro and Capo, which are loud, ancient and full of food. For practical riding, Palermo means traffic: scooters in packs, narrow lanes, and limited-traffic zones in the centre. Park on the edge and walk for an hour, and you will see far more than you would by bike.

From here the ride heads inland toward the Roman villa near Piazza Armerina, a long day across the interior of Sicily on the A19 and quieter local roads. The first sixty kilometres out of the city can be busy; after that the land opens into hills of wheat and almond, and the roads become a pleasure. The sensible months are April to June and September to October.
t.punic town of kerkuane and its necropoli:
The way to Kerkuane from Tunis is a ride through three Tunisias in a day. You leave the capital on the motorway, with the Gulf of Tunis on one side and the red-roofed suburbs thinning out, and within an hour you are on the Cap Bon peninsula, where the country turns surprisingly green. Hammamet and Nabeul come first, tourist towns with beaches and a famous ceramics trade; Nabeul's pottery workshops and Friday market are worth a pause, and orange and lemon groves fill the plain around them. Beyond that the road bends north-east toward Kélibia, with the fortress that overlooks the harbour, and then runs out along the coast to a flat, windy corner of the peninsula.

What waits at the end is Punic Kerkuane and the necropolis beside it, listed by UNESCO in 1985. It is a town of the Carthaginians, abandoned in the third century BC and never lived in again, so the streets, wells and houses survive in an unusually complete state. The most memorable details are domestic: a bathroom with a built-in tub, a courtyard where someone once ate dinner, a seaside quarter where purple dye was made from murex shells. It is humbling to realise how comfortable these people were.

On the bike, the road is flat and mostly straightforward, with the occasional rough edge, so there are no great technical demands, but there are surprises: sand blown across a bend, a lorry heading to the fish market, a donkey cart on the shoulder. Take it steady. Fuel is plentiful in Hammamet, Nabeul and Kélibia, but there is little between Kélibia and the site, so fill in town. Lunch in Kélibia of grilled fish, salad with tuna and a pot of mint tea is a good reward, and the harbour is lively at the end of the day.

The return to Tunis runs back along the same corridor and ends at the medina, so leave in good time. In July and August the heat is heavy, and the wind from the sea can be strong, so spring and autumn are the best seasons for this ride.
t.palermo@38.1,13.4:
Leaving Palermo for Agrigento is a ride that begins in noise and ends in silence. The first few kilometres are the city at its most insistent, with scooters, fumes, a market spilling onto the road and a strong chance of being cut up by a delivery van. Persevere. Once you are through the western suburbs and onto the road south, the island begins to open out into the great rolling interior that most visitors never see: hills of wheat, scrubby ridges, hilltop villages, and long, empty views to ranges blue in the distance.

The road crosses a country that once powered the Mediterranean economy. Sicily was the granary of Rome, and the old sulphur mines around Lercara Friddi supplied much of the world's sulphur in the nineteenth century, a story of brutal labour and sudden wealth. The old estates, the masserie, still stand in the fields, and in spring the slopes are green and scattered with red poppies and yellow broom. By late summer the same land turns the colour of toast.

At the end of the road is the Valley of the Temples, which is not really a valley but a ridge above the sea, where the Greek colonists of Akragas built a line of Doric temples in the sixth and fifth centuries BC. The Temple of Concordia is one of the best-preserved Greek temples anywhere, standing almost intact because it was later used as a church. The scale and the golden stone of the site are striking, and the sunset light on the columns is something to plan for.

Practically, the ride is around a hundred and thirty kilometres each way, and you should plan an early start and a long day. Palermo has fuel everywhere, and so do the towns along the route, but pick up a litre or two of water before the interior stretches. In summer the heat in the afternoon is intense, and the best months are April to June and late September. A sandwich with fresh ricotta in a village bar on the way is a small pleasure.
t.torra bay@-20.5,13.2:
Torra Bay is a name on a map, a dot on the Skeleton Coast of Namibia, and a place you need a plan to reach. It lies on the stretch of Atlantic shore where the cold Benguela Current meets the desert, and the sea's chill produces thick fog that rolls in most mornings and burns away by noon, giving the coast an eerie, silvery look. Sailors named it the Skeleton Coast for the shipwrecks and the bones of whales and seals scattered on the sand, and in the early days, ships that ran aground rarely saw rescue.

The bay itself is a campsite and fishing spot inside the Skeleton Coast National Park, and it is open only in the summer holiday season, from December to January, when anglers arrive to catch kob and steenbras from the surf. For the rest of the year it is closed, and the shore is empty. Permits are needed to enter the park, and they must be bought in advance, with fixed entry and exit gates, so check the regulations. The coastal road is a salt road, firm when damp, with sand drifts and the occasional soft patch, and it is wise to ride with others.

The landscape is stark and beautiful. To the east, the Namib desert rises in gravel plains and distant dunes, and on the shore, colonies of Cape fur seals bark and jostle, while jackals and brown hyenas patrol the tideline at night. Gemsbok, springbok and even desert-adapted elephants can be found in the dry riverbeds to the north. The silence is deep and the horizon is huge, and the feeling of being on the edge of the world is no exaggeration.

Fuel is the main concern. There are no reliable stations at the bay, and the nearest towns, such as Henties Bay to the south and Khorixas or Uis inland, are long distances away, so fill every tank and carry spare fuel, along with plenty of water, food and a tow strap. Carry a satellite messenger if you can, since phone coverage is almost non-existent, and tell someone your plans. The cool foggy mornings give way to bright afternoons, so bring layers.
t.rondane@59.5,10.9:
This stop is called Back to Rondane, which is a slight misnomer, because the point actually lies in Østfold on the eastern side of the Oslofjord, near Rygge and the town of Moss. Rondane's high plateaus are a long day's ride north. What you have here is a very different side of Norway, gentle, farmed and close to the sea.

Moss, with about thirty-four thousand people, is the main town, and it is a good place to know. It sits on a narrow strait with a working harbour and an industrial past in paper and iron, and its main claim to fame in the history books is the Convention of Moss in 1814, when Norway's brief independence after the break with Denmark was settled in a deal that brought it into a union with Sweden. A car ferry runs from Moss across the fjord to Horten, which is a useful shortcut if you are heading to the west side, and the crossing gives you a sea view for free.

Rygge nearby was home to a military air base, later a commercial airport that closed to passenger traffic in 2016, so the sky overhead is quieter than it used to be. The terrain around is gently rolling farmland, with big grain fields, small woods and fjord inlets, and in late summer the whole thing smells of cut hay. It is not dramatic, but it is a pleasant change from high mountain roads.

Riding is relaxed. The E6 runs close by and carries heavy traffic, but the smaller roads to the coast are quiet, with mild bends and occasional farm tractors. Keep to the limits, as Norwegian traffic cameras are everywhere, and watch for deer at dawn and dusk. The weather is milder than in the mountains, though rain can sweep in from the Skagerrak.

For fuel and food Moss is the obvious answer, with several stations and plenty of cafés near the harbour. Smaller places along the way may not be open late, so do not rely on them.

Come in early summer for the long evenings, when the light lingers and the fjord looks like polished metal. A coffee on the harbour front in Moss is a fair reward for a day on the road.
t.silver city@32.8,-108.3:
Silver City is the kind of place that makes people wonder why they did not find it sooner. It sits at about 5,900 feet on the edge of the Gila country in southwest New Mexico, a few miles from the Continental Divide, and its brick downtown still carries the mark of the mining boom that created it in the 1870s. A flood in the 1890s carved out the main street into a ravine, and the Big Ditch park now runs where Main Street once was, which is one of those local facts that stops visitors in the middle of the pavement.

The town's story is wide. Billy the Kid spent part of his boyhood here, and the nearby Santa Rita pit, one of the oldest copper mines in the Southwest, still scars the hills to the east in a vast terraced bowl you can look into from a viewpoint on Highway 152. Pinos Altos, a short ride north, keeps its false-front saloon and old gold camp mood. The university adds a student presence, and the arts scene gives the town better coffee than its size suggests.

The riding is the reason to come. Highway 15 climbs north from Pinos Altos through ponderosa and then threads a long, tight series of bends across ridge after ridge toward the Gila Cliff Dwellings, where the Mogollon people built rooms into cave alcoves in the late thirteenth century. It is slow, narrow and tiring, a thorough two-hour piece of work each way, with no real shoulder and very little traffic. Highway 152 to the east crosses the Black Range through Emory Pass, a high pass with wide views and plenty of hairpins. Elevation keeps the summer manageable, but monsoon storms in July and August are fierce and often arrive after lunch.

Silver City has every service a rider needs, including fuel and a handful of good places to eat, and it is the last real stock-up before the wilder roads. Once you head north into the Gila National Forest the stations are few, the phone signal is patchy and the nearest sizable repair shop is back here. Fill the tank, carry water, and leave early.
t.nakhodka@42.8,132.9:
Nakhodka is a port city on the Sea of Japan, the kind of place that lives by its harbour, and its name means a find or a stroke of luck. In 1859 the Russian corvette America sheltered in the bay during a storm, and the crew noted the deep, protected water as a stroke of luck, so the name stuck. Today the city has around 147,000 people, a long waterfront of cranes and container terminals, and the end of the Trans-Siberian railway's branch to the Pacific nearby. Volchanets is a small neighbour on the road.

For a rider it is a working city and a good stop for supplies. Fuel is plentiful, there are plenty of cafes serving seafood and Korean-influenced dishes, and mechanics are easy to find. The road from Vladivostok runs through Artyom and Partizansk, with rolling forested hills and occasional glimpses of the sea, and the surface is generally good, though traffic of trucks bound for the port can be heavy. The best riding is along the coast and the hills nearby, where the road dips and rises through oak and pine forest, and the air smells of salt and wet leaves. Fog is common in early summer, and winter is cold and windy.

Nakhodka is a young city by Russian standards, and its character is that of a Soviet port town, with blocks of flats on the hills and a busy embankment. It served as a gateway for goods and people leaving and entering the Soviet Union, and in the Cold War years it was closed to foreigners. Today, you will see Japanese and Korean cars on the roads, which come in through the port, and Asian influences in the food and shops. The bay is a lovely sight in the evening, when ships' lights come on and the water goes dark.

The surrounding landscape is wilder than the city suggests. Hills rise steeply behind the town, covered in forest of oak, birch, fir and cedar, with the Sikhote-Alin range beyond. The coast has rocky headlands and small beaches, and in autumn the forest turns a deep red and gold. Tigers and leopards live in the region's forests, though they are far from the city and almost never seen.

Fill up here before riding on to the Lazovsky coast, where villages are small and supplies thinner. Pack a rain layer, since sea mist can come in quickly.
t.arsenyev@44.2,133.3:
Arsenyev is named after Vladimir Arsenyev, the explorer and writer who mapped much of the Russian Far East in the early twentieth century and whose book about his guide Dersu Uzala became a classic, later filmed by Akira Kurosawa. The town of fifty-eight thousand sits on the Daubikhe River at the western edge of the Sikhote-Alin mountains, in Primorsky Krai, and it is the natural stop before the climb into the range. Grazhdanka, a small village, lies nearby.

The town itself is practical, with a helicopter factory as its main employer, so do not be surprised if you hear rotors overhead. For riders it is a place to refuel, eat and sleep. Fuel stations are on the main road, there are guesthouses and cafes, and you can find basic mechanics. The road from Ussuriysk runs north through hilly country, with a decent surface and long, easy bends, and the forest closes in as you approach. From Arsenyev the road climbs into the Sikhote-Alin, with more twists, patchy surface in places and fewer services, so fill the tank and carry water.

The Sikhote-Alin is one of the great forest ranges of Asia, and the mixture of species is remarkable. Siberian and subtropical plants meet here, so spruce and cedar grow alongside oak, lianas and Manchurian walnut, and the animals include the Amur tiger, the Amur leopard further south, brown and Asiatic black bears, and sika deer. You will not see tigers from the saddle, but the sense that they are somewhere in the forest changes how you ride. Autumn is lovely, with red and gold slopes, and spring brings a bright, damp green.

Arsenyev's story is a good one to carry with you. The explorer travelled by foot, boat and horse through this country with Nanai and Udege guides, recording the landscape, the peoples and the animals, and his writing remains the best portrait of the region. The little museum in town is devoted to his work, and is worth a visit if open.

Bring warm and waterproof layers, since the weather in the mountains can turn wet and cold at short notice. Ticks are common in spring and early summer, and mosquitoes in midsummer, so pack repellent.
t.clifton arizona@33.1,-109.3:
Clifton is a copper town squeezed into a narrow canyon in eastern Arizona, where the San Francisco River cuts through red rock, and it looks the part: old brick storefronts, tin roofs, and houses climbing the hillsides in terraces. It has about thirty-seven hundred residents and a main street that still carries the character of a frontier mining camp. Just up the road is the huge Morenci mine, one of the largest copper operations in North America, and its open pit and its terraced waste dumps change the shape of the landscape for miles.

The town's history is rough and colourful. The old jail, hacked into the rock face in the 1870s, was said to be escape-proof, and visitors can still see the cells. Floods have damaged the town repeatedly, and the dry canyon beds nearby can turn into torrents in minutes after a storm. Chase Creek Street, the historic strip, is a good place for a walk and a cold drink before you start.

From here, the Coronado Trail begins. US 191 climbs out of the desert in a long run of tight bends, and its reputation rests on the count, about four hundred and sixty curves in just over a hundred miles, with hardly a straight section. The road gains thousands of feet, from the dry canyon through juniper and oak to pine and aspen forests, and the temperature falls with it. It is named for the Spanish explorer Francisco Vásquez de Coronado, who marched through the region in 1540 in search of golden cities, though the exact route he took is still debated.

Top the tank in Clifton, since there is almost nothing along the road, and the next supplies are in Alpine, a small village high on the plateau. Bring water and warm clothing, and expect rain in the summer afternoons. The road is narrow, with little shoulder, and logging trucks, elk and sometimes bears are on it, so keep alert. The best time is late spring or early autumn, when the air is clear and the forests are colourful. Sunsets in this part of the state are long and spectacular.
t.skeleton coast road point 3@-21.8,14.0:
Cape Cross is the place on this coast where history, wildlife and smell all arrive at once. The seal reserve here hosts one of the largest colonies of Cape fur seals in the world, with tens of thousands of animals crowded on the rocks and beaches, barking, squabbling and basking. You will notice the colony long before you see it, because the odour is strong, a mix of fish, ammonia and salt that carries on the wind, and the sound is a constant chorus of grunts and bleats.

The site is also historic. In 1486 the Portuguese navigator Diogo Cão landed here and planted a stone cross to claim the coast for his king, one of the pillars that marked the progress of Portuguese exploration around Africa. The original cross was later taken to Germany, and replicas now stand on the headland, with a small memorial to the voyage. It is a remote, windswept spot, and it is easy to imagine how strange and forbidding the Namib shore must have looked to those sailors.

The road here, the C34, is a graded salt and gravel route that follows the coast from Henties Bay. The surface is generally good, though it can be rutted or slick after fog, and the wind and glare require attention. A turn-off leads to the reserve, where there is an entrance fee, a parking area and a boardwalk from which you can watch the seals at a respectful distance. Do not approach the animals, because the bulls can be aggressive and bite, and the smell clings to clothing and bikes for days.

Pups are born in November and December, and the colony is at its busiest then, though the seals are present all year. Black-backed jackals and brown hyenas prowl the edges, picking off weak pups, and seabirds wheel above the rocks. The cold Benguela Current brings nutrients that feed the entire coast, which is why so many animals can live in what looks like a desolate place.

Henties Bay, about sixty kilometres south, is the last reliable source, so arrive with a full tank and some reserve. There are toilets and a small shop at the reserve, but not much else, and the next services lie far to the north. Bring a layer for the wind, and a bag to keep your gloves and helmet from absorbing the smell.
t.skeleton coast road point 4@-21.0,13.7:
North of Cape Cross the C34 enters a different Namibia, a stark, empty coast where the desert comes right to the water and the number of people drops to almost none. The land here is part of the Skeleton Coast, a name that has been given to the whole shoreline, and the stretch of road around these coordinates leads toward the Ugab River gate of the Skeleton Coast Park.

For a rider, the salt road is the story. It is a pale, hard-packed surface that runs straight for kilometres, with the Atlantic on one side and gravel plains on the other. Long, uneventful sections demand attention, because the view hardly changes, and the fog can come in without warning, cutting visibility to a few metres. The surface can be slick when damp, and the corrugations on the gravel sections can shake loose a poorly fastened pannier. Keep your speed moderate, and watch the horizon for approaching vehicles, because the road is shared with the occasional safari truck.

The wreck of the Zeila, a fishing vessel stranded on the beach, is one of the landmarks near here, and the coast holds many other wrecks, some visible, some buried by sand. Shipwrecks, strong currents and fog have given the Skeleton Coast its reputation as one of the most dangerous shores for sailors. Rusty hulks, whale bones and the dark outline of stranded vessels give the beach a haunting atmosphere, and the cold wind off the sea makes it feel even more remote.

The Skeleton Coast Park requires a permit, which should be arranged in advance, and the gate has controlled opening hours. Without a permit you cannot continue north, so check requirements before you set out. There are no services along this part of the road, and the nearest fuel is at Henties Bay, to the south. Carry spare fuel, a good amount of water and food, tools and a first aid kit, and let someone know your plan.

Wildlife is sparse but remarkable. Desert-adapted oryx, springbok and jackals are sometimes seen, and a lucky traveller might spot brown hyenas or desert elephants in the river valleys. The cold air and constant wind make this a place to treat with respect, and the stillness when you stop the engine is memorable.
t.skeleton coast road point 5@-20.5,13.2:
Torra Bay lies far up the Skeleton Coast, so remote that the stretch of coast around these coordinates feels like the end of the road. It is a small seasonal campsite within the Skeleton Coast Park, open only for a short period around the Christmas and New Year holidays, when anglers from across Namibia drive up to fish the surf. For the rest of the year the bay is empty, and the wind has the place to itself.

The riding is demanding in a quiet way. The C34 salt road continues north, a long white line across dark gravel, and the combination of distance, wind and fog makes it a test of preparation and patience. Mechanical problems or a fall can be serious here, since help is far away, and mobile coverage is almost nonexistent. Ride within your limits, carry a satellite messenger if you have one, and keep a close eye on your fuel and water.

The coast is some of the most inhospitable in Africa, and yet it has a stark beauty. The cold Benguela Current brings fog that waters the desert and supports lichen fields on the gravel plains, tiny plants that wake up in the damp and turn the ground a pale green and orange. Dunes lie inland, and the surf is heavy, with strong rip currents that make swimming dangerous. Seals and seabirds are common, and jackals patrol the beach looking for scraps.

The history of this coast is one of wrecks, with ships that ran aground in fog and sailors who struggled ashore into a waterless desert. The name Skeleton Coast has been used for centuries, and it is easy to see why. Bleached bones, rusting hulks and the sound of the surf at night create a spare, haunting atmosphere. Few places on earth feel so completely cut off from ordinary life.

Entry to the park requires a permit, and gate hours and rules are strict, so confirm details in advance. Fuel is the main concern: supplies in the park are limited and not always available, and the last dependable source is Henties Bay, far to the south. Carry enough fuel for the round trip plus a margin, and bring all the water and food you need. Nights are cold, and the fog can soak everything, so pack waterproofs and warm layers, and then enjoy the silence.
